title: moon run --profile / moon test --profile report Samples: 0 on Linux

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
<!-- A brief summary if possible -->
On Linux, `moon run --profile` reports `Samples: 0`. The `perf record` command it builds does not pass `--sample-cpu`, and the report parser looks for the `[cpu]` field in `perf script` output, so the sample headers are skipped. Adding `--sample-cpu` makes them parse and the report fills in.

## Actual behavior

<!-- What has happened? What's going wrong?
Paste logs and/or screenshots here -->

```console
$ moon run --profile naive -- 2000 70
Profile: native Linux perf
Executables: 1
Samples: 0, sample weight: 10.00ms
...
Warnings:
  No profiled running samples with MoonBit/runtime symbols were found.
```

`profile.json`:

```json
"summary": { "executables": 1, "observed_rows": 0, "running_samples": 0,
             "profiled_samples": 0, "sample_weight_ms": 10.0, "profiled_time_ms": 0.0 }
```

`perf-script.txt` has the sample lines, but no `[cpu]` field:

```console
$ head -1 _build/native/release/profile/naive/<stamp>/perf-script.txt
naive.exe   17116  7564.509311:   10000000 cpu-clock:u:
```

perf also reports that the CPU attribute is not set:

```console
$ perf script -i _build/native/release/profile/naive/<stamp>/perf.data -F +cpu
Samples for 'cpu-clock:u' event do not have CPU attribute set. Cannot print 'cpu' field.
```

## Expected Behavior

<!-- What should happen instead? -->

`moon run --profile` shows a report on Linux.

With `--sample-cpu` added to the `perf record` invocation (and a `perf` that can unwind stacks), the header carries the CPU field and the report fills in:

```console
$ PATH=<wrapper-dir>:$PATH moon run --profile naive -- 2000 70
Profile: native Linux perf
Executables: 1
Samples: 110, sample weight: 10.00ms
...
```

The relevant pieces, from `crates/moon/src/cli/profile.rs`:

- `perf_record_command` passes `record --quiet -F <hz> -e cpu-clock --call-graph dwarf -o ...`, without `--sample-cpu`.
- `is_perf_sample_header` / `is_perf_cpu_token` expect the token before the timestamp to be `[NNN]`.
- `perf` sets the CPU sample bit only when `target__has_cpu(&opts->target) || opts->sample_cpu` holds (`tools/perf/util/evsel.c`), and `target__has_cpu` is true for `-a` / `-C`, which moon does not pass.

Passing `--sample-cpu` is one option; accepting headers without `[cpu]` would be another. I'd appreciate a fix upstream.

## Steps to Reproduce

<!-- How to trigger it? Does it happen every time? -->

1. On Linux with `perf` on `PATH`, using a native executable package: `moon run --profile <exe> -- <args>` reports `Samples: 0`.
2. `head -1 _build/native/release/profile/<pkg>/<stamp>/perf-script.txt` shows a header without `[cpu]`.
3. `perf script -i _build/native/release/profile/<pkg>/<stamp>/perf.data -F +cpu` prints `Samples for 'cpu-clock:u' event do not have CPU attribute set. Cannot print 'cpu' field.`
4. A small `perf` wrapper that appends `--sample-cpu` to `record` makes the headers parse (`observed_rows` becomes non-zero). In my environment the stacks were still empty because that `perf` was built without libdw/libelf; that part seems separate.

## Environment

Operating System: Linux

<!-- Please copy and paste the output of `moon version --all` below. -->

```

moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12)

```

Tested on WSL2 (Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, x86_64) with `perf 7.0.14`. I have not tried other environments.

## Checklist

- [x] (Optional) My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: Cross-compiling `--target native` with `MOON_CC`: host-only objects are linked, and `platform` cfg comes from the host
body:
Tested with moon 0.1.20261012, MoonBit 0.10.15+943464bfa, zig 0.17.0 (`zig cc` as `MOON_CC`, `zig ar` as
`MOON_AR`), on macOS arm64 and ubuntu-latest as build machines.

We build release binaries for 5 targets on one Linux runner with `zig cc` as `MOON_CC`. Two moon behaviours block this.
A third problem (`rand_s` include order in `env.c`) is reported in https://github.com/moonbitlang/moonbit-native-runtime/issues/2.

## 1. prebuilt host-only objects are linked when `MOON_CC` targets another architecture

### Problem

Moon always compiles the runtime with `-DMOONBIT_USE_SIMDUTF`. It puts the prebuilt objects
`~/.moon/lib/moonbit_simdutf.o` and `~/.moon/lib/simdutf.o` into the runtime library. On Apple targets it also
links the prebuilt `~/.moon/lib/libbacktrace.a`. These files are built for the machine that runs moon. When
`MOON_CC` targets another architecture, the link fails or the objects are unusable.

### Repro

1. Install zig 0.17.0. Create a wrapper `cc` that runs `zig cc -target x86_64-linux-musl "$@"`, and a wrapper
   `ar` that runs `zig ar "$@"`. Make both executable. The build machine is macOS arm64.
   The same failure happens with `aarch64-linux-musl`. The target `x86_64-macos` fails with a different message
   (see the result).
2. Run:

   ```sh
   MOON_CC=/path/to/cc MOON_AR=/path/to/ar moon build --target native --release
   ```

3. Result:
   - Linux targets: `ld.lld` reports `undefined symbol: moonbit_simdutf_*`.
   - `x86_64-macos`: the linker reports `invalid cpu architecture: aarch64 ... while parsing lib/libbacktrace.a(...)`.
     The prebuilt `libbacktrace.a` is for the arm64 host.
4. Workaround that passes: the `cc` wrapper drops `-DMOONBIT_USE_SIMDUTF` and every argument that ends in
   `/moonbit_simdutf.o`, `/simdutf.o` or `/libbacktrace.a`. The `ar` wrapper drops the two simdutf objects. The
   runtime then uses its scalar UTF code path. All 5 targets then build and run (darwin-arm64 natively,
   darwin-x64 under Rosetta).

   Do not drop `libbacktrace.a` when the target is the host: debug test builds need it.

### Proposed fix

Link these objects only when the target is the host. When `MOON_CC` (or the `cc` setting of the package) is
set, either:

- build `simdutf` and `libbacktrace` from source with that compiler, or
- do not define `MOONBIT_USE_SIMDUTF`, do not link the prebuilt objects, and use the scalar UTF code path.

An explicit switch, for example `MOON_NO_PREBUILT=1`, would also be enough.

### Impact

A user cannot cross-compile a MoonBit native binary with a plain `MOON_CC="zig cc -target ..."` wrapper. The
wrapper must know which arguments to drop. This depends on the moon version and can break with an update.

Reference: <https://github.com/moonrockz/smithy/tree/main/apps/zig-cross> (the wrappers that carry the
workarounds).

## 2. the `platform` cfg comes from the host, so a cross-built Windows binary has wrong `OsString` code

### Problem

`core/internal/os_string` selects its Windows code with `#cfg(platform="windows")`. Moon resolves `platform` from
the host OS, and `core` is prebuilt for the host. When we cross-compile for Windows on Linux or macOS, the binary
holds the POSIX `OsString` code. Arguments, environment variables and paths are then handled wrongly.

### Repro

1. Cross-build a CLI that prints its arguments (with `MOON_CC` set to a `zig cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu`
   wrapper) on macOS or Linux.
2. Run the `.exe` on Windows: `smithy.exe version`.
3. Result: the program prints its usage text, as if it had no valid argument. The same source built on Windows
   works.

### Request

A way to set the target platform for the `platform` cfg (for example a `--target-platform` option or a value
derived from the cross compiler), and a `core` bundle for each platform.

title: `moon install user/module`: install all `cmd/` executables of the module
body:
## Question

Could `moon install user/module` — a bare module path — install all of the module's executables under `cmd/`, instead of requiring `moon install user/module/cmd/...`?

I understand from #1501 that install-all was made opt-in on purpose, because selecting module or repo roots used to install multiple binaries unexpectedly. This asks whether a narrower, convention-based default is worth revisiting: `cmd/` is where CLI tools live by convention, and the caller usually cannot know the module's internal package layout up front.

## Current behavior

A bare module path installs exactly the module-root package. For the typical CLI layout (library root + executables under `cmd/`), that fails:

```console
$ moon install user/module
Error: Package `user/module` not found or is not a main package (is-main: true required)
```

And when the root package *is* `is-main: true`, it installs only that one binary, silently skipping the `cmd/` tools.

Today's alternatives require knowing and typing the module's internal layout:

```console
$ moon install user/module/cmd/...   # all mains under cmd/
$ moon install user/module/...       # all main packages anywhere in the module
```

## Discoverability

This is the usability problem behind the request. A user who just wants a module's tools has two awkward options today:

- know in advance that the module happens to keep them under `cmd/` (and that the `cmd/...` wildcard exists), or
- install them one by one (`moon install user/module/cmd/tool1`, `.../tool2`, …), which requires looking up each tool name first.

There is no way to ask `moon` which executables a module provides; the answer lives on external pages (mooncakes.io listing, repository, docs). The `cmd/<name>` → binary `<name>` convention itself is fine — the problem is that a user cannot know that the tool is named `<name>` (or that it exists at all) without an external lookup.

A concrete case: `kupas/notionsdk` publishes exactly one executable, at the internal path `cmd/main`. `moon install kupas/notionsdk` fails, and nothing in the error tells the user that the tool lives at `cmd/main` — or that it will be installed as a binary named `main` (see console output below).

Established installers treat a package as declaring its own binaries and surface all of them:

- `cargo install <crate>` installs every binary the crate declares by default; `--bin` narrows the selection (`--bins` is documented as "Install all binaries. This is the default behavior.").
- `uv tool install <package>` makes all of the package's executables available — "Tool executables include all console entry points, script entry points, and binary scripts provided by a Python package".
- `npm install -g <pkg>` / `pnpm add -g <pkg>` link every `bin` entry declared by the package.

## Verification

Reproduced with `moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12)` on Linux x86_64 using a module with a library root plus `cmd/main`, `cmd/foo`, `cmd/bar`:

```console
$ moon install --dry-run ./test-cli-suite
Error: Path `/tmp/opencode/test-cli-suite` is not a main package (is-main: true required)

$ moon install --dry-run ./test-cli-suite/cmd/...
Dry-run: Would build `testuser/cli-suite/cmd/bar`
Dry-run: Would install `bar` to `~/.moon/bin/bar`
Dry-run: Would build `testuser/cli-suite/cmd/foo`
Dry-run: Would install `foo` to `~/.moon/bin/foo`
Dry-run: Would build `testuser/cli-suite/cmd/main`
Dry-run: Would install `main` to `~/.moon/bin/main`
```

Registry sources filter by relative package path (`PackageFilter` in `crates/moon/src/cli/install_binary.rs`), so a published module laid out the same way behaves the same; `user/module/cmd/...` and `user/module/...` are the documented wildcard forms for fan-out. With the published module `kupas/notionsdk@0.1.2` (library root package, executable at `cmd/main`):

```console
$ moon install kupas/notionsdk
Using cached kupas/notionsdk@0.1.2
Error: Package `kupas/notionsdk` not found or is not a main package (is-main: true required)

$ moon install --dry-run kupas/notionsdk/cmd/main
Dry-run: Would build `kupas/notionsdk/cmd/main`
Dry-run: Would install `main` to `~/.moon/bin/main`
```

Another layout example: `mizchi/actrun` publishes `cmd/actrun`, `cmd/wasi_runner`, and `cmd/wasi_worker` next to its library root package.

## Suggestion

Make the bare module path mean "install this module's tools", without reintroducing the surprise that #1501 removed:

1. `moon install user/module` → install every main package under `cmd/`.
2. If there is no main package under `cmd/`, keep the exact behavior: install the root package when it is `is-main: true`; otherwise report that the module has no installable executables.
3. Leave the explicit selectors unchanged for precise selection (`user/module/pkg`, `user/module/cmd/...`, `user/module/...`).

If the bare path should stay exact, any of these would still remove the guesswork:

- `moon install user/module --all` (or `--cmd`) to install all `cmd/` mains explicitly — non-interactive and script-friendly.
- A way to see and choose: on an interactive terminal, `moon install user/module` could list the module's `cmd/` executables and let the user multi-select which ones to install, with `--list` for non-interactive listing — the discovery-side counterpart of #1484's `moon install --list` for installed binaries. Interactive decisions during tool installation are common in this space: pnpm blocks dependency build scripts by default and, when a global package's native binary is produced by such a build step, prompts the user to approve it interactively (`pnpm approve-builds`); `pnpm update -g --interactive` similarly lets the user select which global installs to update.

title: bug(moonx): Interrupted Wasm response body downloads are not retried
body:
## Actual behavior

`moonx` uses an HTTP retry policy when acquiring a registry Wasm asset, but a transient failure while reading the response body is not retried. If the server returns `200 OK` and then closes the connection before the body is complete, `download_registry_asset()` propagates the `.bytes()` error and the command fails with `failed to read registry asset response from ...`.

The existing policy retries request errors and HTTP 408/429/500/502/503/504 up to three times. It does not wrap the subsequent response-body read. Both the checksum file and the Wasm artifact use this download helper.

Source references at commit `40f18d297259f24a8c6466e8f36b377ede7cb868`:

- [HTTP retry policy](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/40f18d297259f24a8c6466e8f36b377ede7cb868/crates/mooncake/src/registry/download.rs#L21-L49)
- [Response-body read outside the retry policy](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/40f18d297259f24a8c6466e8f36b377ede7cb868/crates/mooncake/src/registry/client.rs#L473-L491)
- [Checksum and Wasm acquisition](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/40f18d297259f24a8c6466e8f36b377ede7cb868/crates/mooncake/src/registry/client.rs#L357-L404)

## Expected Behavior

Retry the full download attempt, including reading the body, on transient transfer failures with a bounded retry budget. A later successful attempt should be verified and cached as usual; exhausted retries should return an error without publishing a partial artifact. Preserve non-retryable behavior for missing assets (404).

## Steps to Reproduce

Suggested regression-test scenario (not yet executed):

1. Start with no cached executable artifact and serve a valid checksum file.
2. For the first Wasm request, return `200 OK` with the full `Content-Length`, write only part of the body, and close the connection.
3. Serve the complete valid Wasm body on the next request.
4. Acquire the asset through the registry client used by `moonx`.

Current code returns the body-read error without issuing the second Wasm request. Expected behavior is to retry and successfully acquire the artifact. Also cover repeated body failures and verify that no partial cache entry is published.

## Environment

Identified by source inspection at the commit linked above, rather than a captured runtime failure. No OS-specific reproduction or installed-toolchain version is claimed.

title: Fresh installs and `moon publish` fail on dependencies still shipping `moon.mod.json`
body:
`moon add <pkg>` fails when any package in the graph still ships the legacy `moon.mod.json` manifest, and `moon publish`'s validation fails the same way with no way to migrate inside it. Not a corner case: of 213 modules probed on 2026-10-15, 60 fail to install with this error, across 24 owners and including `moonbit-community/starter` — the module the docs' own "Add dependencies" example tells you to add.

## Actual behavior

Fresh module, nothing cached locally:

```console
$ moon new repro && cd repro
$ moon add moonbitlang/quickcheck@0.14.0
Using cached moonbitlang/quickcheck@0.14.0
Error: When installing packages

Caused by:
    `moon.mod.json` at '/tmp/repro/.mooncakes/moonbitlang/quickcheck' is no longer supported. Run `moon fmt` to migrate to `moon.mod`.
```

Transitive dependencies hit the same wall, and the error names one package at a time: `moon add mizchi/parquet@0.2.2` stops on quickcheck and only reaches `mizchi/duckdb@0.6.4` (also legacy) once that one is migrated.

I probed the registry on 2026-10-15 — every `moonbitlang/*` and `moonbit-community/*` module plus a seeded random sample of 60 of the other ~2,873 — one fresh `moon new` + `moon add <pkg>` per package, latest versions:

| group | probed | fail |
|---|---|---|
| `moonbitlang/*` + `moonbit-community/*` | 153 | 34 |
| random sample of other modules | 60 | 26 |
| total | 213 | 60 |

28 of the 60 ship the legacy manifest themselves:

| owner | failing modules |
|---|---|
| `moonbitlang` | 9 — `std`, `arduino`, `esp32`, `json_deriving`, `json_deriving_codegen`, `lex-runtime`, `mbt-lexer`, `wasm4`, `dummy_abort` |
| `moonbit-community` | 4 — `starter`, `raylib`, `harfbuzz`, `dom_sanitizer` |
| `tonyfettes` | 2 — `base64`, `tree_sitter_yaml` |
| 13 further owners | one each — `hackwaly/redis`, `emadurandal/sdl3`, `bzy-debug/json_parser`, `kesmeey/immut_IntervalTree`, `tiye/cirru-parser`, `mizchi/kagura_cli`, `0Ayachi0/math`, `HCHogan/btree`, `AdUhTkJm/u8str`, `SupremeHuaji/moonsmiles`, `lijunchen/hello2`, `oboard/apple_silicon_accelerometer`, `ryota0624/circuit_breaker` |

The other 32 reach it through a dependency, and the offenders are concentrated: `moonbitlang/x` (8 — versions up to 0.4.43 ship `moon.mod.json`, 0.4.44 and later ship `moon.mod`), `moonbit-community/prettyprinter` (4), `moonbitlang/async` (4), `moonbitlang/quickcheck` (2, i.e. `@0.14.0`), `mizchi/tempfile` (2), then single cases from `moonbitlang/{regexp, ulex-runtime}`, `moonbit-community/{cmark, miniio}`, `Yoorkin/{prettyprinter, trie}`, `rami3l/js-ffi`, `BigOrangeQWQ/wit-ffi`, `myfreess/casefold`, `mizchi/signals`, `Milky2018/moon_accesskit`, `yatsuna827/pk-rng-lcg32`. All 60 last published before 2026-10-12, so this reads as a migration backlog rather than a string of packaging mistakes — the other 152 modules in the probe resolve normally.

`moon publish` has no recovery path: validation extracts the zip into a temp dir and runs `moon check` there with a fresh resolution, and that dir has no `.mooncakes` to migrate, so `--frozen` does not help either. The publish-side output below is from a module whose dependency graph reaches `mizchi/duckdb@0.6.4`:

```console
$ moon publish --dry-run
extracting packaged zip to .../verify/mooncake_publish_check...
running moon check on extracted package
Caused by: `moon.mod.json` at '.../.mooncakes/mizchi/duckdb' is no longer supported
Error: `moon publish` failed
```

Alternating `moon install` with `moon fmt` inside every `.mooncakes/*/*/` that still has `moon.mod.json` does get local builds and CI past it, but nothing equivalent exists inside publish validation.

## Expected Behavior

Either these artifacts resolve (migrated on download, or a warning instead of a refusal), or republishing is the expected path for every author — in which case the publish-side error could say what to do, since "run `moon fmt`" points at a directory the publisher does not control.

Two things already in the tree could serve here: `read_module_desc_file_in_dir_with_legacy(dir, allow_legacy)` in `crates/moonutil/src/manifest.rs`, and the JSON→DSL migration that `write_module_dsl_to_file` already runs (the same `moonfmt -file_type mod_json` step `moon fmt` uses). Today the strict `read_module_desc_file_in_dir` is what runs in `crates/mooncake/src/dependency_source/global.rs` (`validate_source`, immediately after the registry archive is extracted), and `resolver/context.rs` reads local modules strictly too — so no path tolerates a legacy manifest.

If there is a preferred direction here I can follow up with a patch.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `moon new repro && cd repro`
2. `moon add moonbitlang/quickcheck@0.14.0`, or `moon add mizchi/parquet@0.2.2` for the transitive case
3. publish half: a module whose graph contains one of these artifacts, then `moon publish --dry-run`

Every time, on a clean module with no `.mooncakes`.

## Environment

Operating System: Linux (Arch/CachyOS), x86_64

```console
moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12)
moonc v0.10.15+943464bfa (2026-10-12)
moonrun 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12)
```

`cli.moonbitlang.com/version.json` reports 0.1.20261012 as latest, so there is no newer toolchain to retry on.

## Checklist

- [x] (Optional) My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: bug(moonrun): macOS async conformance snapshots depend on timer interleaving
body:
The macOS Moonrun conformance job can fail because upstream async snapshots require an exact ordering between independently scheduled tasks separated by short real-time delays. A controlled process pause reproduces the failure without changing source code or test snapshots.

## Actual behavior

On PR #2286, head `c134c40b57fa5fbbd3d11679048b51e7642d3a9f`, [the macOS conformance job failed](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/actions/runs/38339204351/job/115106453719) in `test_moonrun_against_upstream_async`: 544 of 546 upstream tests passed.

`group_defer_test.mbt`, test `group defer cancelled`:

```diff
 tick
 tick
+tick
 start group termination
 tick
 protected async defer completed
 group terminated
-tick
```

`cancellation_test.mbt`, test `multiple scope`:

```diff
 ctx 1 task 2 cancelled
+ctx 2 task 2 finished
 ctx 1 received error Err
-ctx 2 task 2 finished
 ctx 2 received error Err
```

The cancellation and cleanup messages still occur. The failure is an exact-output-order mismatch, not a compilation error or a missing cancellation outcome.

The Ubuntu V8, Ubuntu Wasmtime, and Windows conformance jobs passed in that run. A [macOS-only retry](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/actions/runs/38339204351/job/115120922779) was in progress when this issue was filed.

## Expected Behavior

Conformance tests should preserve checks for cancellation, protected cleanup, and required causal ordering without assuming that an independent task cannot run before another task's cleanup finishes merely because their timers differ by 100ms.

## Steps to Reproduce

With an existing toolchain and initialized async submodule, build the repository's V8 Moonrun and the upstream test artifact:

```sh
cargo build -p moon -p moonrun
MOON_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT="$HOME/.moon" target/debug/moon \
  -C third_party/moonbitlang_async --target-dir /tmp/moon-ci-timing-probe \
  test src/group_defer_test.mbt src/cancellation_test.mbt --target wasm --build-only
```

Run either test alone with `target/debug/moonrun` and `--test-args`:

```json
{"package":"moonbitlang/async","file_and_index":[["group_defer_test.mbt",[{"start":2,"end":3}]]]}
```

The artifact is `/tmp/moon-ci-timing-probe/wasm/debug/test/moonbitlang/async/async.blackbox_test.wasm`. For `multiple scope`, replace the filename with `cancellation_test.mbt`; its index is also 2 in the checked-out submodule.

Wait until the subprocess emits the JSON record with `"type":"start"` before measuring the delay, so the pause affects execution rather than WASM startup:

- `group defer cancelled`: wait 450ms, send SIGSTOP to that subprocess, wait 350ms, then send SIGCONT. Two consecutive attempts reproduced the exact CI diff above.
- `multiple scope`: wait 150ms, pause for 350ms, then resume. Two consecutive attempts moved `ctx 2 task 2 finished` before both ctx 1 messages. This differs in precise interleaving from CI but reproduces the same cross-group ordering assumption being violated.

Unpaused runs of both tests passed. These were controlled delay experiments, not a measurement of what stalled the CI runner.

## Analysis

`Timer::new` records a deadline, and `EventLoop::handle_timers` wakes all expired timers before rescheduling coroutines. `Coroutine::wake` appends to the ready queue; `reschedule` executes only the queue length captured at the beginning of that round. Coroutines woken by cancellation and task-group completion therefore run in later rounds.

In the first test, a stall spanning the 500ms timeout and the third tick's deadline makes both ready together. Processing the timeout initiates cancellation; it does not synchronously finish the nested cleanup. The already-ready tick can print before `start group termination`.

In the second test, the 200ms error requires cancellation, child completion, and parent wakeup before the parent prints its error. That chain is not guaranteed to finish before the independent 300ms task prints.

The PR does not change timer, coroutine scheduling, or kqueue implementations, and these tests use ambient runtime configuration. The controlled reproduction shows execution delay is sufficient to cause these failures; the CI log does not identify whether the actual delay came from OS scheduling, runtime pauses, or another cause. A main-branch differential reproduction has not been performed.

A possible fix is to use explicit synchronization where ordering is intended, or assert necessary per-group ordering while permitting unrelated events to interleave. Updating the snapshot to one observed ordering would leave the timing dependency intact.

## Environment

CI: `macos-latest`, V8 backend, nightly MoonBit toolchain, Rust 1.95.0.

Local controlled reproduction: macOS 26.7 (25G229), repository-built V8 Moonrun, existing compiler/toolchain:

```text
moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12)
moonc v0.10.15+943464bfa (2026-10-12)
moonrun 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12) [installed CLI; reproduction used target/debug/moonrun]
```

## Checklist

- [x] My case is minimal enough to be reproducible: each affected upstream test is run independently with a controlled pause.

title: Publish precompiled native CLI binaries to Mooncakes, install per-platform in `moon install`
body:
## Motivation

MoonBit developers publish packages to Mooncakes with `moon publish` and consume them with `moon install`. For CLI tools (native `is-main` packages), installation currently means **compiling the package locally** on the user's machine and placing the resulting binary into `~/.moon/bin` (#1850 documents exactly this: the installed `~/.moon/bin` binary is a locally built MoonBit artifact).

Unlike npm, Go modules, or Rust's `cargo-binstall` / `cargo-dist`, Mooncakes provides no standardized way for a package author to distribute **precompiled native binaries** for multiple operating systems and CPU architectures. A Windows or macOS user who only wants a MoonBit CLI tool must set up a working local toolchain and wait for a local build, even when the author already produced a release binary in CI.

To be clear about scope: this is not about distributing the MoonBit toolchain itself (that was discussed in moonbit-docs#203) — it is about third-party CLI packages on Mooncakes.

Notably, Mooncakes already serves **prebuilt Wasm** artifacts for CLI execution via `moonx` under the `prebuild/` layout proposed in #2113:

```text
<download>/prebuild/<owner>/<module>@<version>/<executable>.wasm
<download>/prebuild/<owner>/<module>@<version>/<executable>.wasm.sha256
```

Extending that same mechanism to per-platform **native** binaries is a natural next step. Meanwhile, the community already works around the gap with external distribution channels — e.g. mizchi/moon-component ships install scripts for macOS/Linux prebuilt binaries alongside local compilation.

## Proposal

### 1. Publishing

Allow package authors to upload precompiled native binaries alongside their MoonBit packages, for one or more platform triples, for example:

- `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`
- `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`
- `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`
- `x86_64-apple-darwin`
- `aarch64-apple-darwin`
- `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`

The exact CLI surface is open — it could be a flag on `moon publish` (e.g. attaching artifacts produced by a CI matrix, potentially driven by `moon generate-build-matrix`), with the platform triple inferred from or attached to each artifact.

### 2. Registry storage and index

Store artifacts under the existing `prebuild/` endpoint, with one sub-path per platform, and record checksums plus the available platform list in the Git index:

```text
<download>/prebuild/<owner>/<module>@<version>/
├── <executable>.wasm                          # existing: executed via moonx
├── x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/
│   ├── <executable>
│   └── <executable>.sha256
├── aarch64-apple-darwin/
│   ├── <executable>
│   └── <executable>.sha256
└── x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/
    ├── <executable>.exe
    └── <executable>.exe.sha256
```

This stays consistent with the decoupled `download` / `index` / `api` registry layout proposed in #2113, so mirrors only serve immutable static artifacts.

### 3. Installation

When a user runs:

```console
moon install username/mytool
```

`moon` should:

1. Detect the user's operating system and architecture.
2. Look up a matching prebuilt binary and its checksum in the index.
3. Download the artifact from the `download` endpoint.
4. Verify its checksum.
5. Install it into the user's global binary directory (`~/.moon/bin`).
6. Fall back to building from source only when no compatible prebuilt binary exists.

## Benefits

- Installing a MoonBit CLI tool becomes fast — no local compilation for consumers.
- npm-style native binary distribution on Mooncakes.
- Removes the local-toolchain requirement for users of CLI tools (nice for end users and CI pipelines alike).
- CI pipelines can publish multi-platform release artifacts from one package.
- Makes Mooncakes more useful as a general-purpose CLI package registry.

This requires no changes to the MoonBit language itself; it is an extension of the `moon` package manager and the Mooncakes service. **Would the MoonBit team consider supporting native binary artifact publishing on Mooncakes, integrated with `moon install`?**

title: moonrun: allow writable directory contents without granting removal of the root
body:
A host may grant `fs.write` on a scratch directory so a guest can manage its contents. Currently, that grant also permits removing the directory itself.

Could moonrun support allowing creation, modification, deletion, and renaming **inside** the directory without granting removal, renaming, or replacement of the root itself?

For example, granting `/session/scratch` should allow deleting `/session/scratch/output.txt`, but should not by itself allow deleting `/session/scratch`.

[Landlock](https://docs.kernel.org/userspace-api/landlock.html#filesystem-flags) provides a useful precedent: directory-entry mutation rights apply to a directory's contents, not the directory itself. Could moonrun adopt similar semantics, or offer an explicit content-only grant if compatibility requires it?

title: Native builds do not disable FP contraction (-ffp-contract=off), so floating-point results change under GCC
body:
**Describe the bug**
moon compiles native targets with `cc ... -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing -O2` and does not pass `-ffp-contract=off`. GCC defaults to `-ffp-contract=fast` in GNU C mode, so it fuses `a * b + c` into a single FMA instruction across statements wherever the target has FMA. That changes floating-point results bit for bit, so the same MoonBit program gives different results on native than on wasm, wasm-gc and js, and different results depending on which C compiler is used.

**To Reproduce**
1. Build a program that uses `@math` functions or plain `a * b + c` arithmetic for `--target native --release`. I compiled the generated C both with Apple clang (the default on macOS) and with `gcc-16 -O2`, using the same flags as moon.
2. Compare the bit patterns of the results.

With GCC, more than 30 core math functions produce different bits on about 1,000 of every 1.5 million inputs: `sinf`, `cosf`, `hypotf` and `hypot` (about 1,000 rows each), `acos`, `acosf`, `asin`, `tan`, `ln`, `log2`, `log10`, `expm1` and others. Ordinary user arithmetic such as `a + (b - a) * u` changes too. Recompiling the same C with `gcc -ffp-contract=off` makes the output byte-identical to clang's.

Apple clang defaults to `-ffp-contract=on`, which only fuses within one C expression. moonc emits each operation as a separate statement, so clang happens not to contract today. With `-ffp-contract=fast`, clang shows the same differences.

**Expected behavior**
Floating-point semantics that do not depend on the C compiler and match the other backends. IEEE 754-2019 §10.4 treats contraction as a value-changing optimization that the language must control. Pass `-ffp-contract=off` by default for gcc-like compilers, for example next to `-fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing` in `crates/moonutil/src/compiler_flags/gcc_like.rs`, and the MSVC equivalent `/fp:precise` with no contraction.

**Affected setups**
GCC as `cc` on Linux aarch64, and GCC on x86-64 whenever FMA is enabled (`-march=haswell` or newer, or `-march=native`). The default x86-64 baseline has no FMA, so it is not affected there.

**Environment**
moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da), moonc v0.10.14, macOS arm64; gcc-16 (Homebrew) to simulate a GCC toolchain. Checked `moonbitlang/moon` `main` (b5159421): `gcc_like.rs` still adds only `-fwrapv` and `-fno-strict-aliasing`.

title: moon test fails to parse results when a failure message contains a control character (ANSI color codes)
body:
## Summary

`moon test` stops with a parse error when a failed test's message contains a control character, such as the ESC (`\x1b`) in an ANSI color code. The generated test driver builds each result event as JSON with `String::escape`, which writes MoonBit escapes (`\u{1b}`) instead of JSON escapes (`\^[`). `moon` then cannot parse the event, and the whole run fails. The results of all the other tests are lost too.

## Reproduction

```moonbit
test "failure message with an ANSI color code" {
  fail("a\u{1b}[31mred\u{1b}[0m")
}
```

```text
$ moon test --target native
Error: failed to run test for target Native

Caused by:
    0: Failed to parse test results for moonrockz/expect WhiteboxTest
    1: Failed to parse test driver event: {"type":"result","file":"zz_probe_wbtest.mbt","index":0,"message":"src/zz_probe_wbtest.mbt:3:3-3:34@moonrockz/expect FAILED: a\u{1b}[31mred\u{1b}[0m"}
```

The same happens with `--target wasm-gc` and `--target js`.

Version: `moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20)`, macOS.

## Cause

In the generated driver (`_build/<target>/debug/test/__generated_driver_for_*_test.mbt`), `handle_result` does:

```moonbit
let file_name = filename.escape()
let message = message.escape()
println(
  "{\"type\":\"result\",\"file\":\{file_name},\"index\":\{index},\"message\":\{message}}",
)
```

`String::escape` is not a JSON encoder. For most messages the two agree, but control characters come out as `\u{..}`, which JSON does not allow. The file name has the same problem in principle.

## Expected

Encode the event with a JSON encoder (for example `message.to_json().stringify()`, or `Json` for the whole event), so that any message reaches `moon` and is reported as a normal failure.

## Why it matters

Assertion libraries want colored failure messages (red and green for expected and received values, and for diff lines), as Jest, pytest and cargo do. Today a colored message turns one failed assertion into a failed test run with no results. This blocks color support in [moonrockz/expect](https://github.com/moonrockz/expect/issues/37).

title: Windows Defender quarantines official moonfmt.exe as Trojan:Win32/Bearfoos.B!ml
body:
The moonfmt.exe included in an official Windows MoonBit toolchain archive is repeatedly quarantined by Microsoft Defender Antivirus. I cannot determine whether this is a false positive, so I would appreciate an investigation of the distributed binary and its build process.

Environment

Windows 11 Pro, build 26200

MoonBit compiler: v0.10.12+1634b282e; moon: 0.1.20260904

Official archive: https://cli.moonbitlang.com/binaries/0.10.12%2B1634b282e/moonbit-windows-x86_64.zip

Archive SHA-256: 3E5449E862D4979B2FC64E6A248EC5BABBD110440C8F2A7BF813C6FA01D8581F (matches the published checksum)

bin/moonfmt.exe SHA-256: DB779273339C2FC3E1AEF5064995662D62EEE3605A01EFC9E0279A8A555B83CE

Defender detection: Trojan:Win32/Bearfoos.B!ml

Defender security intelligence version during the latest detection: 1.459.424.0; engine: 1.1.26080.3

Observed behavior

Defender quarantined moonfmt.exe during toolchain extraction/installation. After reinstalling the checksum-verified archive, invoking moon fmt caused Defender to quarantine the same file again. The latest event occurred on 2026-09-27 at 17:04 local time. The executable itself was also uploaded to VirusTotal and reportedly received 0 detections out of 71 engines; this result does not establish that the file is safe.

Expected behavior

The official Windows toolchain should be installable and moon fmt should run without the executable being quarantined.

I would also appreciate it if you could investigate ways to reduce false-positive detections in future Windows releases.

title: [native/windows] moonc's moonbit_init (18.5k-line flat init block) makes cl /O2 ~5-10x slower than clang; MSVC 14.51 regressed ~1.4-1.6x on this shape
body:
## TL;DR

- `moonc` emits the entire module's global initialization as **one ~18.5k-line C function** (`moonbit_init` — a single straight-line basic block: 18,457 statements, one `if`, no loops).
- On Windows that function makes MSVC `cl /O2` spend **~60–130 s compiling a 10.8 MB file that clang compiles in 12–16 s and gcc in 30 s** (measured **~5–10× vs clang**, toolset- and thermal-dependent); the cost sits ~100% inside cl's backend (`/Od` = 1 s; `/Bt+`: c1.dll 0.33–0.37 s vs c2.dll 86–119 s) and is single-threaded (parallelism 0.99).
- MSVC 14.51 additionally regressed **~1.4–1.6× vs 14.50 on exactly this shape** (interleaved A/B; with the function emptied — or with reduced optimization enabled — 14.51 is *faster* than 14.50, so the regression is shape-specific, not general).
- Workarounds verified today: `MOON_CC=clang` (rc=0 on two machines), package-level `link.native.cc-flags`, and MSVC's own `/d2ReducedOptimizeHugeFunctions` (**119.8 s → 32.1 s on 14.51, 3.7×**; on this file it can only hit `moonbit_init` — the next-largest function is 1,050 lines — and init runs once at startup). Suggested upstream directions: split `moonbit_init` (per-package init chaining, mirroring #1958 on the runtime side) and/or expose a native opt-level (#1378).
- Repro: **a 3.7 KB zero-dependency minimal project** (Option A below) reproduces the cliff standalone; or tag `perf-cliff-repro-20260926` of [rustin-beep/Vitro](https://github.com/rustin-beep/Vitro) (MIT, full sample) — building it yields `run.c`; **path-independent fingerprint: the `moonbit_init` region (`void moonbit_init() {` … closing `}`, 602,899 bytes) has sha256 `08943e7c…`, identical across clean clones** (the whole-file sha is not portable — emitted `#line` directives embed the absolute build path).

---

## Actual behavior

On Windows, `moon build --release --target native` compiles the C emitted for an executable as a **single translation unit** (compile+link fused in one `cl` invocation, no `/c`), with `/O2` applied by default.

For a larger module nearly the entire build cost concentrates in **one generated function**:

- `moonbit_init` — the whole-module global-initialization function emitted by moonc — is **18,498 lines / 589 KB**, and it is essentially **a flat constant-table initializer**: of its 18,495 statements, **18,347 are array-element stores** (`base[i] = value`), **18,157 of them pure integer literals**, filling one **17,425-element heap array** (`moonbit_make_int32_array_raw(17425)`) plus two smaller ones (644 / 88 elements). Exactly **one** `if`, **zero** loops, zero `goto`. Nothing here is a loop the optimizer could skip. It is also one straight-line basic block — but we probed that, and **the block shape is a symptom, not the cause** (item 1c): forcing K−1 opaque branches into the body splits it into K blocks and recovers only ~35%, while splitting the *function* into 4 pieces recovers ~15×. What actually drives the cost is the **instruction count carried by a single function**.
- Emptying **only this function** (keeping `moonbit_layout_table = moonbit_layout_table_data;`) shrinks the file by just **5.6%** (602,900 / 10,776,823 bytes) yet removes **~95% of cl /O2 time**: 101.1 s → 4.93 s interleaved A/B on the same machine (45× from the cold first run, 223.2 s → 4.93 s).
- **The same function is harmless for gcc/clang**: full file 30 s (gcc) / 13.0 s (clang); with `moonbit_init` emptied gcc only drops to 21 s (**1.4×**). Only MSVC blows up on this shape.
- Within one module, only the executable with the large init is slow: `dump_compile.c` is 7.7 MB but its `moonbit_init` is 155 lines → 4.26 s with cl /O2.

End-to-end (`moon build --release --target native`, rc=0):

| Machine | default (cl) | `MOON_CC=clang` | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Author (AI Max 395, MSVC 14.51.36231) | 101 s (interleaved-A/B mean, hot; range 87–126 s; first ever run 223 s) | 17.1 s | 5.9× |
| Second contributor's machine (i9-14900HX, MSVC 14.50.35717) | 82.3 s | 23.2 s | 3.5× |

Single-file matrix (same 10.8 MB emitted `run.c`, `cl /nologo /utf-8 /c /Z7 /O2 -c run.c`):

| Compiler | Author machine | Reporter-2 machine |
|---|---|---|
| clang 22.1.4 (msvc-target) -O2 | 12.96–16.0 s | 13.5 s |
| clang-cl /O2 (same ABI, same headers) | 17.38 s / 12.25 s | 16.7 s |
| MinGW gcc -O2 | 30 s / 28.5 s (16.2.0) | 31.3 s (14.2.0) |
| **cl /Od (14.51)** | **0.93–1.32 s** | — |
| **cl /O1 (14.50)** | 50.8 s | 62–65 s |
| **cl /O1 (14.51)** | 72.7–80.4 s | — |
| **cl /O2 (14.50.35717)** | **68–81 s (interleaved A/B: 67.97 / 69.35)** | 71–73 s |
| **cl /O2 (14.51.36231)** | **96–126 s (interleaved A/B: 106.67 / 95.60)** | (not installed) |
| cl /O2 (14.44.35207) | — | 76 s |

Three facts sharpen the picture beyond the well-known "MSVC is slower than clang on large TUs":

0. **~99% of the cost is inside the optimizer**: `cl /Od` compiles the same 10.8 MB file in ~1 s (`/O2` ≈ 100 s). Parsing/lowering is a non-issue; debug builds (`/Od`) were never slow. Also note cl compiles a single file **single-threaded** — measured parallelism **0.99** (Δcpu-time 44.8 s ÷ Δwall 45.1 s), i.e. exactly one core on a 32-thread host; the wall-clock cost is purely serialized optimizer time.

1. **The blowup is one generated function, and it is shape-specific to MSVC.** Emptying `moonbit_init` costs gcc only 1.4× but MSVC ~13× (14.50) / ~20× (14.51). After emptying it, 14.51 is consistently *faster* than 14.50 across independent runs on both sides (author: 4.9 s vs 5.4–5.6 s; reporter-2 re-run: 4.3–4.4 s vs 4.9–5.3 s) — i.e. the 14.51 regression is specific to this function's shape, not a general slowdown. Absolute values of this sub-6-second comparison drift with thermal state; only the ordering is stable.
1b. **Direct measurement of where the time goes** (MSVC's own `/Bt+`), same input, same machine:

    | Toolset | c1.dll (front end) | c2.dll (back end / optimizer) |
    |---|---|---|
    | 14.51.36231 | 0.370 s | **119.35 s** |
    | 14.50.35717 | 0.329 s | **85.56 s** |

    The front end parses the 10.8 MB file in ~0.35 s; **99.7% is back-end time**, and the entire 14.51-vs-14.50 delta sits in the back end (1.40×). Independently, MSVC's opt-in `/d2ReducedOptimizeHugeFunctions` (documented in your [VS 2019 16.4 backend post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/msvc-backend-updates-in-visual-studio-2019-versions-16-3-and-16-4), instruction threshold 20,000) collapses the cost: **14.51 → 32.1 s (–73%), 14.50 → 40.1 s (–53%)** — and with it enabled, 14.51 is again *faster* than 14.50. This is the same function-shape sensitivity seen in the deletion experiment, now measured without modifying the input.

1c. **Intervention ladder: what actually moves the needle.** We probed several independent interventions on the same input (cl /O2 14.51.36231; interleaved where noted; normalized to each machine's own baseline):

    | intervention | normalized | notes |
    |---|---|---|
    | baseline: one function, 18,467 statements | 1.00 | 87–91 s (author machine, interleaved) |
    | split into K=16 basic blocks (opaque branches, function size unchanged) | **0.65–0.67** | reproduced independently on a second contributor's machine (68 s baseline); saturates by K≈16, K=256 does not help further |
    | `/O1` | 0.75–0.88 | |
    | `/d2ReducedOptimizeHugeFunctions` | 0.42 | **no source change at all** |
    | **split into 2 functions** | 0.22 | |
    | **split into 4 functions** | **0.07** | 5.88 / 5.96 s vs 87.09 / 91.49 s baseline (interleaved) |
    | split into 64 functions | 0.05 | saturating |
    | empty the function body (all 18,467 statements deleted) | 0.06–0.10 | |

    Reading:
    - Cutting the **control-flow graph** into blocks recovers only ~35%. Cutting the **function** into 4 recovers ~15× — and **splitting into 4 functions is as fast as deleting all the code**. The cost is driven by the instruction count carried by a single function (the size of the function-level optimization domain); "one flat basic block" is how the init is emitted, not why it is expensive.
    - The gain saturates very early: 4 functions already capture essentially all of it.

    How the split was made (mechanical, semantics-preserving): hoist the body's local declarations to file-static variables, cut at top-level statement boundaries into N chunks, emit one `static void moonbit_init_pJ(void)` per chunk, and call them in order. We linked a 4-way split build and ran it against the original on 5 baseline cases — **identical stdout and return codes (5/5)**.

    Practical warning for anyone acting on this report: an implementation that only inserts block boundaries (dummy branches and the like) would recover at most a third of the cost.

2. **MSVC 14.51 regressed ~1.5× on this shape vs 14.50** (interleaved A/B: session 1 — 101.14 s vs 68.66 s, non-overlapping ranges 96–126 vs 68–81; session 2 — 1.52×, 92.03 s vs 60.67 s; session 3 on a clean clone — 1.59×, 154.91 s vs 97.63 s; cold first run up to 1.94×). Plausible cause: 14.50/14.51 replaced loop optimizations with a new SSA-based loop optimizer plus many new algebraic patterns ([MSVC Build Tools v14.51 performance post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/c-performance-improvements-in-msvc-build-tools-v14-51)) — a plausible window for a shape-specific regression.

This also matches Microsoft's own diagnosis guidance: the C++ Build Insights post [*Improving code generation time*](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/improving-code-generation-time-with-cpp-build-insights) describes exactly this class — a huge dynamic-initializer function (Chakra's `??__E` for a 450+-element global array) pressing on the optimizer — and prescribes splitting the function ("This splitting technique can also be used for large global arrays"). Our `moonbit_init` is the same class of function at ~70× that size; reducing the optimizer's work on functions above the (opt-in) 20,000-instruction threshold measurably fixes our case (sec. 1b above), which is consistent with that diagnosis.

## Expected Behavior

- Build times closer to the clang/gcc parity the same emitted C already enjoys, and/or a supported knob for the Windows native optimization level.
- Today `link.native.cc-flags` (package-level, documented as overriding default flags) can bypass the hardcoded `/O2` — but it is per-package, requires hand-writing the full flag set, and is CLI-invisible; a first-class `--opt-level` (tracked as #1378) would be the ergonomic fix.

## Steps to Reproduce

Option A (minimal — zero dependencies, no repo clone): download
<https://github.com/rustin-beep/Vitro/releases/download/perf-cliff-repro-20260926/mb_probe.zip> (3.7 KB), unpack, `moon build --target native --release`. The whole project is `moon.mod` + `moon.pkg` + one source file whose entire content is a single literal table:

```
let big_table : Array[Int] = [ …17,425 values… ]
```

The emitted C is 562 KB with a **17,431-statement `moonbit_init`**; one build reproduces the cliff by itself: cold `cl /O2` **201.6 s**, warm **109–142 s**, versus **clang 1 s** on the same file (author machine, MSVC 14.51.36231). One-liner to generate the literal without the download:

```
python -c "print('let big_table : Array[Int] = ['+','.join(str(i%251) for i in range(17425))+']')" > main.mbt
```

**Caveat (measured)**: the table must be a **literal**. Building the same array at runtime with a top-level `let big_table : Array[Int] = build_table()` (function-constructed) emits an init of **3 lines / 2 statements** and does **not** reproduce the cliff.

Option B (single file, **no MoonBit toolchain needed**): download the prebuilt input directly —
<https://github.com/rustin-beep/Vitro/releases/download/perf-cliff-repro-20260926/run.c> (10,776,823 bytes; probe scripts and fingerprint notes in the `perf-cliff-repro-kit.zip` asset of the same release) — or take the emitted `run.c` after any release build of the repo.

Option C (full sample, needs moon + VS): `git clone https://github.com/rustin-beep/Vitro` (MIT), **`git checkout perf-cliff-repro-20260926`** — this report's numbers are pinned to that tag; current `main` has renumbered temporaries so its init fingerprint differs while structure does not (see the note at the end) — then `cd moonbit`, delete `_build`, `moon build --release --target native`; compare with `MOON_CC=clang`. That tag still carries the old `moonbitlang/x` dependency; current `main` is dependency-free and builds offline. `MOON_CC` applies on the generated-C path; for direct-object MSVC targets a non-cl-compatible `MOON_CC` is ignored with a warning.

Root-cause isolation: delete the body of `moonbit_init` (keeping `moonbit_layout_table = moonbit_layout_table_data;`), recompile with `cl /O2` — 101 s → 4.93 s.

Measurement note when reproducing: there is a monotone warm-up drift (first-run penalty from AV/defender scanning, file cache and CPU frequency settling) — on our machines cl /O2 drifted from ~159 s (first ever run) down to a stable ~87–97 s plateau over repeated runs, clang from 16.0 s to ~12 s; **a hot machine can drift the plateau up again (~182 s observed after sustained load)**. **Discard first runs, prefer interleaved A/B (A→B→A→B), and compare numbers taken under comparable thermal state** — otherwise the drift inflates whichever compiler runs first.

For optimizer-side attribution we used MSVC's built-in instrumentation directly: `/Bt+` separates front end (0.37 s) from back end (119.35 s), and the deletion experiment plus `/d2ReducedOptimizeHugeFunctions` both isolate `moonbit_init` (sec. 1b). A `vcperf` Functions-view WCTR trace would be a nice cross-check if you want one, but we believe the attribution is already measured, not inferred.

## Environment

- Author: Windows 11 26200 / AMD AI Max+ 395 / VS 18 Community, MSVC **14.50.35717 + 14.51.36231**; clang 22.1.4; gcc 16.2.0; moon 0.1.20260920
- Second contributor's machine: Windows 10 25H2 / i9-14900HX / VS 18.5, MSVC **14.44.35207 + 14.50.35717**; clang 22.1.4; gcc 14.2.0; moon 0.1.20260920

(`moon build --release --target native --dry-run` shows 43 commands for this module: 25 build-package + 5 link-core + 13 C-toolchain commands; the run executable's link line is a single `cl.exe ... /O2 run.c ... /link` with the user C as the only source file.)

## Context: who is hitting this

This report comes from [Vitro](https://github.com/rustin-beep/Vitro) — a teaching-oriented, white-box C-subset engine written entirely in MoonBit, with the full memory model of the programs it runs under its own control (own address space, heap state machine, checked access on every load/store). Its test suite holds byte-for-byte output parity with Clang across 443 cases, so we are reasonably confident the emitted C is correct and this is purely a build-time problem.

Being a teaching-scale project, we did not expect to hit a build-time cliff of this size. We have since isolated the trigger, and it is **not** "how many packages a module links": it is whether some global constant array literal is large enough that moonc flattens it into thousands of per-element stores inside the single `moonbit_init`. In our case that array is a 17,425-element `Array[Int]` (the precompiled libc bytecode stream), which alone accounts for **99.4%** of the function's 18,457 statements. We measured the cost curve over the statement count (cl /O2, single runs — expect ±10–15% run-to-run scatter): ~1 statement ≈ 0.1–0.3 s, 4k statements ≈ 3 s, 8k ≈ 13 s, 12k ≈ 30–39 s, 17.4k ≈ 110–142 s. The cost **per statement grows superlinearly** (~2× from 4k→8k, ~1.5× from 8k→12k, ~2.5× from 12k→17.4k) — the curve steepens toward the top rather than kicking in at a single point.

If it is addressed, we are happy to keep serving as a regression sample: the repo is MIT, the case reproduces with one command, and we can run pre-release toolchains against it and report timings.

## Notes / possible directions (non-prescriptive)

1. Emit `moonbit_init` in chunks (e.g. per-package init functions chained from the entry) or per-package translation units. We measured this directly (item 1c): chunking into just **4 functions** takes cl /O2 from 87–91 s to 5.9 s (15×) and essentially eliminates the cliff — per-package granularity is not required for the win. The runtime side already moved this way (#1958); the emitted-user-code side is still one unit. This is worth doing beyond the MSVC blowup, because the single-unit shape costs every platform something: gcc is 1.4× slower on the same function (30 s → 21 s), the whole 10.8 MB translation unit is the smallest unit of caching/parallelism (one changed line invalidates the entire ccache entry, and the TU can never occupy more than one core), and it is also the unit handed to LTO and debuggers.
2. First-class opt-level for native release (tracked as #1378). On this shape `/O1` is ~1.15–1.25× faster than `/O2` (14.50: 50.8 s vs 60.7 s author, 62–65 s vs 71–73 s reporter-2; on 14.51 the gap widens to ~1.3×).
3. Document `MOON_CC` as the official mitigation for slow Windows native generated-C builds — verified working on two machines (rc=0, all tasks) — including its precondition: it is ignored for direct-object MSVC targets unless the driver is cl-compatible. Related: #1091 (args support), #1714 (Windows clang coverage).
4. FYI: we plan to file the 14.51-vs-14.50 shape-specific regression with Visual Studio Developer Community separately — it is an MSVC-side matter that MoonBit can only mitigate, not fix.

5. If the MSVC-side path is to be mitigated rather than fixed: `/d2ReducedOptimizeHugeFunctions` is the documented-knob-shaped answer, and we measured it working here (sec. 1b) with a small blast radius on this file (only `moonbit_init` exceeds the threshold; the next-largest function is 1,050 lines) — and since init runs once at startup, its reduced optimization is nearly free at runtime. Note we are not asking MoonBit to pass this undocumented flag by default; we primarily report it as evidence for the shape analysis.

Happy to split the three directions into separate issues if that helps tracking.

~~Scope caveat, stated plainly: **all measurements are Windows-only**; Linux/macOS were not tested (our CI has no non-Windows native job).~~ **Update 2026-09-29: the caveat is now measured, not inferred** — see the table below.

**Linux measurement (2026-09-29, WSL2 Ubuntu 26.04, gcc 15.2.0 / Ubuntu clang 21.1.8, same moon `0.1.20260920`, clean `_build` each run):**

| toolchain | platform | full `moon build --release --target native` |
|---|---|---|
| MSVC 14.51 (cl /O2) | Windows | **60–130 s** (see OP) |
| MinGW gcc -O2 | Windows | 30 s (see OP) |
| gcc 15.2.0 (linux-gnu) | **WSL2 Ubuntu 26.04** | **7.5 s** (minimal variant) / **30 s** (full repo build, incl. /mnt/d 9P I/O overhead) |
| Ubuntu clang 21.1.8 | **WSL2 Ubuntu 26.04** | **3.1 s** (minimal variant) |

The minimal-variant gap (MSVC 60 s+ vs gcc 7.5 s / clang 3.1 s on **the same source, the same moon version, clean caches**) confirms the original inference: the cliff lives in `c2.dll`'s optimizer, not in the emitted shape — the 18.5k-line `moonbit_init` is harmless outside MSVC, including a full-repository native build under gcc (30 s even with the 9P filesystem penalty of building from `/mnt/d`). Practical side note: `wsl + gcc` is a usable local mitigation for Windows users blocked by this cliff (30 s vs 60–130 s), alongside the already-documented `MOON_CC=clang`.

Source baseline: all numbers are against tag `perf-cliff-repro-20260926` of https://github.com/rustin-beep/Vitro (vitro/engine 0.5.0, moon 0.1.20260920). **Building that tag yields `run.c` whose `moonbit_init` region — from `void moonbit_init() {` through the closing `}`, 602,899 bytes, excluding the trailing newline — has sha256 `08943e7ccc296aa625b94d0bbaf11821e0d23297d311c6d3997c774c88fdc2c0`**, identical byte-for-byte across clean clones. The whole-file sha256 is **not** a portable fingerprint: moonc's emitted `#line` directives embed the absolute source path (10,964 lines), so it differs per build directory (e.g. `e9c1d0a…` vs `136ec81c…` for the same tag).

**Current state, for reference**: `main` is now dependency-free (the one external dep was vendored in) and builds offline. Its `moonbit_init` region hashes to `fe7c1f49…` — *structurally identical* to the tag (602,899 bytes, 18,457 statements, same 17,425-element table; a line-by-line diff shows 18,432 differing lines that reduce to **zero once all digits are masked**, i.e. temporary identifiers renumbered only). Timing caveat: single-run scatter on this workload is ±10–15% (109/117.9/142.3 s for the same input), so compare interleaved rather than by absolute numbers. One more measured fact that may be useful to you: MSVC's opt-in `/d2ReducedOptimizeHugeFunctions` switches on somewhere between 4k and 8k statements on this shape (0.99× at 4k, 2.7× at 8k, 3.5× at 12k, 4.2× at 17.4k) — i.e. below the documented 20,000-instruction default once moonc's store sequence is expanded, and the benefit grows monotonically with function size.

## Checklist

- [x] Reproducible from a public repo (MIT) + single-file path; timings stable across ≥2 runs (≤6% spread); regression confirmed by interleaved A/B on one machine and cross-machine toolset comparison.

title: Promote remaining moon.pkg options to dedicated DSL declarations
body:
Several active package settings still require `options(...)`, even though `moon.pkg` has dedicated declarations for imports, package type, formatting, warnings, supported targets, and build rules. Track the remaining fields here so their syntax and migration behavior can be addressed incrementally.

The first step can preserve the existing value types and behavior for eight fields:

- [x] `proof-enabled` → `proof_enabled = true`
- [ ] `bin-name` → `bin_name = "app"`
- [ ] `bin-target` → `bin_target = "native"`
- [x] `max-concurrent-tests` → `max_concurrent_tests = 4`
- [x] `regex-backend` → `regex_backend = "table"`
- [x] `implement` → `implement = "user/module/interface"`
- [ ] `overrides` → `overrides = ["user/module/implementation"]`
- [x] `virtual` → `virtual(has_default: true)`

The remaining fields need separate syntax/design decisions:

- [ ] `targets`: decide whether to retain the filename-to-condition map or introduce dedicated conditional file declarations.
- [ ] `native-stub`: design native stub declarations together with native build configuration.
- [ ] Structured `link`: design declarations for the Wasm, WasmGC, JavaScript, and native configuration fields. The deprecated boolean `link: true` already has `pkgtype(kind: "foreign_library")` as its replacement.

For each migration, preserve existing validation and legacy `options(...)` compatibility, define consistent behavior when both forms are present, add conversion coverage, and update documentation. Coordinate `moonfmt` formatting and JSON-to-DSL migration output with the toolchain implementation; this repository delegates that work to the external `moonfmt` executable.

Deprecated `name` and ineffective `test-import-all` are compatibility leftovers rather than new DSL features.

The Moon-side implementation for the first eight declarations is prepared in draft PR #2252. Compiler and formatter support are also required: local `moonc v0.10.14+7d59c7ec9 (2026-09-18)` rejects the seven assignment declarations with E4192, and the installed `moonfmt` rewrites all eight direct forms into `options(...)`. Moon-side conversion tests and dry-run planning pass; after formatting the same temporary virtual-package project back to legacy options, all three runtime tests pass. Keep this issue open for the companion toolchain changes and the remaining three fields.

title: native: Windows/MinGW builds fail - rand_s include order in env.c, and archiver resolved only as a sibling of the compiler
body:
## Summary

`moon --target native` cannot build at all on Windows with a MinGW-w64 toolchain, for two independent reasons:

1. The bundled C runtime `~/.moon/lib/runtime/env.c` never sees the declaration of `rand_s`, so GCC ≥ 14 rejects it as an implicit function declaration. `env.c` *does* try to opt in with `_CRT_RAND_S`, but the define lands too late — `<windows.h>` has already pulled in `<stdlib.h>`.
2. The native archiver is resolved only as a sibling of the compiler executable, with the name derived from the compiler's own filename, and there is no `PATH` fallback. Any custom compiler name (`mycc.exe`, `moonbit-cc.exe`) breaks the build even when a perfectly good `ar.exe` is on `PATH`.

Both have workarounds, but the only usable workaround for #1 is to wrap the compiler in an executable, which then trips #2. So the two compound: on Windows you cannot install a working `MOON_CC` without putting a renamed copy of `gcc.exe` next to `ar.exe`.

## Environment

```
moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20) ~\.moon\bin\moon.exe
moonc v0.10.14+7d59c7ec9 (2026-09-18) ~\.moon\bin\moonc.exe
moonrun 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20) ~\.moon\bin\moonrun.exe
```

```
gcc.exe (MinGW-W64 x86_64-ucrt-posix-seh, built by Brecht Sanders, r1) 16.2.0
GNU ar (Binutils for MinGW-W64 x86_64, built by Brecht Sanders, r1) 2.47.20260726
```

winlibs release `x86_64-posix-seh-gcc-16.2.0-mingw-w64ucrt-14.0.0-r1`, extracted to `C:\Users\<user>\Tools\mingw64`, added to the user `PATH`. No admin rights, no installer.

## Defect 1 — `rand_s` is never declared

### Symptom

With `cc`/`gcc` on `PATH`, any native build dies inside the bundled runtime:

```
C:/Users/<user>/.moon/lib/runtime/env.c: In function 'moonbit_rt_get_random':
C:/Users/<user>/.moon/lib/runtime/env.c:244:9: error: implicit declaration of function 'rand_s'; did you mean 'rand'? [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
  244 |     if (rand_s(&word) != 0) return -1;
      |         ^~~~~~
      |         rand
```

which surfaces through moon as (note the contradictory summary line):

```
Failed with 0 warnings, 0 errors.
Error: failed to run build for target Native
```

### Root cause

`env.c` opts into the SECURE_API declarations, but after `<stdlib.h>` has already been included:

```c
#elif defined(_WIN32)

#include <windows.h>        // line 37
#include <stdio.h>          // line 38

#ifdef _MSC_VER
...
#else

#ifndef _CRT_RAND_S         // line 51 — too late
#define _CRT_RAND_S
#endif

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdlib.h>         // line 57 — no-op, include guard already closed
#include <time.h>
```

On mingw-w64 14.0.0, `<windows.h>` reaches `<stdlib.h>` transitively through the intrinsic headers, so by line 51 the `stdlib.h` include guard is set and line 57 does nothing:

```
$ gcc -c order_as_env.c -o /dev/null -H
........ C:/.../gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32/16.2.0/include/xmmintrin.h
......... C:/.../gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32/16.2.0/include/mm_malloc.h
.......... C:/.../mingw64/x86_64-w64-mingw32/include/stdlib.h
```

and the declaration in `x86_64-w64-mingw32/include/stdlib.h` is guarded:

```c
#ifdef _CRT_RAND_S
  _SECIMP errno_t __cdecl rand_s(unsigned int *randomValue);
#endif
```

So the header is fine and the symbol is fine — `rand_s` is present in `libucrt.a` (`nm`: `T rand_s`) — only the declaration is missed. This is purely an include-order bug in `env.c`.

### Minimal repro

`order_as_env.c` reproduces `env.c`'s exact include order:

```c
#include <windows.h>
#include <stdio.h>

#ifndef _CRT_RAND_S
#define _CRT_RAND_S
#endif

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>

int use_rand_s(void) {
  unsigned int v = 0;
  return rand_s(&v);
}
```

```
$ gcc -c order_as_env.c -o /dev/null
order_as_env.c: In function 'use_rand_s':
order_as_env.c:17:10: error: implicit declaration of function 'rand_s'; did you mean 'rand'? [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
   17 |   return rand_s(&v);
      |          ^~~~~~
      |          rand

$ gcc -c order_fixed.c -o /dev/null   # same file, #define moved above #include <windows.h>
$                                          # exit 0, no diagnostics
```

### Suggested fix

Move the `_CRT_RAND_S` define above every include in the `_WIN32` / non-MSVC branch — i.e. before `#include <windows.h>` at `env.c:37` — or define it at the very top of the file next to `MOONBIT_BUILD_RUNTIME`. Alternatively declare the prototype locally, or call `SystemFunction036` from `<ntsecapi.h>`, which mingw declares unconditionally.

`-D_CRT_RAND_S` on the compiler command line is confirmed to fix all five bundled runtime units (`env.c`, `runtime.c`, `backtrace.c`, `sync_io.c`, `utf.c`) with zero warnings and no need for `-Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration`, which is why it is what the workaround below injects rather than warning suppression.

## Defect 2 — the archiver is only found as a sibling of the compiler

`MOON_CC` cannot carry flags — the whole string is treated as one executable path:

```
$ MOON_CC="gcc -D_CRT_RAND_S" moon build --target native
Error: failed to run build for target Native

Caused by:
    0: Failed to build a build plan for the modules
    1: Failed to set C compiler when compiling username/nativecheck/cmd/main@0.1.0
    2: failed to resolve native compiler executable `gcc -D_CRT_RAND_S`
    3: failed to find executable `gcc -D_CRT_RAND_S`
    4: cannot find binary path
```

So the fix for defect 1 has to be a forwarding executable. But then the archiver lookup derives the archiver's *name* from the compiler's *filename* and looks for it in the compiler's own directory only:

| `MOON_CC` | archiver moon looks for |
| --- | --- |
| `...\onlybin\cc.exe` | `...\onlybin\ar.exe` |
| `...\onlybin\gcc.exe` | `...\onlybin\ar.exe` |
| `...\onlybin\mycc.exe` | `...\onlybin\myar.exe` |
| `...\onlybin\moonbit-cc.exe` | `...\onlybin\moonbit-ar.exe` |

```
$ MOON_CC=C:/Users/<user>/.moon/tmp/archprobe/onlybin/mycc.exe moon build --target native
Error: failed to run build for target Native

Caused by:
    2: failed to resolve native archiver executable `C:/Users/<user>/.moon/tmp/archprobe/onlybin\myar.exe`
```

In that run `ar.exe` *was* resolvable on `PATH` (`C:/Users/<user>/Tools/mingw64/bin/ar.exe`, GNU ar 2.47.20260726), and moon still failed — so there is no `PATH` fallback for the derived name. The `gcc.exe` / `cc.exe` rows above fail the same way when their directory has no `ar.exe`, which is what proves the sibling-only lookup independently of the name derivation.

Note the mixed separators in the diagnostic (`.../onlybin\myar.exe`) — cosmetic, but it makes the message awkward to grep.

### Suggested fix

Any of:

- honour a separate `MOON_AR` / `--ar` override instead of deriving the name,
- fall back to searching `PATH` for `ar.exe` (and `llvm-ar.exe`) when the sibling lookup misses, and say so in the error,
- or at minimum print the lookup order that was tried, so "put your compiler somewhere that also has ar" is discoverable rather than reverse-engineered from four error messages.

## Why this matters together

The path of least resistance on Windows is currently: copy/rename the compiler so that (a) it is found first by the `cc → gcc → clang` probe, and (b) its derived archiver name already exists beside it. That is what I did — a `cc.exe` forwarder in `mingw64\bin` that injects `-D_CRT_RAND_S` — and it works, but it depends on undocumented name-derivation behaviour and on the `cc`-first probe order. Neither is a reasonable thing to expect users to discover.

## Verification that the workaround is sufficient

With the forwarder installed as `mingw64\bin\cc.exe` (i.e. injecting only `-D_CRT_RAND_S`, no warning suppression):

```
$ moon test --target native
Total tests: 2, passed: 2, failed: 0.

$ moon run cmd/main --target native
Hello

$ moon build --target native
Finished. moon: no work to do
```

The tests include a user `extern "c"` stub that calls `rand_s` itself, so the injected define is confirmed to reach project stubs as well as the bundled runtime, and to link against `libucrt`.

## Possibly related

Closed issues around native toolchain resolution that look adjacent, though none covers these two failures: #2145, #1955, #1956, #1904.

title: moon check --json: a failed pre-build command yields status=failure with empty messages and no cause
body:
## Summary

When a `pre-build` command fails, `moon check --json` reports `"status": "failure"` but nothing else: `diagnostics` and `messages` are both empty and every `summary` count is zero. A consumer cannot tell *why* the run failed, or even that a pre-build step was involved. The human output is equally silent about the cause (`Error: failed when checking project`), and the two modes disagree on the exit code (255 vs 1).

Consumers that drive edits from the JSON result (we use it as a guard in [moonbitlang/openseek#1709](https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/pull/1709)) have to treat `status != "success"` with no error diagnostic as "unknown failure", which is workable but leaves the agent with no cause to act on. By contrast, a failed build plan IS messaged (`"Failed to calculate build plan: ... Cannot find import 'x'"`), which is exactly what a consumer needs.

## Reproduction

`moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20)`, macOS.

```
moon.mod:  name = "tmp/prebuild"
in.txt:    (empty)
main.mbt:  pub fn hi() -> Int { 1 }
moon.pkg:
  options(
    "pre-build": [
      { "command": "false", "input": [ "in.txt" ], "output": "generated.mbt" },
    ],
  )
```

```
$ moon check --json ; echo exit=$?
{"version":1,"status":"failure","diagnostics":[],"messages":[],"summary":{"tasks_executed":null,"moon_errors":0,"moon_warnings":0,"diagnostic_errors":0,"diagnostic_warnings":0}}
exit=1

$ moon check ; echo exit=$?
Failed with 0 warnings, 0 errors.
Error: failed when checking project
exit=255
```

For comparison, a manifest importing a package that does not exist is reported well:

```
$ moon check --json
{"version":1,"status":"failure","diagnostics":[],"messages":[{"$message_type":"moon","level":"error","message":"Failed to calculate build plan: Failed to solve package relationship: Cannot find import 'tmp/broken/nonexistent' in tmp/broken/lib@0.0.0"}],"summary":{"tasks_executed":null,"moon_errors":1,"moon_warnings":0,"diagnostic_errors":0,"diagnostic_warnings":0}}
```

## Expected

A pre-build failure surfaces as a moon-level message, so `summary.moon_errors` is nonzero and `messages` names the cause, e.g.

```json
{"$message_type":"moon","level":"error","message":"pre-build command failed (exit 1) in package tmp/prebuild: false"}
```

Ideally with the command's captured stderr (or its first lines) in the message, since that is usually the actual reason. The human output would benefit from the same line. Aligning the exit code between the two modes would also help scripts that check it.

title: native: stack overflow exits with a bare SIGSEGV — no diagnostic, and buffered stdout is lost

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
Deep recursion in a native build overflows the stack and the process dies
with a bare `SIGSEGV` (exit 139): stderr stays empty, and stdout that was
already written with `println` before the crash is lost as well. The same
program on the js backend fails with a readable
`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` plus source locations.

## Actual behavior

With an 8 MiB stack (`ulimit -s 8192`), 100% reproducible on Linux x86-64,
on both `latest` (moon 0.1.20260915) and `nightly` (moon 0.1.20260916):

| case | command | exit | stdout | stderr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| deep 100000 | `deep.exe 100000` | 0 | 38 B | 0 B |
| deep 500000 | `deep.exe 500000` | 0 | 38 B | 0 B |
| deep 1000000 | `deep.exe 1000000` | **139** | **0 B** | **0 B** |
| unbounded recursion | `spin.exe` | **139** | **0 B** | **0 B** |
| release/AOT 20000000 | `deep.exe 20000000` (`--release --strip`) | 0 | 42 B | 0 B |
| js backend 10000 (control) | `moon run deep --target js -- 10000` | 1 | 18 B (kept) | ~0.6–1.4 KB, `RangeError` + `deep/main.mbt:38` |

The crash point depends on the stack limit as expected: 550000 frames already
crash, while the same binary with a 64 MiB stack runs 1000000 frames to
completion.

Where this behaviour comes from: this is native runtime behaviour. The real
sources live in `moonbitlang/moonbit-compiler` (issues are disabled there),
mirrored at `moonbitlang/moonbit-native-runtime`, so I am reporting it here.
The shipped runtime already contains a panic/`SIGABRT` backtrace path
(`backtrace.c`: `moonbit_panic`; `include/backtrace.h`: `backtrace_print`;
libbacktrace is linked), but there is **no `SIGSEGV`/`sigaltstack` handler at
all** — `grep -rn "sigaction\|sigaltstack\|SIGSEGV" ~/.moon/lib/runtime`
matches only a comment mentioning `SIGABRT` — so a guard-page overflow never
reaches that existing path. `moonbit_println` (runtime `env.c`) writes through
stdio `fwrite` without flushing, which is why the pre-crash output is lost too.

One observation I could not verify: with `--release --strip` the 20000000
frame case completes, which I assume is the recursion being optimized into a
loop; I did not check the assembly.

## Expected Behavior

At least a clear diagnostic instead of a bare `SIGSEGV` — for example routing
the stack overflow through the existing backtrace path (or printing a short

title: import all: two `"@pkg" *` imports in one .mbtx conflict even when their exports are disjoint
body:
### Summary

In `.mbtx` script mode, two import-all declarations in the same file are rejected as an alias conflict, even when the two packages export no names in common. Only one `"@pkg" *` is usable per script.

### Repro

```mbtx
///|
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
  "moonbitlang/async/fs" *,
  "moonbitlang/async/shell" *,
}

///|
async fn main {
  println(readdir(".").length())
  println(Cmd("echo", ["hi"]).status())
}
```

```
$ moon run both.mbtx
Error: Failed to solve package relationship
    Error 1: Conflicting import alias: Both moonbitlang/async/fs@0.21.3 (Source) and moonbitlang/async/shell@0.21.3 (Source) are imported into moon/test/single@0.0.1 with the same alias '*'.
```

Either glob alone works, and one glob alongside ordinary qualified imports works:

```mbtx
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
  "moonbitlang/async/fs",
  "moonbitlang/async/shell" *,
}
// @fs.readdir(".") and Cmd("echo", ["hi"]) both resolve
```

### Expected

Two import-all declarations should coexist. A conflict should be reported only when a name that is actually exported by both packages is *referenced* — the way `use a::*; use b::*;` behaves in Rust, where ambiguity is an error at the use site (E0659) rather than at the import.

### Why this looks like an implementation artifact

`*` appears to be modeled as an import *alias* string, so the package solver's "two packages, same alias" check fires on it. But `*` is not a name — it means "bind this package's names unqualified" — and two such imports are only genuinely in conflict when a referenced name is ambiguous.

The two packages above have **no** overlapping exports. From their `pkg.generated.mbti`, `async/fs` exports 35 top-level names and `async/shell` exports 6 (`Cmd`, `Output`, `Pipeline`, `Redirect`, `Stdin`, `glob`); the intersection is empty. `readdir` and `Cmd` cannot collide, yet the import is still refused.

The wording reinforces this: "Conflicting import alias ... with the same alias `'*'`" describes the implementation's data structure rather than anything a user wrote.

### Impact

Import-all exists to make short scripts shorter, and the common shape of a script is exactly the combination that cannot use it — `shell` to run a command, `fs` to read the result, `env` to find a path. Capping it at one package per script means the author picks one to shorten and qualifies the rest, which is the situation the feature was meant to remove.

### Acceptable outcomes, in preference order

1. Allow several `*` imports; report ambiguity at the reference site when a name is exported by more than one of them.
2. If the one-per-file limit is deliberate, say so in the diagnostic. Something like "at most one import-all per file; `x` and `y` both use `*`" would be actionable, where the current message reads as an internal conflict the author is expected to resolve with an alias.

### Workaround

Glob at most one package per script and qualify the others.

### Environment

```
moon    0.1.20260915 (2e1a46d 2026-09-15)
moonc   v0.10.13+cbb11c36f (2026-09-15)
moonrun 0.1.20260915 (2e1a46d 2026-09-15)
moonbitlang/async 0.21.3
```

### Routing note

The message text is present in the `moon` binary and absent from `moonc`, and it surfaces as a package-resolution failure, so this may belong in `moonbitlang/moon`. Filed here at the reporter's direction — please transfer if that is the better home.

title: moon fmt silently skips .mbtx scripts, even when explicitly specified

labels.name: pending-triage
