body:
While migrating a prebuild script to `.mbtx` following #2165, I found that `moon fmt` silently skips the script. The behavior also reproduces in a minimal module without a configured prebuild hook or external dependencies.

## Actual behavior

- `moon fmt build.mbtx` exits with status 0 and prints `Finished. moon: ran 1 task, now up to date`, but leaves the unformatted script unchanged.
- `moon fmt --check build.mbtx` also exits with status 0 while the script is still unformatted.
- Running `moon fmt` without a path also leaves the script unchanged.

As a separate control, I copied the same source to a neighboring `control.mbt`. Running `moon fmt build.mbtx` formatted `control.mbt` while still leaving `build.mbtx` unchanged.

## Expected Behavior

`moon fmt build.mbtx` should format the explicitly requested script:

```moonbit
///|
fn main {
  println(1)
}
```

`moon fmt --check build.mbtx` should return a nonzero status when that script needs formatting.

## Steps to Reproduce

In an empty directory, create these three files.

`moon.mod`:

```moonbit
name = "repro/mbtx-fmt"
version = "0.0.0"
```

`moon.pkg`: an empty file.

`build.mbtx`:

```moonbit
///|
fn main{println(1)}
```

Run:

```sh
moon run build.mbtx --target wasm  # Prints 1; the script is valid.
moon fmt build.mbtx
cat build.mbtx                    # Still contains fn main{println(1)}.
moon fmt --check build.mbtx       # Exits 0.
moon fmt
cat build.mbtx                    # Still unchanged.
```

Operating System: macOS, arm64.

`moon version --all`:

```text
moonc v0.10.12+ef027fb8a (2026-09-11) ~/.moon/bin/moonc
```

## Actual behavior

```text
���ڴ����� ...encoding-probe.lib �Ͷ��� ...encoding-probe.exp
```

Raw-byte capture confirms that MSVC emits GBK bytes, while Moon's stderr already contains UTF-8-encoded U+FFFD replacement characters. This is not merely a terminal rendering problem.

The likely loss point is `String::from_utf8_lossy(&result.output)` in n2's [`src/progress.rs`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/n2/blob/79d275ef051cf0d4864ae3b4f4947e3f3f035899/src/progress.rs), before invoking Moon's output callback.

title: `moon.pkg` lexer panics on integer literals ≥ 2^31 (e.g. `heap-start-address` above 2 GiB)
body:
The experimental `moon.pkg` format (`rr_moon_pkg`) lexes every integer
literal as `i32`, so any value at or above 2147483648 crashes `moon`
instead of producing a config value or an error. The same value in
`moon.pkg.json` works.

## Actual behavior

With the `moon.pkg` below, `moon build --target wasm` panics:

```
thread 'main' panicked at crates/moonutil/src/moon_pkg/lexer.rs:115:30:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: ParseIntError { kind: PosOverflow }
```

followed by the "`moon` has accidentally crashed" banner.

Cause: `crates/moonutil/src/moon_pkg/lexer.rs` declares the only number
token as `INT((Loc, i32))` and fills it with `s.parse::<i32>().unwrap()`.
The parser forwards the `i32` with `json!(i)`. There is no float token and
no string-to-number path, so no spelling of a large value gets through:
`2214592512` and `2214592512.0` panic in the lexer; `0x84000000`,
`"2214592512"`, and `2.214592512e9` are rejected downstream. `2147483647`
builds, `2147483648` panics. This is still the case on current `main`
(commit `ba0c3b15`, 2026-09-04).

## Expected Behavior

`moon.pkg` accepts the same numeric values as `moon.pkg.json`.
`heap-start-address` is a wasm32 linear-memory address, a `u32` that
legitimately reaches 4 GiB. A value the lexer cannot represent should
produce a diagnostic, not a panic.

Suggested fix: lex integers as `i64` (or `u64`) and return an error
instead of unwrapping.

Context: we import a host memory (`import-memory`) whose lower 2 GiB is
a GPU-shared arena, so the MoonBit heap has to start at 2214592512
(`0x84000000`). Because `moon fmt` migrates `moon.pkg.json` to
`moon.pkg` automatically, such a package stops building after a format.

## Steps to Reproduce

Happens every time.

1. `moon new repro` (or any module), then replace the root moon.pkg with:

   ```
   options(
     link: { "wasm": { "heap-start-address": 2214592512 } },
   )
   ```

2. Run `moon build --target wasm`.
3. Observe the `PosOverflow` panic above.
4. Change the value to `2147483647`: the build succeeds. Change it to
   `2147483648`: it panics again.

## Environment

Operating System: macOS

```
moon 0.1.20260427 (48d7def 2026-04-27) ~/.moon/bin/moon
moonc v0.9.1+cd5b07232 (2026-04-28) ~/.moon/bin/moonc
moonrun 0.1.20260427 (48d7def 2026-04-27) ~/.moon/bin/moonrun

Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_pkg
```

## Checklist

- [x] (Optional) My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: Support test blocks in .mbtx scripts (they compile today, then never run)
body:
### Summary

A `test` block inside a `.mbtx` script compiles, and then is silently
ignored. `moon run` never executes it, and `moon test` cannot reach it
because it rejects the `fn main` that every script necessarily has. So a
single-file script can *look* tested while nothing runs.

I would like `moon test some_script.mbtx` to run that file's `test`
blocks.

### Reproduce

`probe.mbtx`:

```moonbit
///|
fn double(x : Int) -> Int {
  x * 2
}

///|
test "double doubles" {
  assert_eq(double(21), 42)
}

///|
fn main {
  println(double(21))
}
```

**`moon run probe.mbtx`** — the test block compiles and is skipped
without a word:

```
42
```

Note it is not rejected. A deliberately failing assertion behaves the
same way, so nothing tells the author the block is inert.

**`moon test probe.mbtx`** — gets far enough to compile the file, then
refuses it for having a `main`:

```
Error: [4069]
    ╭─[ probe.mbtx:12:1 ]
    │
 12 │ ╭─▶ fn main {
 14 │ ├─▶ }
    │ ╰─────── Unexpected main function in the non-main package.
────╯
```

Every `.mbtx` is a script, so every `.mbtx` has a `main`, so this path
can never succeed today.

`moon 0.1.20260901 (56d55cd 2026-09-01)`, macOS.

### Why it matters

`.mbtx` is a good fit for a workflow script that binds published modules
and is run with `moon run` — no package directory, no `moon.pkg`, one
file to read. We use them for the examples in
[moonbitlang/workflow](https://github.com/moonbitlang/workflow).

The scripts are not all thin, though. One of ours parses `moon ide
analyze` output, decides which findings need no judgement, locates a
declaration in a package, and rewrites the line. That logic wants unit
tests: the parser, the name anchor that must match `run` but not
`run_cli`, the rewrite that must drop exactly one export marker.

It had those tests while it was a package. Converting it to a script to
match the other examples dropped all of them, and the only alternatives
are to keep a package that exists solely to hold tests, or to go
untested. Being able to write `test` in the script and run
`moon test the_script.mbtx` would remove that choice.

### Suggested behaviour

- `moon test path/to/script.mbtx` compiles the file as a test target,
  runs its `test` blocks, and ignores `fn main` rather than erroring on
  it.
- Failing that, at minimum reject a `test` block in a `.mbtx` at compile
  time. Silently accepting a block that never runs is the worst of the
  three outcomes — a passing suite that is not a suite.

Happy to help with a PR if the direction is agreed.

title: `MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD` does not disable `--moonbit-unstable-prebuild` scripts

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
## Actual behavior

`MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD=1` prevents package-level `pre-build` / `dev_build` actions from running, but it does not prevent the module-level `--moonbit-unstable-prebuild` script in `moon.mod.json` from running.

Consequently, `moon build` can execute arbitrary JavaScript or Python supplied by the module author even when both of these variables are set:

```sh
MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD=1
MOON_IGNORE_POSTADD=1
```

This also happens with `moon build --dry-run`.

This is security-relevant for hosted services that build untrusted modules. Mooncakes.io currently sets both variables while building published modules, but its Wasm artifact path invokes:

```sh
moon build --target wasm --release
```

A published module can therefore execute its `--moonbit-unstable-prebuild` script in the Mooncakes.io build worker. The current worker uses a disposable container without database or AWS credentials, which limits the impact, but the script still has access to the container's filesystem, processes, resources, and permitted network. More importantly, the current environment variables do not provide a complete no-user-scripts boundary for hosted or long-running build workers.

There is a related edge case for `moon check`: the root module's unstable prebuild is skipped, but installing a `bin-deps` dependency can enter a child build and execute that dependency's unstable prebuild script.

## Expected Behavior

Moon should provide a documented, fail-closed way to guarantee that no user-defined install or build script will execute.

Either:

1. `MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD` should also suppress or reject `--moonbit-unstable-prebuild`, including child builds used to install `bin-deps`; or
2. Moon should provide a separate flag or environment variable for hosted builds that covers package-level `pre-build` / `dev_build`, module-level `--moonbit-unstable-prebuild`, `postadd`, and child build paths.

For a hosted build service, failing when such configuration is encountered may be safer than silently ignoring it.

## Steps to Reproduce

Create `moon.mod.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "example/unstable-prebuild-repro",
  "source": "src",
  "--moonbit-unstable-prebuild": "prebuild.js"
}
```

Create `prebuild.js`:

```js
process.stderr.write("UNSTABLE_PREBUILD_EXECUTED\n");
process.exit(1);
```

Create `src/lib/moon.pkg.json`:

```json
{}
```

Create `src/lib/lib.mbt`:

```moonbit
pub fn answer() -> Int {
  42
}
```

Run:

```sh
MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD=1 MOON_IGNORE_POSTADD=1 moon build --dry-run
```

Actual output includes:

```text
UNSTABLE_PREBUILD_EXECUTED
Error: Failed to run prebuild script for module example/unstable-prebuild-repro
```

The script was executed despite `MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD=1` (and despite `--dry-run`).

## Environment

Operating System: macOS 14.1, arm64

```text
moon 0.1.20260827 (d0aaa07 2026-08-27)
moonc v0.10.11+8f8e8db1e (2026-08-27)
moonrun 0.1.20260827 (d0aaa07 2026-08-27)

Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

The current `main` branch at `56d55cd7654f8deef5f5409439390e123473fed0` appears to have the same behavior: the module-level prebuild path is not guarded by `MOON_IGNORE_PREBUILD`.

## Checklist

- [x] My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: moon doc plans moonc checks differently from moon check
body:
## Description

Before invoking `moondoc`, `moon doc` runs `moonc check` to prepare package metadata and interface files. The packages checked in this phase are not selected consistently with `moon check` for the same target backend.

`moon check` selects local packages that support the requested backend and expands only the dependencies needed by those packages. In contrast, `BuildDocs` currently requests `CheckMi` for every discovered non-stdlib package through `all_packages(true)`. This includes unrelated dependency packages and packages whose `supported_targets` excludes the selected backend.

## Reproduction

Using `moonbit-community/rabbita` with `moonbitlang/async@0.21.0`:

```console
$ moon doc --target wasm --dry-run | rg 'async/src/raw_fd/raw_fd.mbt'
moonc check .../async/src/raw_fd/raw_fd.mbt ... -target wasm ...

$ moon check --target wasm --dry-run | rg 'async/src/raw_fd/raw_fd.mbt'
# no output
```

The package explicitly supports only the native backend:

```moonbit
supported_targets = "-all+native"
```

Executing the commands produces the same difference:

- `moon check --target wasm` succeeds.
- `moon doc --target wasm` checks `moonbitlang/async/raw_fd` and fails because `fd_is_nonblocking` is not available for Wasm.
- The JS target also checks unrelated packages such as `hackwaly/moonback` and `moonbitlang/async/raw_fd`, producing undefined-type/value errors, while `moon check --target js` succeeds.

The dry-run package-set comparison showed 27 packages checked only by `moon doc` for Wasm and 36 packages checked only by `moon doc` for JS. Raw action totals are not directly comparable because `moon check` also creates test and doctest check actions.

## Relevant implementation

- `crates/moonbuild-rupes-recta/src/build_plan/builders.rs`: `build_build_docs` requests source `CheckMi` for `pkg_dirs.all_packages(true)`.
- `crates/moon/src/cli/check.rs`: normal `moon check` intents start from local packages filtered by `package_supports_backend`.

## Expected behavior

The compiler-check phase used to prepare documentation should respect the selected backend and should not check packages excluded by `supported_targets`. Ideally, its package selection should share the applicable behavior with `moon check`; any intentional documentation-specific differences should be explicit.

title: Decouple registry API, Git index, and artifact download endpoints
body:
## Motivation

The current registry configuration couples API operations and artifact downloads under a single registry URL. This makes it difficult to use a read-only mirror for package downloads while continuing to use the official `mooncakes.io` service for login, publishing, search, and other dynamic operations.

A mirror should only need to:

1. Clone and periodically update the public Git index.
2. Use `aws s3 sync` to synchronize all public objects served by `download.mooncakes.io`.

An advantage of this design is that mirrors do not need to understand how packages, prebuilt artifacts, symbols, or future content are organized.

## Detailed Description

Introduce three independent fields in `$MOON_HOME/config.json`:

```json
{
  "download": "https://download.mooncakes.io",
  "index": "https://mooncakes.io/git/index",
  "api": "https://mooncakes.io"
}
```

The fields have the following responsibilities:

- `download`: Base URL for immutable downloadable artifacts, including package ZIP archives, `symbols.zip`, prebuilt Wasm files, and checksum files.
- `index`: Git Smart HTTP URL of the Mooncakes package index.
- `api`: Base URL for dynamic registry operations, including login, registration, publishing, search, and metadata queries.

Users should be able to override only `download` and `index` while continuing to use the official API:

```json
{
  "download": "https://example.mirror/mooncakesio-download",
  "index": "https://example.mirror/mooncakesio-index",
  "api": "https://mooncakes.io"
}
```

The expected download layout is:

```text
<download>/
├── user/
│   └── <owner>/<module>/<version>.zip
├── prebuild/
│   └── <owner>/<module>@<version>/
│       ├── <executable>.wasm
│       └── <executable>.wasm.sha256
└── symbols.zip
```

The client should construct normal hierarchical paths under the configured `download` URL.

### `moon add`

For example:

```console
moon add moonbitlang/async@0.1.0
```

The client should:

1. Resolve the package version and checksum from the local Git index.
2. Download:

   ```text
   <download>/user/moonbitlang/async/0.1.0.zip
   ```

3. Verify the downloaded archive against the checksum recorded in the index.
4. Store it in the local registry cache.

With the example mirror configuration, the URL would be:

```text
https://example.mirror/mooncakesio-download/user/moonbitlang/async/0.1.0.zip
```

### `moonx`

For example:

```console
moonx Yoorkin/cowsay
```

The client should:

1. Query package and executable metadata from:

   ```text
   <api>/api/v0/modules/Yoorkin/cowsay
   ```

2. Download the prebuilt Wasm file from:

   ```text
   <download>/prebuild/Yoorkin/cowsay@0.1.0/cowsay.wasm
   ```

3. Download its checksum from:

   ```text
   <download>/prebuild/Yoorkin/cowsay@0.1.0/cowsay.wasm.sha256
   ```

4. Verify the Wasm file before caching or executing it.

The mirror therefore serves only static artifacts, while package queries continue to use the official API.

### `moon update`

The command should:

1. Clone the configured index when it is not available locally:

   ```console
   git clone --depth 1 --single-branch --no-tags <index>
   ```

2. Update an existing index from its `main` branch:

   ```console
   git pull origin main
   ```

3. Download:

   ```text
   <download>/symbols.zip
   ```

The configured index endpoint must support Git Smart HTTP and shallow clones. It is not required to implement the Cargo sparse-index protocol.

### Mirror requirements

A read-only mirror only needs to maintain two datasets.

#### Git index

The mirror can clone and periodically fetch the official index:

```console
git clone --mirror \
  https://mooncakes.io/git/index \
  mooncakesio-index.git

git -C mooncakesio-index.git fetch --prune origin
```

It can then expose this repository through Git Smart HTTP at an address such as:

```text
https://example.mirror/mooncakesio-index
```

#### Download artifacts

The official public S3 bucket should allow a mirror operator to synchronize all objects served by `download.mooncakes.io` using `aws s3 sync`:

```console
aws s3 sync \
  s3://<official-public-download-bucket>/ \
  /srv/mirrors/mooncakesio-download/ \
  --no-sign-request \
  --only-show-errors
```

The public S3 bucket must grant anonymous:

- `s3:ListBucket`, so `aws s3 sync` can list objects.
- `s3:GetObject`, so `aws s3 sync` can download objects.

The synchronized dataset should contain all content served by `download.mooncakes.io`, including:

```text
user/
prebuild/
symbols.zip
```

A mirror does not need to synchronize or implement:

- User accounts or credentials.
- Login and registration.
- Package publishing.
- Search and query APIs.
- The Mooncakes database.
- Download statistics.

Those operations continue to use the configured `api` endpoint.

None known.

title: Proposal: publish backend-specific `packages.json` inventories
body:
## Motivation

`packages.json` describes one concrete Target Backend, but it is currently published at the global path `_build/packages.json`.

This becomes ambiguous when one command produces more than one Build Target Projection:

- `moon check` without an explicit target can split local packages by their owning module's preferred target.
- `moon check --target all` and `moon bundle --target all` materialize several backends.
- Every plan rewrites the same file, so only the last backend remains visible to IDE and documentation tooling.
- The current package list is broader than the actual plan, while artifact paths and check commands are backend-specific. This can expose packages or artifacts that were not produced for the selected backend.
- Consumers must interpret file-level compile conditions themselves, duplicating MoonBuild target-selection logic.

A language service should be able to load all metadata produced by one check, then keep each request in one self-consistent backend context. It should not merge incompatible package variants or rerun `moon check` merely to switch backends.

## Proposed metadata contract

Publish one inventory per backend and a small authoritative index:

```text
_build/
  index.json
  js/
    packages.json
  native/
    packages.json
```

For standalone files, use `_build/<backend>/<filename>.packages.json`.

`_build/index.json` is a JSON array containing the backends materialized by the current metadata-producing command:

```json
["native", "js"]
```

Each backend `packages.json` remains a single-module-shaped document for compatibility, but becomes a materialized backend inventory:

- Top-level `backend` identifies the backend projection. The top-level `opt_level` field is removed: optimization-level selection is already materialized in file membership, artifact paths, and check commands, so consumers do not need to interpret it.
- `packages` contains only packages participating in that backend's plan, including checked transitive dependencies. If a virtual implementation participates, retain its virtual interface package as well.
- `files`, `wbtest-files`, `test-files`, and `mbt-md-files` become arrays already filtered by the same backend and optimization-level rules used by the build plan.
- File presence is authoritative; consumers do not reevaluate conditional compilation expressions.
- `artifact` and the check-command fields belong to the same backend plan.
- Package-level `supported-targets` is no longer needed in this materialized format: inclusion in the indexed backend inventory is the relevant fact.
- All other existing top-level and package-level fields remain present for compatibility; the concrete before/after example below lists the complete field set.

This represents simultaneous backend snapshots, not one merged cross-backend type environment.

## Implementation plan

1. **Generate plan-scoped metadata**

   In `crates/moonbuild-rupes-recta/src/metadata.rs`, pass the planned output set into metadata generation. Seed Source, WhiteboxTest, and BlackboxTest targets whose `.mi` output is present in the plan, close that set over package dependencies, and retain virtual interface packages required by participating implementations.

   Reuse the normal file classifier with the plan's Target Backend and optimization level. Serialize the resulting Package File Sets as arrays rather than exporting conditions for consumers to interpret.

2. **Publish backend-specific files**

   In `crates/moon/src/rr_build/mod.rs`, write metadata to `_build/<backend>/packages.json` and add one helper that writes the authoritative `_build/index.json`. Keep the backend field validation-friendly so consumers can reject an inventory whose contents do not match its index entry.

3. **Publish once at the command boundary**

   Update `moon check` and `moon bundle` so the per-backend planning path only writes its own inventory. The outer command publishes the complete backend set after all requested inventories are available. A single-backend or automatically selected invocation publishes a one-element index; `--target all` publishes `wasm`, `wasm-gc`, `js`, and `native` (LLVM remains explicit).

4. **Migrate consumers together**

   IDE, LSP, MoonIDE, and moondoc consumers should read `index.json`, load every indexed inventory, and include the backend in package/cache identity. Request routing chooses a backend first (explicit target, owning module preference, then the existing default policy) and only then chooses the Normal/Wbtest/Bbtest view.

   During toolchain skew, new consumers can fall back to the legacy `_build/packages.json` when `index.json` is absent. New Moon versions should stop presenting one arbitrarily selected backend at the legacy global path as if it described the whole workspace.

5. **Document and test the contract**

   Add the layout and publication rules to the MoonBuild architecture reference. Cover:

   - a workspace whose local modules prefer JS and Native;
   - explicit single-target and `--target all` checks/bundles;
   - backend-filtered source files and package closures;
   - standalone-file metadata names;
   - virtual implementations and checked transitive dependencies;
   - stale backend files omitted from a newer index;
   - planning/materialization failure preserving the previous index;
   - watch mode and dry-run behavior.

## Non-goals

- Changing command target-selection or build execution semantics.
- Adding backend-scoped dependency declarations.
- Combining several backends into one package/type environment.
- Eagerly deleting stale backend directories; the index defines visibility.

## Related issues

- #1667: unbuilt sibling virtual implementations can appear as usable metadata.
- #1680: artifact paths can point at missing outputs. Plan-scoped inventories remove unplanned entries; artifact-location correctness itself should remain tracked there.

## Checklist

- [x] I have added the proposed contract, implementation boundaries, migration path, and acceptance coverage.

title: Registry module names have inconsistent case semantics on case-insensitive filesystems
body:
Moon registry module names are treated as case-sensitive, but the registry index stores them directly as filesystem paths. The current index contains these entries:

- `user/xunyoyo/Permutation.index`
- `user/xunyoyo/permutation.index`
- `user/youyong5/MoonTetris.index`
- `user/youyong5/moontetris.index`

On a default case-insensitive macOS filesystem, a system Git clone reports that these paths collide, materializes only one path from each group, and leaves the checkout dirty:

```text
 M user/xunyoyo/Permutation.index
 M user/youyong5/MoonTetris.index
```

The username component is also stored directly as a path and permits uppercase letters, so its case semantics have the same inconsistency even though the current index does not contain two usernames differing only by case.

body:
Update: I have some new findings, but editing this post would break the historical context, so I will submit my new findings as a comment instead.

`moon ide doc "@async/fs"` returns only `unimplemented` when run outside a MoonBit module (no `moon.mod`). The package is fully functional when actually imported and used — it has `read_file`, `open`, `File::read_all`, and many other APIs.

This is misleading in `.mbtx` script scenarios, where users probe package availability with `moon ide doc` before writing imports.

I discovered this issue while observing the behavior of the pi-coding-aget. I originally planned to have the agent submit this issue itself, but the submitted issue structure lacked two labels, which might not comply with the repository’s workflow. Therefore, I closed #1914 as "no plan." I apologize for the confusion.

## Actual behavior

```bash
$ cd /tmp && moon ide doc "@async/fs"
package "moonbitlang/async/fs" // moonbitlang/async@0.19.1

pub let unimplemented : Unit
```

Same result for `@async/process`. No exported functions shown.

## Expected Behavior

Should list exported symbols: `read_file`, `open`, `File`, `CreateMode`, etc. — same as when `moon ide doc` is run inside a module that imports `moonbitlang/async/fs`.

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
cd $(mktemp -d)
moon ide doc "@async/fs"          # → only unimplemented
moon ide doc "@async/process"     # → only unimplemented

# Compare: these work correctly
moon ide doc "String"             # → full method list
moon ide doc "@json"              # → full symbol list
```

Every time, in any directory without `moon.mod`.

## Environment

Operating System: Linux (Arch)

```
moon 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)
moonc 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)
moonrun 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)
Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

title: Run tests and benchmarks affected by changed paths (`--related`)
body:
## Motivation

When changing or optimizing a local package, running only that package's own tests or benchmarks can miss regressions in downstream dependents. A repository-local affected-test selector would make it easier to validate behavior and performance across the packages that use the changed code.

This is inspired by Vitest's [related command](https://vitest.dev/guide/cli.html#vitest-related).

## Detailed Description

The proposed interface is:

```console
moon test --related PATH...
moon bench --related PATH...
```

The implementation in #1855 currently maps each ordinary source path to its owning local package, then selects that package and its reverse local package-dependency closure. It is deliberately package-graph based: precise same-package file or symbol dependencies would require additional compiler/build metadata.

Manifests are handled conservatively by selecting the corresponding module or workspace. Explicit `*_test.mbt` and `*_wbtest.mbt` inputs currently use the existing file-level test filter.

Before finalizing the implementation, we should agree on the user-facing contract:

1. Should `--related` be supported by both `moon test` and `moon bench`?
2. Which dependency edges define “related”? In particular, should link-time relationships such as virtual-package overrides participate alongside ordinary package imports?
3. When the input itself is a test file, should Moon run only that file, the owning package, or the reverse package closure?
4. Should paths outside local packages be ignored with a diagnostic or rejected as errors?
5. Which existing selectors should compose with `--related` (for example `--filter`, target selection, and package scoping)?

A future, more precise version could use compiler-provided file-to-file or symbol-to-file dependency information, but that is not required for the initial package-level behavior.

## Related Issues

- Implementation: #1855

- [x] I have added all necessary details to make it easy for the maintainers to understand my request.

title: `moon.work` lacks a way to exclude workspace members
body:
> Disclaimer: This issue was generated by AI. However, I have reviewed it carefully and believe it is better
  > written than what I would have produced myself, while accurately reflecting my intent.
 
**`moon.work` lacks a way to exclude workspace members, causing external path dependencies to participate in `moon fmt` / `moon test`**

## Description

We maintain a monorepo containing multiple MoonBit modules. The project also depends on a MoonBit module from another repository. At the moment, the external module can only be introduced through a relative path in `moon.work`:

```toml
members = [
  "module-a",
  "module-b",
  "module-c",
  "../external/shared-lib",
]
```

`../external/shared-lib` is an external dependency outside the current repository. It is needed for dependency resolution and builds, but it is not part of the current repository's source maintenance, formatting, or test scope.

However, once this external module is declared as a `moon.work` member, workspace-level commands also include it in operations such as `moon fmt` and `moon test`.

There currently seems to be no way to express the following requirement:

> Allow an external module to participate in dependency resolution and builds, without including it in the current workspace's batch formatting, checking, and testing commands.

## Actual behavior

Given the following `moon.work`:

```toml
members = [
  "module-a",
  "module-b",
  "../external/shared-lib",
]
```

Running:

```bash
moon fmt
moon test
```

processes all of the following modules:

```text
module-a
module-b
../external/shared-lib
```

As a result, changes to the external dependency's source code, tests, configuration, or compatibility can affect the current repository's formatting workflow, test results, and CI.

## Current workaround

The current workaround is to bypass workspace auto-discovery and manually enumerate the packages that should be processed:

```bash
moon -C module-a test . src/core src/model src/utils test cmd/tool --target native
moon -C module-a test . src/core src/model src/utils test cmd/tool --target js
moon -C module-a test . src/core src/model src/utils test cmd/tool --target wasm-gc

moon -C module-b test cmd/main src/api src/service src/support test_cases --target native
```

This approach has several problems:

- The commands are verbose and difficult to read.
- The same package list must be maintained repeatedly for different targets.
- Adding, moving, or removing a package requires updating build scripts manually.
- It is difficult to ensure that `fmt`, `check`, and `test` use the same package scope.
- The workspace's package auto-discovery cannot be used conveniently.
- Maintenance costs increase as the number of packages grows.

## Expected behavior

Moon should distinguish between the following two concepts:

1. External modules that participate in dependency resolution and builds.
2. Local modules that participate in batch commands for the current workspace.

Any of the following solutions would address the problem.

### Option 1: Support exclusions in `moon.work`

For example:

```toml
members = [
  "module-a",
  "module-b",
  "../external/shared-lib",
]

exclude = [
  "../external/shared-lib",
]
```

Alternatively, a member could have an explicit attribute:

```toml
members = [
  "module-a",
  "module-b",
  { path = "../external/shared-lib", workspace_commands = false },
]
```

The external module would still be available for dependency resolution and builds, but would not participate by default in:

```bash
moon fmt
moon check
moon test
moon info
```

If explicitly specified, the module could still be processed directly.

### Option 2: Provide `--exclude` for workspace commands

For example:

```bash
moon fmt --exclude ../external/shared-lib
moon check --exclude ../external/shared-lib
moon test --exclude ../external/shared-lib
```

Exclusion by module name or glob would also be useful:

```bash
moon test --exclude external/shared-lib
moon test --exclude "../external/*"
```

If the same exclusion applies to multiple commands, it would also be helpful to configure it in `moon.work` as a default, so that local scripts and CI do not need to repeat it.

### Option 3: Distinguish workspace members from external path dependencies

An external path dependency is not necessarily a member of the current workspace.

It would be useful to allow a module to reference a dependency outside the workspace without adding that dependency to `moon.work.members`. For example:

```toml
import {
  "example/shared-lib" {
    path = "../external/shared-lib"
  },
}
```

The external module could participate in dependency resolution and builds, but would not automatically be included in the current workspace's `fmt`, `check`, and `test` traversal.

This would also make ownership boundaries clearer:

- `moon.work.members` represents modules maintained by the current repository.
- A path dependency represents a locally available dependency maintained elsewhere.

### Option 4: Support Git dependencies

Another solution would be to allow dependencies to be fetched directly from Git, instead of requiring the repository to be checked out next to the current repository and added to `moon.work`.

For example:

```toml
import {
  "example/shared-lib" {
    git = "https://example.com/example/shared-lib.git"
    rev = "0123456789abcdef"
  },
}
```

Tag and branch references could also be supported:

```toml
import {
  "example/shared-lib" {
    git = "https://example.com/example/shared-lib.git"
    tag = "v1.2.3"
  },
}
```

```toml
import {
  "example/shared-lib" {
    git = "https://example.com/example/shared-lib.git"
    branch = "main"
  },
}
```

It would also be useful to support a subdirectory within a Git repository:

```toml
import {
  "example/shared-lib" {
    git = "https://example.com/example/monorepo.git"
    rev = "0123456789abcdef"
    subdir = "libs/shared-lib"
  },
}
```

Recommended reference types would include:

- `rev`: a fixed commit, suitable for reproducible builds;
- `tag`: a version tag;
- `branch`: useful during development, but less reproducible;
- `subdir`: a module located in a subdirectory of a Git repository.

With Git dependencies, the external module would not need to be added to the current project's `moon.work`, and therefore would not be traversed by the current workspace's `moon fmt` or `moon test` commands.

Git dependencies would also provide the following benefits for CI and collaborative development:

- No dependency on a particular local directory layout;
- No need for developers to prepare a neighboring checkout manually;
- The ability to pin a commit for reproducible builds;
- A clear distinction between current-repository source code and external dependencies;
- A better fit for cross-repository development than local path dependencies alone.

If Git dependencies cannot be supported in the short term, workspace member exclusions or an independent path-dependency syntax would still be very valuable.

## Relation to #1716

This issue is related to [#1716](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/issues/1716), but the focus is different.

Issue #1716 primarily discusses:

- Path dependencies being lost during the `rr_moon_mod` migration;
- The lack of a usable way to represent path dependencies in the new `moon.mod` format;
- External path dependencies not being preserved correctly during migration.

This issue focuses on the following additional problem:

- Even when an external module is introduced through `moon.work`, there is no way to exclude it from workspace-wide operations;
- A module needed for dependency resolution should not necessarily be treated as a module maintained by the current workspace;
- Moon lacks a convenient cross-repository dependency mechanism such as Git dependencies.

In short:

- #1716: How should external dependencies be represented and migrated correctly?
- This issue: How can external dependencies be prevented from affecting the current workspace's batch operations?

## Minimal reproduction

Directory structure:

```text
workspace/
├── moon.work
├── module-a/
│   └── moon.mod
├── module-b/
│   └── moon.mod
└── ../external/
    └── shared-lib/
        └── moon.mod
```

`moon.work`:

```toml
members = [
  "module-a",
  "module-b",
  "../external/shared-lib",
]
```

Run:

```bash
moon fmt
moon test
```

### Actual result

Moon processes both local modules and the external module:

```text
module-a
module-b
../external/shared-lib
```

### Expected result

Any of the following behaviors would be acceptable:

1. Allow `../external/shared-lib` to be marked as excluded in `moon.work`;
2. Allow it to be excluded from an individual command using `--exclude`;
3. Allow it to be declared as a path dependency without making it a workspace member;
4. Allow it to be fetched as a Git dependency without adding it to the current workspace.

## Use cases

This issue commonly occurs in the following situations:

- Several repositories share a local MoonBit module;
- One monorepo depends on a module from another monorepo;
- Git submodules or neighboring checkouts are used for local development;
- CI needs to build an external dependency but should not run all of its tests;
- An external dependency has not yet been published to a registry;
- A development version of a dependency needs to be tested temporarily;
- A private module cannot be published to a public registry.

## Summary

At present, `moon.work.members` appears to serve two different purposes:

1. Declaring the dependency-resolution scope;
2. Declaring the execution scope for workspace-wide commands.

For cross-repository dependencies, these scopes are not always the same.

It would be helpful if Moon provided at least one of the following:

- Workspace member exclusions;
- A `--exclude` option for `fmt`, `check`, and `test`;
- Path dependencies that do not become workspace members;
- Git dependencies supporting commits, tags, branches, and subdirectories.

This would avoid manually enumerating every local package in build scripts merely to exclude an external dependency.

moonc syncheck: support moon.work (currently rejected as unsupported input)
body:
## Summary

`moonc syncheck` accepts `.mbt`, `.mbt.md`, `moon.pkg`, and `moon.mod`, but **not `moon.work`**. Running it against a `moon.work` file fails outright rather than syntax-checking it:

```
$ moonc syncheck -error-format json moon.work
moon.work: unsupported input file type for syncheck; supported suffixes: .mbt, .mbt.md, moon.pkg, moon.mod
$ echo $?
2
```

`moon.work.json` is likewise rejected.

## Environment

```
$ moonc -v
moonc v0.10.3+0225ff0ff-nightly (2026-07-03)
```
(Feature flags: `rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg`)

## Why it matters

We use `moonc syncheck` as a standalone, project-less pre-write **syntax gate** for agent-authored edits — it validates candidate file content in a scratch file before it lands on disk, with no build lock or project context. It already covers `.mbt`, `.mbt.md`, `moon.mod`, and `moon.pkg`. `moon.work` is the one workspace file we cannot gate this way, so a malformed `moon.work` can be written unchecked.

## Request

Add `moon.work` (and, if applicable, its textual form) to the set of `moonc syncheck` inputs, parsing it with the same workspace-file grammar `moon` uses, and emitting the same JSON lex/parse diagnostics as the other kinds.

## Repro

```
printf 'members = [ "a",\n' > moon.work   # unterminated
moonc syncheck -error-format json moon.work
# expected: a lex/parse diagnostic; actual: "unsupported input file type"
```

title: moon install: reinstalling a native binary in place → macOS "Killed: 9" (SIGKILL) from stale code-signing cache
body:
## Summary

On macOS (arm64), running `moon install` **again** for a native `is-main` package — overwriting a binary that already exists in `~/.moon/bin` and has been executed before — produces a binary that the kernel **SIGKILLs at exec** (`Killed: 9`, exit 137, no output), *before* `main` runs. The on-disk code signature is still reported *valid*; the kill is the macOS code-signing/AMFI cache rejecting the in-place-replaced binary. A fresh install (or re-sign / fresh inode) runs fine.

This bit a user of a MoonBit CLI: after `moon install`, every invocation (`--help`, subcommands, etc.) was killed with no output.

## Environment

- `moon 0.1.20260624 (99b20c1 2026-06-24)`, `moonc v0.10.1+1f52b86e1-nightly`
- macOS 26.4.1 (build 25E253), Apple Silicon (arm64)
- Binary: `Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64`, `Signature=adhoc` / `flags=0x20002(adhoc,linker-signed)` (the normal state for a moon-built arm64 binary)

## Symptom

```
$ openseek --help          # (a moon-installed native is-main binary)
zsh: killed     openseek --help
$ echo $?
137                         # 128 + 9 = SIGKILL, and zero stdout/stderr
```

Every invocation is killed identically — the process never reaches `main` (hence no output), so it is not a bug in the program.

## Evidence that it's the code-signing cache, not the binary

```
# The on-disk signature is VALID, yet the binary is killed when run:
$ codesign -v --verbose=2 ~/.moon/bin/openseek
~/.moon/bin/openseek: valid on disk
~/.moon/bin/openseek: satisfies its Designated Requirement
$ ~/.moon/bin/openseek --help ; echo $?      # 137 (killed)

# Re-signing the SAME file in place fixes it immediately:
$ codesign -s - --force ~/.moon/bin/openseek
$ ~/.moon/bin/openseek --help ; echo $?      # 0, runs correctly

# A plain copy of the (killed) installed binary to a NEW path also runs fine
# after an ad-hoc re-sign — i.e. the bytes/logic are correct.
```

So the file is a correct, validly-signed binary; the kernel kills it only at the path it was reinstalled over.

## Root cause (analysis)

`moon install` appears to install by writing/overwriting the binary **in place** at `~/.moon/bin/<name>` (same vnode/inode). macOS caches a code-signing decision (CDHash) tied to the file; when a previously-executed binary is overwritten in place with **different content**, the cached hash no longer matches the new content and AMFI kills the process at exec (`SIGKILL`) rather than re-validating. This is a well-known macOS gotcha for tools that replace an executable in place (e.g. `cp` over a running/previously-run binary). It only reproduces when a binary already existed at that path *and had been run*; a first-time install is fine.

## Reproduction

1. `moon install` a native `is-main` package on macOS arm64; run the installed binary (works — caches the signature).
2. Change the source, rebuild, and `moon install` **again** (overwrites `~/.moon/bin/<name>` in place with different content).
3. Run the installed binary → `Killed: 9` / exit 137, no output.
4. `codesign -s - --force ~/.moon/bin/<name>` (or `rm` it before step 2) → runs again.

## Suggested fix

Make `moon install` not overwrite the executable in place. Any of:

- **Atomic install via rename**: write to a temp file in the same dir, then `rename(2)` over the destination (new inode ⇒ no stale cache). This is also crash-safe.
- **Re-sign after copy**: `codesign -s - --force <dest>` on macOS post-install (ad-hoc is fine; it refreshes the cached CDHash).
- At minimum, `unlink` the destination before writing the new file.

Atomic rename is the cleanest and also avoids partially-written binaries.

## Workaround (for users hitting this today)

```bash
codesign -s - --force ~/.moon/bin/<name>     # or:  rm ~/.moon/bin/<name> && moon install
```

title: moon check --output-json: emit machine-applicable fix suggestions for fixable diagnostics
body:
## Summary

`moon check --output-json` emits the location and message of a diagnostic, but for **fixable** diagnostics it carries neither the source text of the span nor a structured, machine-applicable fix. Tools (and LLM agents) that want to *apply* the fix therefore have to re-read the source just to reconstruct text the compiler already has.

## What `--output-json` gives today

```json
{
  "$message_type": "diagnostic",
  "level": "warning",
  "error_code": 20,
  "path": ".../argparse/help_render.mbt",
  "loc": "128:44-128:50",
  "message": "Warning (deprecated): `length` is deprecated, use `len` instead"
}
```

Source line 128 is:

```
  let parts = Array::new(capacity=cmd.args.length())
```

So the JSON knows precisely: at `128:44-128:50` the token `length` should become `len`. But a consumer that wants to apply that has:
- no source text of the span (must read the file to learn it’s `cmd.args.length()`), and
- no structured replacement — only the prose `use \`len\` instead`.

The column-based `loc` also isn’t directly usable by line/text-anchored editors.

## Why it matters

Migrating deprecations is a common, mechanical task. Driving it through an agent today, fixing ~264 `length` → `len` warnings across a tree, the agent spends **dozens of `read` round-trips** reconstructing exactly the text `moon` already computed — pure overhead. A tool/CI script wanting to auto-migrate has the same problem.

## Ask

1. **(Primary) Machine-applicable fix suggestions in `--output-json`.** For diagnostics with an obvious mechanical fix (deprecations, simple renames), include structured suggestions, e.g.:

   ```json
   "suggestions": [
     { "loc": "128:44-128:50", "replacement": "len", "applicability": "machine-applicable" }
   ]
   ```

   This mirrors rustc’s `--error-format=json` (`spans[].suggested_replacement` / `suggestion_applicability`) and Clang fix-its. It lets a thin tool — or `moon` itself — apply the fix directly, no source re-read, no model in the loop.

2. **(Fallback, also useful) Source snippet in the JSON.** Include the span’s source text (and/or the full line) so consumers can construct an edit without a separate read, even when a structured replacement isn’t available.

3. **(Bonus) `moon check --fix`** that applies machine-applicable suggestions in place — deprecation migrations become one command.

#1 is the high-leverage one: with applicability metadata, `moon` (and tooling) can auto-apply the safe ones and leave the rest to a human/agent.

title: moon doc drops labels from labelled enum constructor arguments
body: `moon doc` drops labels from labelled enum constructor arguments when generating documentation signatures. ## Actual behavior `moon info` preserves labelled enum constructor arguments in `pkg.generated.mbti`, but `moon doc` drops those labels in the generated documentation signature. Reproduction repository: https://github.com/shiguri-01/moon-doc-issues Source enum: ```moonbit ///| pub(all) enum Shape { Circle(radius~ : Double) Rect(width~ : Double, height~ : Double) RoundedRect(Double, Double, radius~ : Double) } derive(Debug, Eq) ``` `moon info` output preserves the labels: ```moonbit ///| pub(all) enum Shape { Circle(radius~ : Double) Rect(width~ : Double, height~ : Double) RoundedRect(Double, Double, radius~ : Double) } derive(Eq, @debug.Debug) ``` However, `moon doc` writes this to `_build/doc/shiguri-01/moon_doc_issues/package_data.json`: ```json "signature": "pub(all) enum Shape {\n Circle(Double)\n Rect(Double, Double)\n RoundedRect(Double, Double, Double)\n} derive(Eq, @moonbitlang/core/debug.Debug)" ``` So the generated documentation displays the constructors as positional arguments: ```moonbit pub(all) enum Shape { Circle(Double) Rect(Double, Double) RoundedRect(Double, Double, Double) } derive(...) ``` ## Expected Behavior The generated documentation signature should preserve labelled enum constructor arguments. For example: ```moonbit pub(all) enum Shape { Circle(radius~ : Double) Rect(width~ : Double, height~ : Double) RoundedRect(Double, Double, radius~ : Double) } derive(...) ``` This matters because labels are part of the public API information. For example, `Rect(Double, Double)` does not tell users which argument is `width` and which is `height`, especially when multiple fields have the same type. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Clone the reproduction repository: ```sh git clone https://github.com/shiguri-01/moon-doc-issues.git cd moon-doc-issues ``` 2. Enter the dev shell if using Nix: ```sh nix develop ``` 3. Run: ```sh moon info moon doc ``` 4. Compare: ```text pkg.generated.mbti _build/doc/shiguri-01/moon_doc_issues/package_data.json ``` The labels are present in `pkg.generated.mbti`, but missing from the `signature` field in `package_data.json`. This happens consistently in the reproduction repository. ## Environment Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS on WSL2 ```text moon 0.1.20260608 (60bc8c3 2026-06-08) /nix/store/wkfnkjx8ypvdnxcsdk6g0hpzmnj1fd7r-moonbit-toolchains-v0.10.0+e66899a54+60bc8c3/bin/moon moonc v0.10.0+e66899a54 (2026-06-09) /nix/store/iysq2hin8hr86gazbambycw42xy1d7gn-moonbit/bin/moonc moonrun 0.1.20260608 (60bc8c3 2026-06-08) /nix/store/iysq2hin8hr86gazbambycw42xy1d7gn-moonbit/bin/moonrun Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg ``` ## Checklist - [x] (Optional) My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: moon check: report `(no input files changed)` so repeated (and errored) runs are skippable — agent context hygiene
body:
## Motivation

Agentic / LLM tools run `moon check` after almost every edit. The scarce resource isn't compute — incremental check is fast — it's **context**: re-injecting an identical verdict after every action floods the model's context window with redundant, identical output. The agent wants to run check per action but **skip emitting the result when no input changed**.

## Key finding: success is cached, failure is not

Empirically (moon 0.1.20260618), the existing `no work to do` short-circuit only fires when the last check **succeeded**. On **errors**, every run re-checks and re-prints the full diagnostics — there is no "nothing changed" signal:

```
# a package with a type error, NO input change between the two runs:
$ moon check
  ... <full error> ...
  Failed with 0 warnings, 1 errors.
$ moon check                 # no input changed
  ... <full error AGAIN> ... # re-emitted in full, no "no work to do"
  Failed with 0 warnings, 1 errors.

# after fixing the error:
$ moon check
  Finished. moon: ran 2 tasks, now up to date
$ moon check                 # no input changed
  Finished. moon: no work to do   # success path DOES short-circuit
```

So context pollution is **worst exactly where the signal is missing**: while iterating on errors, repeated `moon check` dumps the same diagnostics into context every time, with no marker to skip on.

## The right primitive: input-stability, not "cached"

The signal the agent needs is **"did any input file change since the last check?"** — a pure input-fingerprint comparison. It is *outcome-independent*: available on the error path even though no artifact was cached. The logic:

> no input changed ⟹ compilation is deterministic ⟹ the verdict (incl. diagnostics) is provably identical ⟹ safe to skip.

That holds whether or not the result was cached — which is exactly why `cached` is the wrong word and `no input files changed` is the right one. moon already fingerprints inputs for the success path; it does **not** need to cache failure results to serve this — it only needs to report the input-change flag.

## Proposal

1. **Report input-stability on every run, on both paths**, alongside counts, e.g.:
   ```
   10 errors, 10 warnings (no input files changed)
   ```
   On success this generalizes today's `no work to do`; on the error path it is new (and the most valuable case). A tool gates skipping on the `(no input files changed)` marker.

2. **Machine-readable.** Extend `--output-json` with `inputs_changed: bool` and a `summary { errors, warnings }`, and emit JSON on the no-change / error paths too (today `--output-json` falls back to the human line when there is no work).

3. **(Optional, secondary optimization.)** moon could additionally cache failure diagnostics to *skip re-running* erroring packages on unchanged input — a speed win — but the context goal is fully met by the flag alone, even if moon recomputes.

4. **Naming.** A stats-only mode for just the counts line would pair well, but note `-q/--quiet` is already taken (suppress-all output), so it would need a new name (`--summary` / `--format=summary`).

## Environment

```
moon  0.1.20260618 (afb4494 2026-06-18)
moonc v0.10.1+d1acd7ec2-nightly (2026-06-18)
```

title: `moon.work` should reject or document `preferred_target`
body:
## Summary

`moon.work` accepts a top-level `preferred_target` field without warning or error. This is surprising if `preferred_target` is only intended for `moon.mod`.

If `preferred_target` is intentionally supported in `moon.work`, it should be documented. If it is not supported, the manifest parser should reject it as an unknown field so users do not accidentally introduce a hidden workspace-wide target default.

## Environment

```text
moon 0.1.20260608 (60bc8c3 2026-06-08)
Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

## Repro shape

Create a workspace manifest like this:

```toml
preferred_target = "native"

members = [
  ".",
  "./cmd/app",
]
```

Then run a normal workspace command, for example:

```sh
moon build
```

## Observed

Moon accepts the file without warning or parse error.

In local testing, this was easy to mistake for a supported workspace-level target default while refactoring a workspace with one native module and one JS module.

## Expected

One of these behaviors would be clearer:

- reject `preferred_target` in `moon.work` as an unknown/unsupported field, or
- document that `moon.work` supports `preferred_target`, including how it composes with member modules' own `preferred_target` values.

The current silent acceptance makes it hard to tell whether the field is valid, ignored, or accidentally affecting target selection.

title: `moon run` should use the selected package/module target in mixed-target workspaces
body:
## Summary

In a workspace with multiple local modules that have different `preferred_target` values, `moon run <package>` currently fails before using the selected package's owning module preference or the package's supported target set.

## Environment

```text
moon 0.1.20260608 (60bc8c3 2026-06-08)
Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

## Repro shape

Workspace layout:

```text
root/
  moon.mod                    # preferred_target = "native"
  moon.work                   # members = [".", "./cmd/app"]
  cmd/server/moon.pkg         # supported_targets = "native", is-main
  cmd/app/moon.mod            # preferred_target = "js"
  cmd/app/moon.pkg            # supported_targets = "js", is-main
```

Running the native-only server package without an explicit target:

```sh
moon run cmd/server
```

## Observed

```text
Warning: Multiple local modules specify different preferred targets; pass `--target` to choose one explicitly
Error: Package 'example/root/cmd/server' does not support target backend 'wasm-gc'. Supported backends: [native]
```

## Expected

`moon run` is package-scoped, so after resolving `cmd/server`, it should be able to choose either:

- the selected package's owning module `preferred_target` (`native` here), or
- the package's sole supported target (`native` here).

Only genuinely ambiguous runnable packages should require `--target`.

## Workaround

```sh
moon run --target native cmd/server
```

title: moon check --target native passes, but moon build --target native fails with GCC linker errors

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
## Actual behavior

```plaintext
/home/abc/.moon/lib/core/abort/abort.mbt:54:9: error: redefinition of '_M0FPC15abort5abortGuE'
/home/abc/.moon/lib/core/abort/abort.mbt:49:19: error: '_M0L3msgS1' undeclared (did you mean '_M0L3msgS2'?)
```

`moon check --target native` passes, but `moon build --target native` fails with GCC linker errors:

- core `abort()` functions are defined twice in the generated `main.c` (redefinition)
- additionally, some core symbols reference the old `internal/strconv` path which no longer generate correct C symbols (undeclared)

This blocks all native binary builds for projects that depend on `moonbitlang/async` (the first public package that pulls in a sufficient amount of core modules), but the bug itself is in the build system, not in `async`.

A companion minimal reproduction repository with a working CI pipeline that demonstrates the failure is available at:  
https://github.com/conglinyizhi/moonbit-bug-core-bundle

## Expected Behavior

`moon build --target native` should succeed, producing a native binary — the same way `moon check --target native` passes without errors.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a new MoonBit project with `moonbitlang/async@0.19.2` as a dependency
2. Run `moon check --target native` → passes
3. Run `moon build --target native` → fails

**Minimal reproduction (3 files):**

`moon.mod`  
```moon
name = "repro"
version = "0.1.0"
license = "Apache-2.0"
import {
  "moonbitlang/async@0.19.2",
}
```

`cmd/main/moon.pkg`  
```moon
import {
  "moonbitlang/async/http",
}
options(
  "is-main": true,
)
```

`cmd/main/main.mbt`  
```moon
fn main {
  println("hello")
}
```

Then run:

```bash
moon update
moon check --target native   # ✅ passes
moon build --target native   # ❌ fails
```

Also happens with any project that pulls in core modules beyond the bare minimum. No third-party package is actually required — `moonbitlang/async` just happens to be the simplest trigger.

## Root Cause (diagnosed)

The compiler generates a single `main.c` file (≈176K lines for this trivial project) that includes both:

1. Core source code from `~/.moon/lib/core/` (e.g., `abort.mbt`) compiled to C
2. The pre-compiled core bundle `libmoonbitrun.o` (produced by `moonc bundle-core`)

Both contain identical function definitions (`abort`, `panic_impl` and all their generic variants), causing redefinition errors at the GCC link stage.

Additionally, because both the old `core/internal/strconv` and new `core/strconv` paths coexist in `~/.moon/lib/core/`, the compiler generates two sets of C symbols (`_M0FPC28internal7strconv*` from the old path and `_M0FPC17strconv*` from the new path). The old-path symbols only have references but no definitions in `main.c`, so GCC reports them as undeclared.

`moon check` works because it operates at the Moon IR (type-checking) layer, which doesn't involve C compilation or linking.

## Environment

- **Operating System**: Linux x86_64 (Debian 12-based)
- **moon**: `0.1.20260608 (60bc8c3 2026-06-08)`
- **moonc**: `v0.10.0+e66899a54 (2026-06-09)`
- **Feature flags enabled**: `rr_moon_mod`, `rr_moon_pkg`

## Checklist

- [x] My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: moon check can repeatedly rebuild dev_build outputs after generated files become newer than check DB
body:
## Summary

We saw a report that `moon check --verbose` can repeatedly rebuild/rerun work even when there are no source changes. If true, `--verbose` should only affect logging and should not affect the up-to-date/cache decision.

I tried to reduce this locally and could not reproduce on the latest toolchain, so filing this as a suspected cache invalidation bug with the exact environment and attempts below.

## Environment

```text
moon 0.1.20260604 (156bb5e 2026-06-04)
Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

## Expected behavior

Repeated runs of `moon check --verbose` with no intervening source changes should behave like repeated `moon check` runs: the first run may do work, but the second run should report no work to do.

## Reported behavior

`moon check --verbose` was reported to always rebuild/rerun tasks. The case was noticed while working on a repository with a `moon.mod` rule that generates MoonBit sources from Markdown using a nested `moon run` command.

## Local reduction attempts

### Minimal `moon new` project

```sh
moon check
moon check
moon check --verbose
moon check --verbose
```

Observed:

```text
first plain check:   Finished. moon: ran 5 tasks, now up to date
second plain check:  Finished. moon: no work to do
first verbose check: Finished. moon: no work to do
second verbose check: Finished. moon: no work to do
```

### Clean `moonbitlang/openseek` worktree with generator rule

The project has a `moon.mod` rule shaped like:

```moonbit
rule(
  name: "md_to_mbt_string",
  command: "moon run --quiet --target native scripts/md_to_mbt_string -- \"$input\" \"$output\"",
)
```

Observed:

```text
first verbose check:  Finished. moon: ran 141 tasks, now up to date
second verbose check: Finished. moon: no work to do
```

I also tested changing the rule command to the non-quiet form:

```moonbit
command: "moon run scripts/md_to_mbt_string -- \"$input\" \"$output\""
```

Observed:

```text
first verbose check after rule edit:  Finished. moon: ran 5 tasks, now up to date
second verbose check after rule edit: Finished. moon: no work to do
plain check after that:                Finished. moon: no work to do
```

## Request

Could you confirm whether `--verbose` is intended to be completely excluded from task-cache/rebuild inputs? If there are known cases where verbose mode changes the command environment or task identity, it would be useful to document or fix those because users expect `--verbose` to be diagnostic-only.

I can add a smaller repro if I can capture a workspace where the repeated rebuild is still happening.

title: Windows: Cannot inject the standard library moonbitlang/core after fresh install (v0.1.20260522)
body:
# Bug Report: Windows - Cannot inject the standard library `moonbitlang/core`

## Summary
On Windows, MoonBit CLI v0.1.20260522 fails to load the standard library `moonbitlang/core` for any project, including freshly created ones via `moon new`. The error occurs across all build targets (js, wasm, wasm-gc, native).

## Version

```
moon 0.1.20260522 (84aa893 2026-05-22)
Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 (PowerShell / cmd)
- MoonBit installed via: `irm https://cli.moonbitlang.cn/install/powershell.ps1 | iex`

## Reproduction Steps

1. Fresh install MoonBit on Windows
2. Run `moon new test_project`
3. `cd test_project`
4. Run `moon build --target js` (or `moon test --target js`)

## Expected Behavior

Build/test should succeed using the built-in standard library.

## Actual Behavior

```
Error: failed to run build for target Js

Caused by:
    0: Failed to resolve the module dependency graph
    1: Cannot inject the standard library `moonbitlang/core`: Cannot load the core file
```

## Additional Context

- The standard library source **does exist** at `~/.moon/core/` (cloned from https://github.com/moonbitlang/core, `moon.mod` present)
- Also tried placing it at `~/.mooncakes/moonbitlang/core/` — same error
- Reinstalling the toolchain via the PowerShell script does **not** resolve the issue
- The `.moon/lib/` directory was temporarily deleted during reinstall; manually restoring `runtime_core.c` and other files from the ZIP distribution did not help
- All targets fail with the identical error message
- The `mooncake` CLI does not have an `install` subcommand to manually fetch core

## Suspected Cause

The `rr_moon_mod` / `rr_moon_pkg` feature flags may have changed the standard library discovery path on Windows, causing `moonc` to fail locating/injecting `moonbitlang/core`.

title: `moon fmt` emits invalid byte-escapes for non-ASCII `description`

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
`moon fmt` encodes non-ASCII chars in `description` as decimal byte escapes. An em-dash becomes `\226\128\148`. The TOML lexer then rejects the file `moon fmt` just wrote. This blocks the `moon.mod.json` → TOML migration for any project with non-ASCII text in `description`.

## Actual behavior

`description` with a U+2014 em-dash:

```json
"description": "Canopy — projectional editor"
```

is migrated to:

```toml
description = "Canopy \226\128\148 projectional editor"
```

Those escapes are the raw UTF-8 bytes of U+2014 (`0xE2 0x80 0x94`) in decimal. The lexer then rejects the file:

```
Error: Failed to calculate build plan
Caused by:
    1: failed to load `moon.mod`
    2: Lexing error at 711..806
```

I only verified U+2014, but the encoding path looks generic — Japanese, accented Latin, and emoji should all fail the same way.

## Expected Behavior

Emit non-ASCII chars as raw UTF-8. That's valid in TOML basic strings. If escapes are needed, the right form is `\uXXXX` for the Unicode codepoint. The current decimal byte-escapes target the raw UTF-8 bytes, which the lexer can't parse.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
mkdir repro && cd repro
moon work init
# Write a description including non-ASCII characters.
cat > moon.mod.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "test/proj",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Repro — non-ASCII description"
}
EOF
moon fmt        # produces \226\128\148 byte escapes
moon check      # lexing error on the migrated file
```

## Environment

Operating System: Linux (WSL2, kernel 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2)

```
moon 0.1.20260522 (84aa893 2026-05-22) ~/.moon/bin/moon
moonc v0.9.3+3d4544a9e (2026-05-22) ~/.moon/bin/moonc
moonrun 0.1.20260522 (84aa893 2026-05-22) ~/.moon/bin/moonrun

Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

title: `rr_moon_mod` migration drops path-deps with no opt-out

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
`moon 0.1.20260522` enables `rr_moon_mod`. `moon fmt` then rewrites `moon.mod.json` to TOML `moon.mod`. The rewrite drops the `path` field from every dep. The new `import {}` block has no path-dep syntax. `moon check` fails on the migrated file. I couldn't find an opt-out.

## Actual behavior

`moon fmt` rewrites:

```json
{ "deps": { "dowdiness/loom": { "path": "./loom/loom", "version": "0.1.0" } } }
```

to:

```
import { "dowdiness/loom", }
```

`moon check` then fails:

```
moon.mod only supports versioned registry dependencies in `import`, found `dowdiness/loom`
```

A versioned form (`"dowdiness/loom@0.1.0"`) only resolves if the target is also listed in `moon.work` `members`. The migration tool doesn't promote path-deps into `moon.work`. I also tried inline-table forms on `import {}` (`{ path = "..." }`, `path "..."`) and the lexer rejected all of them.

**Cross-repo path-deps have no fix.** My `loom/loom/moon.mod.json` reaches into canopy's `lib/` from inside a git submodule:

```json
"dowdiness/text_change": { "path": "../../lib/text-change" }
```

`moon.work` can't list a path owned by another repo's workspace, so workspace-promotion doesn't help.

**No opt-out.** None of these disabled `rr_moon_mod`:

```sh
moon -Z=!rr_moon_mod fmt          # Unknown feature
moon -Z=-rr_moon_mod fmt          # Unknown feature
MOON_UNSTABLE="" moon version --all       # still enabled
MOON_UNSTABLE="wasi_link" moon version --all   # still enabled
```

The CDN at `cli.moonbitlang.com/binaries/<version>/...` only serves `latest` and `nightly`. Every versioned URL I tried — `0.1.20260522`, `0.1.20260512`, `stable`, `bleeding` — returns HTTP 403. Pinning to the last working release is not an option.

## Expected Behavior

Add a TOML syntax for path-deps in `import`, e.g.

```
import {
  "dowdiness/loom@0.1.0" { path = "./loom/loom" },
}
```

The legacy `moon.mod.json` loader already understands path-deps. This unblocks both same-repo and cross-repo path-deps.

The migration tool should preserve `path` rather than drop it silently. Until the syntax lands, `rr_moon_mod` needs an opt-out. Default it to off, or expose a `--unstable-feature=no-rr_moon_mod` / `MOON_UNSTABLE` switch. Archiving older CDN builds would also unblock pinning as a temporary workaround.

## Steps to Reproduce

Triggers every time on any module with a path-dep:

```sh
mkdir repro && cd repro
moon work init
# Writing path-deps including moon.mod.json
cat > moon.mod.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "test/proj",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "deps": {
    "moonbitlang/x": { "path": "../x", "version": "0.4.0" }
  }
}
EOF
moon fmt        # drops the path field
moon check      # fails on the resulting import
```

## Environment

Operating System: Linux (WSL2, kernel 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2)

```
moon 0.1.20260522 (84aa893 2026-05-22) ~/.moon/bin/moon
moonc v0.9.3+3d4544a9e (2026-05-22) ~/.moon/bin/moonc
moonrun 0.1.20260522 (84aa893 2026-05-22) ~/.moon/bin/moonrun

Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg
```

title: Bug: internal tcc cannot find libtcc1.a or macOS SDK libraries on macOS when running native tests

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
## Actual behavior

On my macOS machine, `moon test` fails for a project whose preferred target is `native` because MoonBit's bundled `internal tcc` cannot find its own runtime library and the current macOS SDK libraries.

Initial failure from `moon test`:

```
tcc: error: library 'pthread' not found
tcc: error: library 'c' not found
Error: Failed to run the test: /Users/xxx/Desktop/xxxx/_build/native/debug/test/llm/llm.blackbox_test.rspfile
The test executable exited with exit status: 1
```

Directly invoking the bundled compiler also fails:

```
$ ~/.moon/bin/internal/tcc /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke.c -o /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke
tcc: error: library 'c' not found
tcc: error: library 'libtcc1.a' not found
```

I found that:

- MoonBit bundles `internal tcc` at `~/.moon/bin/internal/tcc`
- MoonBit also bundles `libtcc1.a` at `~/.moon/lib/libtcc1.a`
- But this `tcc` binary does not automatically pick up that library path
- Its default SDK search paths also do not match the current Xcode SDK layout on my machine

On this machine, the current SDK path is:

```
/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Platforms/MacOSX.platform/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX26.2.sdk
```

I was able to make `internal tcc` compile a minimal C program only after explicitly passing both a private library dir and the current SDK lib dir:

```
~/.moon/bin/internal/tcc \
  -B$HOME/.moon/lib \
  -L$(xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path)/usr/lib \
  /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke.c \
  -o /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke
```

So this looks like a path-discovery problem in the bundled `internal tcc` flow, not that the system actually lacks the libraries.

As a workaround, I configured the package to use system `clang` for native linking, and then `moon test` passed.

## Expected Behavior

On macOS, `moon test` with the `native` target should work out of the box when MoonBit uses its bundled `internal tcc`, without requiring users to manually patch SDK or `libtcc1.a` search paths.

At minimum, the bundled `internal tcc` should be able to locate:

- MoonBit's bundled `libtcc1.a`
- The active macOS SDK reported by `xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use macOS with full Xcode selected via `xcode-select -p`
2. Install MoonBit and verify version below
3. Create or use a MoonBit project with `preferred-target` set to `native`
4. Run `moon test`
5. Observe that the bundled `internal tcc` fails with missing `pthread`, `c`, or `libtcc1.a`

Minimal extra reproduction:

```
printf 'int main(){return 0;}\n' > /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke.c
~/.moon/bin/internal/tcc /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke.c -o /private/tmp/moonpi_tcc_smoke
```

## Environment

Operating System: macOS 15.7.7 (24G720), arm64

```
moon 0.1.20260512 (81d40e3 2026-05-12)

Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_pkg
```

Additional environment details:

```
$ xcode-select -p
/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer

$ xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path
/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Platforms/MacOSX.platform/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX26.2.sdk

$ uname -a
Darwin zhengliulideMacBook-Air.local 24.6.0 Darwin Kernel Version 24.6.0: Tue Apr 21 20:18:14 PDT 2026; root:xnu-11417.140.69.710.16~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T8103 arm64
```

title: `moon run -c <script>` should default to `--target native`
body:
## Summary

When using `moon run -c '<inline script>'`, the default target is `wasm-gc`.
For inline scripts this is almost always the wrong default — most packages
that someone would reach for in a one-liner (e.g. `moonbitlang/async` and
its subpackages, anything doing IO/FS/process) declare `supported_targets = "+native"`,
so the script fails to build with a confusing error.

I propose `moon run -c` default to `--target native`. Users who want a different
target can still pass `--target wasm-gc` explicitly.

## Repro

```bash
moon run -c "$(cat <<'INNER'
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
}

async fn main {
  @async.sleep(10)
  println("hi")
}
INNER
)"
```

Fails with:

```
Error: [4020]
... Package "async" not found in the loaded packages.
... Cannot use `async fn main`: package moonbitlang/async is not imported.
```

Adding `--target native` makes it succeed.

## Why this is the right default for `-c` specifically

- Inline scripts have no `moon.mod.json`, so they can't inherit `preferred-target`
  (issue #865) the way project-based `moon run` already does.
- Native is the most fully-supported target across the standard library and
  `moonbitlang/*` ecosystem packages — wasm-gc deliberately excludes IO-heavy APIs.
- The use case for `-c` is overwhelmingly "quick experiment / one-liner,"
  which biases toward "make the common dependencies work out of the box."
- Project-based `moon run` is unaffected — it still respects `preferred-target`
  from the manifest.

## Scope

This proposal is narrowly about `moon run -c <script>` and `moon run -` (stdin).
It does **not** propose changing the default for `moon run <package>`, `moon build`,
`moon test`, etc.

## Alternatives considered

- **Target directive inside the script** (e.g. `//! target: native`): more flexible
  but adds new syntax for a niche case.
- **Infer target from `supported_targets` of imported packages**: too magical,
  could behave unpredictably when packages disagree.

Compared to those, "default `-c` to native" is the smallest, most predictable change.

title: `packages.json` artifact paths can point to missing `.mi` files for supported targets
body:
## Problem

For some dependency packages, `moon check` writes an `artifact` path into `_build/packages.json` even though the referenced `.mi` file does not exist.

This violates the expected invariant:

> When the current backend is included in a package's `supported-targets`, the package's `artifact` path in `packages.json` should point to an existing `.mi` file.

The issue is reproducible with `moonbitlang/parser`.

## Reproduction

Use `moonbitlang/parser` and run a check target such as `wasm-gc`:

```sh
moon check --target wasm-gc
```

Then inspect `_build/packages.json`.

For `Yoorkin/ArgParser`, `packages.json` contains an entry similar to:

```json
{
  "root": "Yoorkin/ArgParser",
  "rel": "",
  "artifact": "_build/wasm-gc/debug/check/.mooncakes/Yoorkin/ArgParser/ArgParser.mi",
  "supported-targets": ["Wasm", "WasmGC", "Js", "Native", "LLVM"]
}
```

The current backend is `wasm-gc`, and `WasmGC` is included in `supported-targets`, so consumers of `packages.json` reasonably expect the `artifact` path to exist.

However, the file at the `artifact` path does not exist.

The actual generated artifact is under the dependency package's own build directory instead, for example:

```text
.mooncakes/moonbitlang/yacc/_build/js/release/build/.mooncakes/Yoorkin/ArgParser/ArgParser.mi
.mooncakes/moonbitlang/yacc/_build/js/release/build/.mooncakes/Yoorkin/ArgParser/ArgParser.core
```

This path is not the path recorded in the root project's `_build/packages.json`.

## Expected Behavior

If a package appears in `_build/packages.json` with:

- the current backend included in `supported-targets`, and
- an `artifact` field pointing to a `.mi` file,

then that `artifact` path should exist after `moon check --target <target>` succeeds.

Alternatively, if the package was not actually checked for the current target, `packages.json` should not expose a misleading `artifact` path for that package.

## Actual Behavior

`packages.json` records an `artifact` path under the root project's `_build/<target>/debug/check/...` directory, but the `.mi` is not there.

The `.mi` may have been generated elsewhere, such as inside a dependency module's own `.mooncakes/.../_build/...` directory, or it may not have been generated for the current root check at all.

## Impact

Any tool that consumes `packages.json` and follows the `artifact` path can fail or lose functionality, because the path may point to a missing `.mi`.

This affects more than documentation generation. Language services and other tooling that rely on `packages.json` to resolve package `.mi` artifacts can fail to load package information for affected packages.

In particular, LSP features for packages whose `.mi` paths are wrong or missing may not work correctly.

## Why This Is a Build System Issue

The problem is in the consistency of the build metadata emitted by the build system.

`packages.json` presents `artifact` as the path to the package's `.mi` artifact for the current build context. For packages whose current backend is supported, that path should either be valid or the package should not be represented as having a usable artifact in this build.

Consumers should not have to guess whether an `artifact` path is real, search unrelated dependency build directories, or special-case packages whose artifacts were generated outside the root project's `_build` tree.
