title: Technical Inquiry: Compiler-level verification and the AI-Native definition
body:
## The Hook (Context)
MoonBit presents a fast compiler/build-system stack focused on developer productivity and high-performance output, with a clear language and tooling ecosystem.

## The Challenge (Technical Wedge)
For AI-generated workflows, how are non-deterministic outputs constrained at compiler boundaries? In particular:
- At which phase are structural constraints applied before lowering and bundling?
- What AST/grammar checks reject invalid or unsafe generated edits deterministically?
- How is compiler trust maintained when generation occurs upstream of your native compiler pipeline?

## The Comparison (The Sley Standard)
In evaluating true AI-native architectures, we are using Sley (a self-hosted language with a native compiler that enforces safe change boundaries at the root syntax level) as the baseline. Since MoonBit is currently understood as a fast compiler/toolchain platform for generated codeflows, not yet evidenced as a full compiler-for-AI-native change boundaries in syntax itself, how is the AI-native label technically justified versus AI-friendly compiler tooling?

## The Call to Action
Please clarify whether MoonBit should be framed as an AI-native language system or a fast AI-friendly compiler/toolchain. If AI-native terminology remains, please document the boundary model for non-deterministic generation, including parser/AST checks that enforce safe change envelopes before compilation proceeds.

title: moondoc: crashes opening missing *.impl.mi for sibling implementation packages of a virtual package (js vs native)
body:
### Summary
When documenting a module that uses a **virtual package** with **two implementation packages** (e.g. browser `js` and `native`), `moondoc` fails with `Sys_error: No such file or directory` because it tries to open an `.impl.mi` file that was never produced for the **currently selected build target**.
`moon check` succeeds for each target, but the documentation step fails for **all** targets tried by the registry pipeline.
### Background (third-party library maintainer)
We maintain [`emadurandal/rhodonite_webgpu`](https://github.com/emadurandal/RhodoniteMBT) on [mooncakes.io](https://mooncakes.io). The module exposes WebGPU bindings with:
- A **virtual** package `…/webgpu_objects`
- Implementations under `…/webgpu_objects/js` (JS / browser) and `…/webgpu_objects/native` (`Milky2018/wgpu_mbt`, desktop)
This layout matches MoonBit’s documented virtual-package pattern and passes `moon check --target all` locally and in CI.
We wanted **mooncakes-hosted API docs** to build successfully for published versions. Today the package installs fine, but **“Documentation failed to generate”** appears on the registry because `moondoc` exits with an error (see logs below).
### Actual behavior
The mooncakes doc pipeline (simplified):
1. `moon update`
2. For each backend in order: `native` → `wasm-gc` → `wasm` → `js`:
   - `moon check --target <backend>` → **OK** (warnings only)
   - `moondoc . -packages-json ./_build/packages.json -o ./build` → **FAIL**
Representative failures:
**After `check --target native`, `doc (native)`:**
```
Fatal error: exception Sys_error("/source/_build/native/debug/check/webgpu_objects/js/js.impl.mi: No such file or directory")
```
**After `check --target js`, `doc (js)`:**
```
Fatal error: exception Sys_error("/source/_build/js/debug/check/webgpu_objects/native/native.impl.mi: No such file or directory")
```

So `moondoc` appears to iterate implementation packages listed in `packages.json` and unconditionally open each implementation’s `*.impl.mi`, even when that implementation was **not built** for the active target.
Locally we also observe `packages.json` listing an `artifact` path for `webgpu_objects/js` pointing at `…/js.impl.mi` while `os.path.exists(artifact)` is **false** after a **native-only** check—consistent with the registry error path.
### Expected behavior
One of (non-exclusive):
1. **`moondoc` should only process implementation packages / artifacts that actually exist** for the current `_build` layout and target (skip missing `*.impl.mi`, or filter using the same rules as the checker).
2. **`packages.json` should not reference `.impl.mi` paths for packages that were not built** for the selected backend.
3. Registry doc pipeline could run **`moondoc` only for a target where all listed implementation artifacts exist**, or document a supported pattern for virtual + multi-backend libs.
### Environment (from mooncakes log)
- `moon` 0.1.20260509  
- `moonc` v0.9.1+2ef9d1932-nightly (2026-05-09)  
- Feature flags: `rr_moon_pkg`  
- Project layout: single published module root `/source` (no workspace)
### Minimal reproduction idea
Any minimal module with:
- `webgpu_objects` (virtual, `has-default: false`)
- `webgpu_objects/js` (`implement`, `supported_targets = "js"`)
- `webgpu_objects/native` (`implement`, `supported_targets = "native"`)
Then:
```bash
moon check --target native
moondoc . -packages-json ./_build/packages.json -o ./build
```
Expected to reproduce missing js.impl.mi on native.

### Impact
Published packages remain installable, but hosted docs are broken, which hurts discovery and API reference for multi-backend libraries using virtual packages.
Thank you for considering a fix or documenting the intended workflow for this case.

title: Bug: incorrect minutes conversion in bench output
body:
## Description

`auto_select_unit` in `crates/moonbuild/src/benchmark.rs` uses `us / 6e10` to convert microseconds to minutes, but `6e10` µs = 60,000 seconds = 1,000 minutes. The correct divisor is `6e7` (60 × 1e6).

As a result, any benchmark duration that reaches the minutes branch displays a value 1000× too small.

Additionally, the seconds-to-minutes cutoff is at `1e9` µs (1,000 seconds). A cutoff of `6e7` µs (60 seconds) would be more natural — otherwise durations like 999 seconds display as `"999.00 s"` instead of minutes.

## Steps to reproduce

```rust
// current behavior
auto_select_unit(60_000_001.0) // expects "  1.00 min", actually returns " 60.00 s"
auto_select_unit(1_000_000_001.0) // returns "  0.02 min" (should be " 16.67 min")
```

## Expected behavior

```rust
auto_select_unit(60_000_001.0)    // "  1.00 min"
auto_select_unit(1_000_000_001.0) // " 16.67 min"
```

Found while working on #1588.

title: Support custom host imports in moonrun for wasm-gc testing.
body:
<!--
    NOTE

    While we appreciate all feature requests, please understand that not all
    requests can be accepted. Providing detailed information will help us better
    evaluate your suggestion.
-->

<!-- A brief summary of what you want to add. -->

## Motivation

When a MoonBit package uses wasm-gc host function imports (via fn name = "module" "function" syntax), moon test fails because moonrun only provides a hardcoded set of import namespaces. This affects not only the package itself but any downstream package that transitively depends on it.

  For example, a cryptographic random number generator needs Web Crypto API access:
```
  #external
  priv type JsUint8Array
  fn js_new_uint8array(len : Int) -> JsUint8Array = "crypto" "newUint8Array"
  fn js_get_random_values(buf : JsUint8Array) -> Unit = "crypto" "getRandomValues"
  fn js_read_byte(buf : JsUint8Array, idx : Int) -> Int = "crypto" "readByte"
```

  Running moon test (wasm-gc target) produces:
```
  TypeError: WebAssembly.Instance(): Import #2 "crypto": module is not an object or function
```

We're building https://github.com/moonbit-crypto/mb-crypto, a cryptographic library for MoonBit. Since MoonBit positions itself as a wasm-native language, shipping wasm-gc support is important. The library works correctly at runtime (the host provides imports when instantiating the WASM module), but the testing story is incomplete.

  Our current workaround is moon test --target wasm-gc --build-only followed by a custom Node.js test harness that instantiates the WASM module with the missing imports. This works, but adds friction for every downstream user.

## Detailed Description

Any of the following would solve this:

  1. Built-in crypto namespace in moonrun — similar to how __moonbit_rand_unstable is already provided, add crypto.getRandomValues backed by Node.js webcrypto. This is the most impactful since secure randomness is a fundamental primitive.
  2. User-provided import modules — allow specifying a JavaScript file in moon.pkg.json or via a CLI flag (e.g., moon test --target wasm-gc --imports host.mjs) that exports additional import namespaces for moonrun.
  3. Plugin system for moonrun — a moonrun.config.js or similar that lets packages declare their host import requirements.

  This is analogous to the situation Rust's getrandom crate faced with wasm32-unknown-unknown — the ecosystem eventually added the necessary support.

## Related Issues

 - https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/issues/356 (related but different — that's about conditional deps, this is about test runtime imports)

- [ x ] I have added all necessary details to make it easy for the maintainers to understand my request.

title: cc-link-flags from external dependency in .mooncakes not propagated to main package
body:
When an external dependency declares cc-link-flags in its moon.pkg,
the flags are not propagated to the consuming main package at link time.

## Reproduction

My project imports `mizchi/tui/io` which declares in its moon.pkg:

```
options(
  link: { "native": { "cc-link-flags": "src/io/tui_native.c" } },
)
```

My main package imports `mizchi/tui/io` (transitively).
`moon build --target native` fails with:

```
Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:
  "_tui_flush", "_tui_get_terminal_cols",

title: Windows native build fails because -lm is passed to MSVC linker when using clang.exe

labels.name: pending-triage

body:
<!-- A brief summary if possible -->

Windows native build fails when Moon selects clang.exe by default. The generated native link command contains -lm, which becomes m.lib under the MSVC linker. Setting MOON_CC=clang-cl works around the issue.

## Actual behavior

Running:

```powershell
moon build --target native -v
```

fails on Windows with:

```text
LINK : fatal error LNK1104: cannot open file 'm.lib'
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1104
```

The verbose command includes -lm when clang.exe is selected.

From investigation, the issue seems to be that on Windows Moon treats clang.exe as a gcc-like compiler and unconditionally appends -lm. In this environment clang.exe ultimately uses the MSVC linker, so -lm becomes a request for m.lib and the build fails.

This is not project-specific. I reproduced it in multiple MoonBit projects, including one under a pure ASCII path.

Workaround:

```powershell
$env:MOON_CC="clang-cl"
moon build --target native
```

With MOON_CC=clang-cl, the same project builds successfully.

## Expected Behavior

Native build on Windows should succeed without requiring MOON_CC to be overridden manually.

Moon should not append Unix-style -lm for Windows native builds when the actual toolchain path is MSVC-style.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use Windows with LLVM clang installed and Visual Studio / MSVC linker available.
2. In a MoonBit project, run:

```powershell
moon build --target native -v
```

3. Observe that the generated command includes -lm and fails with m.lib.
4. Then run:

```powershell
$env:MOON_CC="clang-cl"
moon build --target native
```

5. Observe that the build succeeds.

This happens reproducibly in my environment.

title: JS target: abort() in moonbitlang/core (StringView, Array) silently pulls ~5KB dead code into release builds
body:
## Summary

When MoonBit code is compiled to JS with `--release`, `abort()` calls pull in SourceLoc formatting code (SourceLocRepr, StringBuilder, StringView, Int.to_string — about 5KB minified) that bundlers like esbuild cannot tree-shake.

The problem is that **`moonbitlang/core` uses `abort()` internally** for bounds checking in `StringView`, `Array`, and `ArrayView`. Library authors who never write `abort()` themselves unknowingly inherit this overhead just by using standard string/array operations. There is no way to discover this from the MoonBit source — it only becomes visible by inspecting the compiled JS output.

## How we discovered this

In [mizchi/luna](https://github.com/mizchi/luna.mbt) (UI library), I track JS bundle sizes with esbuild tree-shaking. After a compiler upgrade, `signals-only` went from 5,915 to 11,175 bytes (+89%). Investigation showed the entire increase was SourceLoc/StringBuilder code pulled in by a single `abort()` in our dependency (`mizchi/signals`).

I replaced that `abort()` with `panic()` to fix our own code. However, if any code path in the package can reach an `abort()` — even indirectly through `moonbitlang/core`'s `StringView` bounds check or `Array` indexing — the entire SourceLoc/StringBuilder chain is included in the compiled output and cannot be tree-shaken away. This means that any package using standard string or array operations may silently carry this overhead without the author being aware of it.

## Dependency chain

```
User code
  → String.sub() / String.view()
    → StringView constructor (stringview.mbt:399)
      → abort("Invalid index for View")
        → SourceLocRepr.parse()     -- parses "file.mbt:42:5" string
        → StringBuilder             -- Logger trait impls (write_string, write_char, write_view, write_substring)
        → Int.to_string             -- formats line/column numbers
        → Compare impls             -- op_ge, op_le for Int
```

The same applies to:
- `Array` indexing → `abort("index out of bounds: ...")` (arraycore_js.mbt:251)
- `ArrayView` indexing → `abort("index out of bounds: ...")` (arrayview.mbt:135)

## Reproduction

https://github.com/mizchi/repro_abort_size

```bash
bash compare.sh
```

Two packages with identical logic, differing only in error handling:

```moonbit
// src/with_abort/lib.mbt — uses abort()
None => abort("unreachable")

// src/with_panic/lib.mbt — uses panic()
None => panic()
```

```
=== Minified (esbuild --bundle --minify) ===
  with_abort: 4,897 bytes (26 functions)
  with_panic:   136 bytes ( 2 functions)
  overhead:  +4,761 bytes
```

## Suggestion

For JS `--release` builds, consider compiling `abort(msg)` without the SourceLoc formatting machinery — for example, as `throw new Error(msg)` directly. The formatted source location (file:line:column) is valuable during development but adds significant dead weight to production bundles.

This would also benefit `moonbitlang/core` itself, since its bounds checks would no longer pull in StringBuilder/StringView/Int.to_string in release builds.

## Environment

- moon 0.1.20260309 (f21b520 2026-03-09)
- esbuild 0.25.x for tree-shaking measurement

title: moon build links non-main package as executable on native target (missing _main)
body:
### Summary
`moon build --verbose` on a library package can try to link a non-main package as an executable, then fail with missing `_main` on macOS arm64.

### Repro repository
https://github.com/moonbit-community/tonyfettes-raylib

Reproduced on:
- `origin/main` (`2ae71de`)
- local branch `fix/warnings` (`f9886ec`)

### Environment
- `moon 0.1.20260224 (2288f02 2026-02-24)`
- Feature flags: `rr_moon_pkg`
- macOS Darwin 25.0.0 (arm64)
- Apple clang 17.0.0

Full logs + env snapshot:
https://gist.github.com/bobzhang/82a0a6902f3be02488afd42d96d53d8e

### Steps to reproduce
```bash
git clone https://github.com/moonbit-community/tonyfettes-raylib.git
cd tonyfettes-raylib
git checkout 2ae71de
moon version
moon build --verbose
```

### Actual behavior
Build fails during link:
```text
failed: /usr/bin/cc -o .../_build/native/debug/build/internal/raylib/raylib.exe ...
Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:
  "_main", referenced from:
      <initial-undefines>
ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture arm64
```

`moon build --dry-run --verbose` shows:
```text
moonc link-core ... ./_build/native/debug/build/internal/raylib/raylib.core -main tonyfettes/raylib/internal/raylib -o ./_build/native/debug/build/internal/raylib/raylib.c ...
```
which appears to treat `tonyfettes/raylib/internal/raylib` as a main package.

### Expected behavior
For `moon build` on this library module, non-main packages should not be linked as executables requiring `main`, or should otherwise avoid generating a link step that expects `_main`.

### Additional note
On this same machine, `moon test --target native` succeeds (`Total tests: 81, passed: 81, failed: 0`), so toolchain/SDK setup appears generally OK.

1. Create a package with C stubs and a prebuild script that outputs link config
2. Run `moon test` or `moon build`
3. Observe linker error: missing library that should be provided by prebuild link config

## Expected behavior

Prebuild link config (link_flags, link_libs, link_search_paths) should be applied to:
1. The package's C stub compilation/linking (currently missing)
2. The package's final linking
3. Descendant packages (already works via propagate_link_config)

## Current workaround

Use legacy build system: `NEW_MOON=0 moon test`

## Root cause

In `crates/moonbuild-rupes-recta/src/build_plan/builders.rs`, the `propagate_link_config` function only iterates through dependency packages, not the target package itself. Additionally, `build_archive_or_link_c_stubs` does not apply prebuild link config to C stubs.

## Suggested fix

Apply prebuild link config directly to:
1. Target package's C stub link_flags in `build_archive_or_link_c_stubs`
2. Target package's own link config in `build_make_exec_link_core`

title: Split -C/--directory (chdir) from --source-dir; deprecate ancestor moon.mod.json discovery
body:
### Update (2026-02-02)
Final decision after discussion:

- Introduce `--cwd <DIR>` as the real chdir flag (top-level; must appear before the subcommand; applied early so external subcommands inherit it).
- Keep `-C/--directory <DIR>` temporarily with legacy meaning (project discovery only, no chdir); it is deprecated and warns.
- Keep `--source-dir <DIR>` temporarily with legacy meaning (project discovery only, no chdir); it was never exposed/documented, so it stays hidden from help and warns when used.
- Keep ancestor-walk project discovery (supported behavior; no planned breaking change to remove it).

Implementation: PR #1432.

---

### Background
Today `moon`'s common option `-C/--directory` is documented as “source code directory”, but it does **not** actually change the process working directory. Also, `--source-dir` is currently just an alias of `--directory`.

Internally, project discovery walks ancestors to find `moon.mod.json`, which makes invocations from subdirectories “work”, but can lead to surprising runtime CWD for `moon run`/`moon test` (e.g. tests that read `./data/...`).

### Decision
Adopt the conventional meaning of `-C` (make/ninja/cargo): **change to DIR before doing anything else**.

Separate “working directory” from “project root”:
- `-C, --directory <DIR>`: `chdir(DIR)` before any other work. Applies to all subcommands, including external subcommands (`moon-foo`).
- `--source-dir <DIR>`: directory used to locate `moon.mod.json` (project root). This does not change CWD.

### Rollout plan
#### Step 1: split flags + warnings (no breaking behavior yet)
- Split `--source-dir` from `-C/--directory` in clap (stop aliasing `--source-dir` to `--directory`).
- Implement `-C/--directory` as a real `std::env::set_current_dir` performed early (before subcommand dispatch), so external subcommands inherit the cwd.
- Keep the current ancestor-walk project discovery for now, but emit a warning when `moon.mod.json` is found in an ancestor directory rather than the selected `source-dir`/CWD.
  - Warning should clearly state that ancestor discovery will become an error in a future release and suggest using `-C <project-root>` or `--source-dir <project-root>`.
- Update docs/help snapshots accordingly.

#### Step 2: breaking change
- Remove ancestor-walk discovery. Require `moon.mod.json` to exist **exactly** in `--source-dir` (or in the current directory if `--source-dir` is not provided).
- Turn the Step 1 warning into a hard error with an actionable message.
- Update `PackageDirsError::NotInProject` message to match the new semantics.

### Implementation sketch
- `crates/moonutil/src/dirs.rs`
  - Refactor `SourceTargetDirs` to include both `directory` (for `-C/--directory`) and `source_dir` (for `--source-dir`).
  - Step 1: keep `find_ancestor_with_mod`, but warn when `project_root != start_dir`.
  - Step 2: remove `find_ancestor_with_mod` usage; require `start_dir/moon.mod.json`.
- `crates/moon/src/main.rs`
  - After parsing CLI flags and before dispatching any subcommand (including `External`), apply `set_current_dir` if `-C/--directory` is present.
- Tests/docs
  - Update `moon help` snapshots and any test cases using `--source-dir`.
  - Add/adjust coverage for the new warning (Step 1) and new error (Step 2).

### Acceptance criteria
- `moon -C <dir> <cmd>` behaves like `cd <dir> && moon <cmd>`.
- External subcommands inherit the cwd change.
- Step 1: running from a subdirectory still works but emits a single, clear warning.
- Step 2: running from a subdirectory errors with guidance.

title: refactor: extract test runner as a separate package
body:
Currently, the test runner is put together with the tests as if they were in the same package. The alternative solution is to compile the test runner in a separate package, whereas the test entries are treated as public functions exposed from the target packages. The current approach has pros and cons.

Cons:
1. The names used in the test driver must be mangled to avoid collision. This complicates the maintenance of the test driver template
2. This requires conditional handling of test driver templates to avoid depending on `moonbiltang/core/test` or `moonbitlang/core/bench` because the user may have not declared them
3. This requires specific handling of main packages (as #1212)

Pros:
1. This requires one less step of complication, because otherwise there's a new package to be compiled.

title: Improve moon add dependency conflict errors and batch dependency upgrades UX

labels.name: dependencies
labels.description: Pull requests that update a dependency file

body:
When using `moon add`, conflicts may arise during dependency resolution, and the error output is vague and doesn’t explain exactly what prevents resolution.

```
error: Multiple conflicting versions were found for module moonbitlang/async: [Version { major: 0, minor: 16, patch: 0 }, Version { major: 0, minor: 15, patch: 0 }]

// Don't know which modules are actually using moonbitlang/async
```

And, when multiple top-level modules depend on a shared dependency that has a breaking update, it’s currently not possible to easily upgrade both at once.

```
module a -> async@0.15.0
module b -> async @0.15.0
```

But, the current tooling forces users to manually remove and re-add modules one by one to resolve these issues, which is error-prone and cumbersome, and gives no insight into root causes.

```bash
// Currently, you must:
moon remove a
moon remove b
moon add a
moon add b
```

Therefore, please improve conflict error reporting so that it points to the exact source(s) of conflicts,
and provide a way to upgrade mutually-dependent packages in lockstep, to streamline dependency upgrades and debugging.

title: Add optimization level flags (`-Oz`, `-O1`, etc.) and refactor debug/release to profiles in moon build system

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Motivation
Currently, the moon build system uses `debug` and `release` options, which function as presets or profiles, each bundling a set of underlying flags. However, there is no granular control over optimization levels, such as those seen in other language toolchains (e.g., `-O0`, `-O1`, `-O2`, `-O3`, `-Os`, `-Oz` in C/C++, Rust, Swift, etc.). This limits power users and advanced build scenarios who want to tune builds for size, speed, or debugging fidelity. 

## Detailed Description
Investigate how other programming language compilers/build systems expose optimization control and profiles:

### Survey Summary
- **C/C++ (GCC/Clang):** Supports flags like `-O0` (none), `-O1`, `-O2`, `-O3` (increasing optimization), `-Os` (optimize for size), `-Oz` (aggressive size optimization), and `-Og` (debugging with some optimizations).
- **Rust (Cargo):** Profiles include `dev` and `release`, which compose flags like `opt-level` (0–3, `s`, `z`), `debug`, `lto`, etc., and allow further refinement in `Cargo.toml` ([profile.*] tables).
- **Swift (swiftc):** Similar optimization flags: `-O`, `-Ounchecked`, no optimization (debug), and profile concept via Xcode schemes.
- **Zig:** Uses build profiles (ReleaseSafe, ReleaseFast, ReleaseSmall, Debug), each mapped to underlying options, and also exposes individualized flags.

### Recommended Approach for Moon
1. Refactor `debug`/`release` as profiles, not exclusive build modes.
2. Introduce explicit optimization level flags (e.g., `-O0`, `-O1`, `-O2`, `-O3`, `-Os`, `-Oz`), mirroring conventions from C/Rust.
3. Allow users to compose their own profiles with sets of flags, possibly in a config file (akin to `[profile.*]` in Cargo).
4. Document how default profiles (`debug`, `release`) map to specific flag sets and how custom ones can be constructed. 
5. Ensure integration with current build graph and artifact naming logic. 
6. Update documentation and dev references. 

### Benefits
- Improved user control over build output (speed, size, debug info)
- More familiar developer experience for those from C/C++/Rust/Swift backgrounds
- Extensibility for future flags/profiles

## Related Issues
N/A (initial proposal)

<!-- A brief summary of what you want to add. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the problem or use case that this feature would address. Why is
this feature important to you or your team? -->

Want to reduce output binary size as much as possible to run on small embedded devices where memory is extremely limited, so smaller binary size means less memory used on keeping the program in-memory.

My current build target is `wasm`, as I'm trying to make games for https://fireflyzero.com/

I don't want to use `--nostd` as it removes too many essential features.

## Detailed Description

<!-- Provide a detailed description of the feature. Include any relevant
details, diagrams, or examples to help illustrate the feature. -->

In Rust you can set the panic handling method to just `abort` instead of `unwind`, which helps reduce binary size as it doesn't have to generate any abort-handling code: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/panic.html

https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/de28d1d1421bfda3668726d0870e42f1bc68b019/crates/moonutil/src/scan.rs#L827-L832

title: [Compiler Bug] Type system recursion problem?

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
Hey there! I think I found a bug in the compiler, but I'm unsure if I'm doing something wrong.

## Actual behavior

I'm trying to implement the `FingerTree` spec outlined here in this document:

https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/ralf.hinze/publications/FingerTrees.pdf

In order to reproduce the problem, you need to define a type with an indirect recursion like the following example, and then actually use it during a test via `moon test`.

```rs
pub enum FingerTree[T] {
  Empty
  Single(T)
  Deep(Node[T], FingerTree[Node[T]], Node[T])
}

pub fn [T] empty() -> FingerTree[T] {
  Empty
}

pub fn [T] FingerTree::is_empty(self : FingerTree[T]) -> Bool {
  self is Empty
}

test "check if empty" {
   assert_true(Empty.is_empty())
}
```

For type systems like Haskell, this sort of thing is pretty easy because the compiler is mature, but I bet that the recursion into the `FingerTree[Node[T]]` type is causing trouble. This is to say that it tries to work over the `FingerTree` type inside the recursive definition of `Deep`, and then tries to generate a type for `FingerTree[Node[T]]` which recurses into `FingerTree[Node[Node[T]]]`... etc.

Example console output is as follows, because it continues to hang and the linker is stuck in a loop.
```
[==================================------] 6/7 done, 1/1 running
link username/fingertree (inline test) (221s)
```


## Expected Behavior

I assume that `FingerTree[Node[T]]` is also the same as `FingerTree[T1]` where `T1` is `Node[T]` and since that function type already exists, it should continue and not try to unfold the recursive type.

## Steps to Reproduce

See above.

## Environment

Ubuntu linux, but this looks like a compiler type problem.

title: Single-file mode fails when module dependencies have package alias conflicts
body:
## Description

Single-file mode cannot properly handle module dependencies when the dependent module contains packages with conflicting implicit aliases. This prevents users from declaring any module dependency that might have alias conflicts, effectively breaking stdlib usage in single-file mode.

## Background
### Normal package mode:

1. Declare module-level dependency in moon.mod.json
2. In each package's moon.pkg.json, explicitly import specific packages with explicit aliases
3. Build system warns about alias conflicts at the package level

### Single-file mode:

1. Declare module-level dependency in front matter

title: Add --filter flag to moon test for glob-based test name filtering
body:
## Motivation

Running a single test by name from the CLI allows better debugging workflow and enables AI tools to narrow down test scope.

## Detailed Description

Add a `--filter` / `-F` flag to `moon test` that filters tests by name using glob pattern matching.

### Proposed CLI Interface

```
moon test [OPTIONS] [PATH]

Options:
  -p, --package <PACKAGE>    Run test in the specified package
  -f, --file <FILE>          Run test in the specified file
  -i, --index <INDEX>        Run only the index-th test
  -F, --filter <PATTERN>     Run tests matching the glob pattern (NEW)
```

### Usage Examples

```bash
# Run tests matching a glob pattern
moon test --filter "test_add*"        # matches tests starting with "test_add"
moon test --filter "*_error"          # matches tests ending with "_error"
moon test --filter "*parse*"          # matches tests containing "parse"

# Combine with package filter
moon test -p lib --filter "parse*"

# Combine with file filter  
moon test -p lib -f parser.mbt --filter "edge_case*"

# Combine with PATH
moon test src/lib --filter "add*"
```

### Design Notes

- Uses glob pattern matching (supports `*` and `?` wildcards)
- Single pattern only (no multiple `--filter` flags)
- Case-sensitive matching
- Works at runtime after test discovery, before execution
- Integrates with existing filter hierarchy: package → file → name

### Precedent in Other Tools

| Tool | Flag | Pattern Type |
|------|------|--------------|
| Go | `go test -run` | regex |
| Cargo | `cargo test <NAME>` | substring |
| Jest | `--testNamePattern` | regex |
| pytest | `-k` | expression |

title: Avoid stale-loop between pre-build file generation and moon fmt

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
## Actual behavior

In projects where pre-build steps generate source files that are also formatted by `moon fmt`, the two actions can conflict and cause each other to always see files as stale:

- The pre-build step generates files.
- `moon fmt` reformats those generated files.
- On the next run, the pre-build step sees the formatted files as stale compared to its own expected output and regenerates them.
- `moon fmt` then sees the regenerated files as stale again and reformats them.

As a result, both the generator and the formatter keep re-running instead of converging to a stable, up-to-date state.

## Expected Behavior

- Pre-build generated files and `moon fmt` should not continuously invalidate each other.
- The build graph should converge so that:
  - After the first successful run, subsequent runs do not keep re-running both the generator and `moon fmt` for the same files, or
  - Pre-build generated files that are not intended to be formatted are automatically skipped by `moon fmt`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use a project where a pre-build step generates files that are also picked up by `moon fmt`.
2. Run `moon fmt` (or a command that triggers both generation and formatting).
3. Run the same command again.
4. Observe that both generation and formatting keep running because each sees the other's output as stale.

## Environment

OS: Any

Related parent issue context: generated pre-build files should be skipped by `moon fmt` so that they do not fight with the generator.

title: Use windows-specific shlex on windows platform

labels.name: -Z rupes-recta
labels.description: Unstable: Related to the Rupes Recta build backend

body:
Currently, `moon` uses the *nix shlex on all platforms. This causes a problem on Windows platforms because:

- `shlex` (designed for POSIX shells) does not use the same algorithm of quoting as Windows ones.
- For `n2`, on unix platforms the command string is passed to `sh -c`, while on Windows it's passed **verbatim** to [`CreateProcessA`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessa). The different platforms use different rules to parse the string.

This means that our `shlex`-joined string will NOT work on Windows, and it will also cause issues when one wants to reparse it (e.g. for debugging).

## Solution

Use Windows-specific shell joiner & splitter. A splitter is available at https://github.com/chipsenkbeil/winsplit-rs, but no pacakges were found for joining shell yet.

Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments?view=msvc-170

title: Invalid module name is viewed as valid in case-insensitive FS
body:
In case-insensitive file systems, if a provided module name differs from the real one only by case, it is viewed as valid by the build system. However, later stages, such as downloading it from a registry, will fail because object storages like Amazon S3 are usually case-sensitive.

## Actual behavior

In the example below, the actual module name is `TheWaWaR/clap`.

```shell
$ moon add TheWawaR/clap
Downloading TheWawaR/clap
error: When installing packages

Caused by:
    HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://moonbitlang-mooncakes.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/user/TheWawaR%2Fclap%2F0.2.6.zip)
```

## Expected Behavior


```shell
# Successful download
$ moon add TheWaWaR/clap
Downloading TheWaWaR/clap

# Invalid module name report

Error: Cannot find `thewawar/clap`.

title: Change the way to use binary dependencies when building

labels.name: pending-triage
labels.description: This issue is not confirmed yet, and/or hasn't been checked for priority

body:
Binary dependencies currently are compiled on first install via a recursive call to `moon`, working directly in `.mooncakes` directory as a local package, and with their artifacts saved to `.mooncakes/<module_name>/<binary_name>`.

This behavior is pretty cursed, to say the least. A couple of obvious things to name:

- It builds the dependency as a local codebase via a recursive `moon` subprocess call. 
  - It will resolve the dependency's own dependency list, locally, which lives in `.mooncakes/<module_name>/.mooncakes`. This chain can go on forever.
  - It means that the dependency's build scripts will be executed locally, while in reality a package submitted to Mooncakes should be in the state *after* build scripts execution, so it won't need to be executed again in the user's machine.

- The build cache directory lives in `.mooncakes/<module_name>/target`, and the artifact also lives in `.mooncakes`. As a rule of thumb, a build system should prevent modifying data in local folders directly unless asked, even it's a local dependency cache, not to say saving artifacts in it.

- This builds the binary dependency eagerly, every time `moon install` or its in-process equivalents are triggered (so almost every time you run a `moon` subcommand). This might be time-consuming.

## Suggestion

1. Move build cache to `./target`, out of `.mooncakes`.
2. Move build artifact to `./target`, out of `.mooncakes`.
3. If possible, postpone and/or make it incremental. Don't spawn a new `moon` every time you use some subcommand. Change usage to the built binary so that it can be incrementally requested.

title: Add folder lock to `moon install` writing to `.mooncakes`
body:
Reported by @peter-jerry-ye.

During concurrent `moon install` (or install operations when running other `moon` commands), multiple threads/process will try to download and populate `.mooncakes` at once. This will cause a race condition on file system, potentially breaking the folder.

Adding a lock will solve most of the problem, provided that the user doesn't spawn two `moon`s with different package resolving results. Even then, the error should be transient for the one spawned with the stale config.

title: Avoid polluting test results with minor snapshot differences

labels.name: -Z rupes-recta
labels.description: Unstable: Related to the Rupes Recta build backend

labels.name: area/misc
labels.description: Area: Misc, not fitting anything else

body:
Related: #802 (About Rupes Recta)

## The issue

Rupes recta is reaching almost feature parity. However, of the total 288 test cases of `moon`, we still have 96 (at the time of writing) tests that still haven't passed.

Many of these tests are due to minor implementation differences that will not affect the end user, such as two equally valid topo sorting in commands, changes in output messages, etc. These minor differences are being picked up by the *extensive* usage of snapshot tests in the existing tests of the legacy system, and pollutes the output and hides the actual behavior differences.

We need a way to avoid such pollution.


## The solution

I guess we need to do one of these:

- Refactor and fix Rupes Recta to be line-for-line equivalent to the legacy system. This is hard, and only postpones the problem instead of solving it.

- Refactor the tests to focus on the properties of the builds, instead of snapshotting the output (mostly the build graph) and require byte-for-byte equality. This is a large amount of very dirty work, essentially a Pro Max version of the previous test-moving refactor (https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/pull/750).

title: Support OS configs for `moon`
body:
# Feature Request

A partial temporary solution to #972.

## Summary

Add conditional compilation config based on current (running) OS, to and only to the conditional compilation section of `moon.pkg.json`. Will not add them to `#cfg(...)` conditions in code and `moonc`.

## Motivation

Many native MoonBit packages will need to conditional compile based on the current OS. We are not implementing in in-language `#cfg` attributes because we need some more time to handle. At the meantime, to fulfill these packages' requirements, we will be providing these OS-checks as a basic, file-level conditional compilation.

## Detailed Description

The conditional compilation section (`targets`) in `moon.pkg.json` will be added with three directives, `windows`, `macos` and `linux`. These directives become true when the target OS equals the given system.

The target OS is currently defined the OS the build system is currently running on, if the target backend is native (C and LLVM). If the target backend is non-native (WASM, WASM-GC and JS), the target OS should be unknown/none. Cross compilation and overridding is explicitly a future concern and not handled here.

No changes should be done to the commandline options to `moonc`.

## Related Issues

#972.

## Checklist

- [ ] I have added all necessary details to make it easy for the maintainers to understand my request.

cc @Yoorkin

title: `n2` process spawn behavior different in windows and *nix
body:
In Windows it spawns subprocesses using `CreateProcessA`, which does not perform variable replacement.

https://github.com/moonbitlang/n2/blob/1334a10500fd6670115e59f91df31ac902390871/src/process_win.rs#L207-L218

In Unix-like systems it spawns subprocesses using `sh -c`, which supports all `sh` quirks and variable replacements.

https://github.com/moonbitlang/n2/blob/1334a10500fd6670115e59f91df31ac902390871/src/process_posix.rs#L183-L192

This makes it a platform-specific behavior.

This is a `n2` implementation issue, which uses a string to represent the commandline being executed. I suggest that we remove the `sh -c` behavior altogether.

# Bug Report

Follows https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonbit-overlay/pull/4#issuecomment-3194173787

## Environment

Latest moonbit toolchain from moonbit-community/moonbit-overlay

### OS

Operating System: NixOS (GNU/Linux)

### MoonBit CLI Tools Version

```
moon 0.1.20250801 (edae1ae 2025-08-01) /nix/store/1zkmgf3xd2r4pig7h0l0dwk3197l8dvw-moonbit-cli-v0.6.24+012953835/bin/moon
moonc v0.6.24+012953835 /nix/store/1zkmgf3xd2r4pig7h0l0dwk3197l8dvw-moonbit-cli-v0.6.24+012953835/bin/moonc
moonrun 0.1.20250801 (edae1ae 2025-08-01) /nix/store/1zkmgf3xd2r4pig7h0l0dwk3197l8dvw-moonbit-cli-v0.6.24+012953835/bin/moonrun
```

## Steps to Reproduce

Simply `nix run github:jetjinser/moonbit-overlay#moon -- update` and fail in seconds.

## Expected Behavior

`moon update` should write registry into a writable directory.

## Actual Behavior

First clean existing moon registry, e.g. `rm -rf ~/.moon/registry`.

```
nix run github:jetjinser/moonbit-overlay#moon -- update
error: update failed

Caused by:
    0: failed to clone registry index
    1: non-zero exit code: exit status: 128
```

## Detailed Description

After investigating moon implementation, it seems that `moon` tries to find *everything* (libraries, registry index, etc.) under `MOON_HOME`, but the current approach set `MOON_HOME` to the core library path, which is inside the read-only Nix store.

(See directory structure of toolchain provided by moonbit-overlay at https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonbit-overlay/pull/4#issuecomment-3194173646.)

This assumption is not suitable for packaging:
- Core components, such as core libraries, are invariable, and can be bundled with `moon`, `moonc`, `moonrun` in most cases.
- Other components, such as registry index, are runtime-variable. This should be put aside with core components.

So the case is that, `moon` should provide separate path configurations for different usages.

cc @jetjinser

## Checklist
- [x] (Optional) My case is minimal enough to be reproducible.

title: Enhance the `.mbt.md` file's front matter `deps` config
body:
# Feature Request

## Summary

This feature request includes two enhancement in different case:

1. Extend `.mbt.md` file's front matter config `deps` target to local Moonbit module as its dependency.
2. [optional] Allow a `.mbt.md` file refer other `.mbt.md` files (aliasing as its context, like virtual package).

## Motivation

1. Simplify the workaround for markdown test mode, make the `moon test` for `.mbt.md` file works offline.
2. make `.mbt.md` file more flexible on distribution.

<!-- Describe the problem or use case that this feature would address. Why is this feature important to you or your team? -->

## Detailed Description


`.mbt.md` file can run (test) by `moon test` command, which convenience for simple demo and POC. Although the `deps` can be config in Markdown front matter area, it can only refer to the module already published on `mooncakes.io` using module's name and version number, while the `moon.mod.json` can config local Moonbit module as package dependency using a `path` field.

#### case-1: extend deps config

we can extend deps config in this way:
```yaml
moonbit:
    deps:
        moon/bit: 1.0
        moon/bot: {path: ../bot} # <- local deps
```
Since most related code have been implemented, this enhancement would not take a hard work on it.

#### case-2: markdown file as 'virtual package'

First, aliasing each markdown file as a single package:

```yaml
moonbit:
    libs:
        foo: ./foo/export.mbt.md  # local file
        foo.bar: https://example.com/b.mbt.md  # remote file
```

then we can use these package in `.mbt.md` files' Moonbit code blocks:
```mbt
let b = @foo.echo("ok")
```

This enhancement is very different compare to case 1, which need a lot of works on dependency check. Both two case can take a better experience on doc-oriented programming.

# Feature Request

## Summary

Provide a pure subset of MoonBuild that relies on external providers for file I/O, does not perform the building themselves, and can then be compiled to `no_std` WebAssembly for embedding in e.g. browsers.

## Motivation

Currently, MoonBuild requires a native environment to scan files, access timestamps, and spawn subprocesses. However, it doesn't always need to be so heavy. In fact, the part of the build system that generates the build graph can be a **pure function**, if the external file I/O can be extracted and viewed as an immutable input.

If such part is extracted, we can completely separate generating a build graph from actually running the build graph. It would be useful to use the stripped-down version in internal testing, in-browser IDEs and other useful scenarios.

## Related Issues

title: Race condition during `moon test --enable-coverage`
Race condition when building different targets in parallel
body:
https://github.com/moonbitlang/moonlex/actions/runs/16162212422

When building for multiple targets, the build processes run in parallel. However, there are subroutines that access files in the same directory (`.mooncakes`) instead of non-overlapping ones like during build. This causes a race condition when multiple threads are modifying files at once.

https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/62a0c33657eaa33a5f86a7a4ce300c0910d9aea0/crates/moon/src/cli/build.rs#L94-L119

To fix the issue, we will remove all parallel build parts. Each build will use the full number of cores to spawn tasks, so running them in parallel poses no real advantage for a large enoguh project.

title: normal package's diagnostics and its whitebox test package's diagnostics should first be unioned then publish

a.mbt
a_wbtest.mbt

when we do `moon check`, there will be two checks:

```
moonc check a.mbt
moonc check a.mbt a_wbtest.mbt
```

Currently those two check's diagnostics are published independently, we wish that those two sets of diagnostics are first be unioned then published

body:
Dear all,

The MoonBit team is planning a couple of large refactors around the inner workings of MoonBuild (`moon`) during the next few months.

In order to keep the refactoring process smooth and focused, we will be partially freezing the current behavior and feature set of MoonBuild until the refactor is mostly done. This means we will temporarily pause merging pull requests that introduce new features or behavioral changes to core components.

You may find more information in the tracking issue in #802.

### What is frozen

During this period, contributions for the following areas will be (mostly) put on hold:

- Build system core, including how programs are built, and what files are used/generated during the process.
- The main build pipeline around the following top-level commands, including data schema:
  - `moon build`
  - `moon check`
  - `moon run`
  - `moon test`

Notes about contribution:

- Related issues and pull requests will be kept open. We will review them once the new design is finalized, to see whether they can be incorporated into the new design. Your contributions are valued and will not be lost!
- You may still see the core team merging features or interface changes into these "frozen" areas. This will primarily be for the refactor itself, but may occasionally include other urgent updates due to internal requirements.

### What is *not* frozen

We still welcome and encourage contributions in these areas:

- **Bugfixes**, especially those that affect the correctness of the build system.
- **New features** that are not related to the frozen area, e.g. `moonrun`, `moon doc`, `moon coverage`.
- **Documentation improvements.**

### Timeframe

**Current schedule: **From 2025-07-07 to 2025-10-01**, spanning three months.**

Please treat these dates as our current best estimate. The refactoring work is complex, and the timeline may be extended if we encounter unforeseen challenges, or shortened if progress is faster than anticipated. We will post all updates on the schedule and scope in this issue.

Thank you for your understanding and cooperation!

body:
**current output**

```
Generate shell completion for bash/elvish/fish/pwsh/zsh to stdout

Usage: moon shell-completion [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --shell <SHELL>  The shell to generate completion for [default: bash] [possible values: bash, elvish, fish, powershell, zsh]
  -h, --help           Print help

Common Options:
  -C, --directory <SOURCE_DIR>   The source code directory. Defaults to the current directory
      --target-dir <TARGET_DIR>  The target directory. Defaults to `source_dir/target`
  -q, --quiet                    Suppress output
  -v, --verbose                  Increase verbosity
      --trace                    Trace the execution of the program
      --dry-run                  Do not actually run the command
      --build-graph              Generate build graph


Discussion:
    Enable tab completion for Bash, Elvish, Fish, Zsh, or PowerShell
    The script is output on `stdout`, allowing one to re-direct the
    output to the file of their choosing. Where you place the file
    will depend on which shell, and which operating system you are
    using. Your particular configuration may also determine where
    these scripts need to be placed.

    The completion scripts won't update itself, so you may need to
    periodically run this command to get the latest completions.
    Or you may put `eval "$(moon shell-completion --shell <SHELL>)"`
    in your shell's rc file to always load newest completions on startup.
    Although it's considered not as efficient as having the completions
    script installed.

    Here are some common set ups for the three supported shells under
    Unix and similar operating systems (such as GNU/Linux).

    Bash:

    Completion files are commonly stored in `/etc/bash_completion.d/` for
    system-wide commands, but can be stored in
    `~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions` for user-specific commands.
    Run the command:

        $ mkdir -p ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions
        $ moon shell-completion --shell bash >> ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/moon

    This installs the completion script. You may have to log out and
    log back in to your shell session for the changes to take effect.

    Bash (macOS/Homebrew):

    Homebrew stores bash completion files within the Homebrew directory.
    With the `bash-completion` brew formula installed, run the command:

        $ mkdir -p $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d
        $ moon shell-completion --shell bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/moon.bash-completion

    Fish:

    Fish completion files are commonly stored in
    `$HOME/.config/fish/completions`. Run the command:

        $ mkdir -p ~/.config/fish/completions
        $ moon shell-completion --shell fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/moon.fish

    This installs the completion script. You may have to log out and
    log back in to your shell session for the changes to take effect.

    Elvish:

    Elvish completions are commonly stored in a single `completers` module.
    A typical module search path is `~/.config/elvish/lib`, and
    running the command:

        $ moon shell-completion --shell elvish >> ~/.config/elvish/lib/completers.elv
    
    will install the completions script. Note that use `>>` (append) 
    instead of `>` (overwrite) to prevent overwriting the existing completions 
    for other commands. Then prepend your rc.elv with:

        `use completers`
    
    to load the `completers` module and enable completions.

    Zsh:

    ZSH completions are commonly stored in any directory listed in
    your `$fpath` variable. To use these completions, you must either
    add the generated script to one of those directories, or add your
    own to this list.

    Adding a custom directory is often the safest bet if you are
    unsure of which directory to use. First create the directory; for
    this example we'll create a hidden directory inside our `$HOME`
    directory:

        $ mkdir ~/.zfunc

    Then add the following lines to your `.zshrc` just before
    `compinit`:

        fpath+=~/.zfunc

    Now you can install the completions script using the following
    command:

        $ moon shell-completion --shell zsh > ~/.zfunc/_moon

    You must then open a new zsh session, or simply run

        $ . ~/.zshrc

    for the new completions to take effect.

    Custom locations:

    Alternatively, you could save these files to the place of your
    choosing, such as a custom directory inside your $HOME. Doing so
    will require you to add the proper directives, such as `source`ing
    inside your login script. Consult your shells documentation for
    how to add such directives.

    PowerShell:

    The powershell completion scripts require PowerShell v5.0+ (which
    comes with Windows 10, but can be downloaded separately for windows 7
    or 8.1).

    First, check if a profile has already been set

        PS C:\> Test-Path $profile

    If the above command returns `False` run the following

        PS C:\> New-Item -path $profile -type file -force

    Now open the file provided by `$profile` (if you used the
    `New-Item` command it will be
    `${env:USERPROFILE}\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1`

    Next, we either save the completions file into our profile, or
    into a separate file and source it inside our profile. To save the
    completions into our profile simply use

        PS C:\> moon shell-completion --shell powershell >>
        ${env:USERPROFILE}\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1

    This discussion is taken from `rustup completions` command with some changes.

```

title: Phantom "`moonc` can't read JSON" bug caused by repeated writing to a build file
body:
# Background

Occasionally a bug like this will pop up in the CI:

```
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.

A bug report containing the error description and relevant code would be
greatly appreciated. You can submit the bug report here:

  https://github.com/moonbitlang/moonbit-docs/issues/new?template=ice.md

Error: parse_patch: json is not a map

Compiler args: moonc gen-test-info -json /home/rynco/Projects/core/result/panic_test.mbt /home/rynco/Projects/core/result/result_test.mbt -patch-file /home/rynco/Projects/core/target/wasm-gc/debug/test/result/__moonbit_internal_md_test.json

moonc version: v0.1.20250528+9637a5d8a
error: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0
```

`moonc` reads a patch JSON file, which happens to be empty. This file is written during package `scan`ning, which is way before `moonc` is invoked during build, so it shouldn't be the files not synced.

# Findings

The following is a debug log captured by `strace`, when trying to trigger the bug from building https://github.com/moonbitlang/core: [11.txt.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/20516184/11.txt.gz)

From the trace file, we can find that `/result/__moonbit_internal_md_test.json` **has been read once, but written ~90 times**, which is not normal. The file should have been only written once in the main process, and read once by `moonc`. We can find these reads and writes:

```
# line 1909, by main `moon` process (1208708)
1208708 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rynco/Projects/core/target/wasm-gc/debug/test/result/__moonbit_internal_md_test.json", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_CLOEXEC, 0666) = 6

# line 134607, by `moonc` (1208957)
1208957 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rynco/Projects/core/target/wasm-gc/debug/test/result/__moonbit_internal_md_test.json", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC <unfinished ...>
```

Where do the 90 other reads come from?

Take the read at line 130340 as an example:

```
# line 130340
1208934 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rynco/Projects/core/target/wasm-gc/debug/test/result/__moonbit_internal_md_test.json", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_CLOEXEC, 0666 <unfinished ...>
```

This read is initiated by process 1208924, which, if we search for it...

```
# line 118998
1208934 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/dev/null", O_RDONLY <unfinished ...>
1208922 <... openat resumed>)           = 5
1208934 <... openat resumed>)           = 0
1208934 execve("/bin/sh", ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/home/rynco/.moon/bin/moon gener"...], 0x7fffd5a577f8 /* 93 vars */ <unfinished ...>
```

...is an invocation of `moon gener...` something. Searching the codebase gives `moon generate-test-driver`.

And indeed, `moon generate-test-driver` invokes `scan`, which writes the file:

https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/daaecb68406d3a829666dc7938ece4f053673c93/crates/moon/src/cli/generate_test_driver.rs#L245

And that's exactly why the file has 90+ writes instead of one, since each `moon generate-test-driver` invoke writes once to the file. And if unfortunate enough `moonc` will read the dirty file truncated but not yet written.

# Summary

So the issue is clear: `moon generate-test-driver`, invoked as a subprocess in `n2` build graph, writes to the file `moonc` is reading when building its module graph. The file truncation happens before `moonc`'s read and writing of the file happens after it, causing `moonc` to read a blank file.

# Fix

- Don't generate any files during `scan`, but only once during actual build graph generation.
- We might want to reduce repetitive module graph generation during `n2` building. Or consider removing `n2` altogether to keep things in once process.

title: Support `pull` mode in `moonyacc` integration
body:
Currently, `moonyacc` supports two input modes of the generated parser. The default one is `array`, but one can enable the `pull` mode by supplementing `--input-mode pull` as a command-line option.

Recently, `moon` supported `moonlex` and `moonyacc` integration by adding user invisible prebuild rules for `.mbx` and `.mby` files. However, it seems conflict with the user-defined prebuild rules. Below is the error message generated when executing `RUST_BACKTRACE=full moon check`:

```
thread 'main' panicked at crates/moonbuild/src/pre_build.rs:147:40:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: pre-build:0: "<project dir>/src/parser/lexer.mbt" is already an output at pre-build:0
```

I tried to remove my own prebuild rules, but it seems that I have no way to enable `pull` mode. As a workaround, I have to change the extension from `.mby` back to `.mbty`.

I would suggest allowing users to customise `moonlex`/`moonyacc` parameters in the automatically generated prebuild rules, or simply allowing users to override the generated rules for `.mbx` and `.mby` files.

title: get `argv` behavior is different between platforms
body:
x's `@sys.get_cli_args()` behaves vastly different betweeen platforms.

- Native: Just C `argv`, the most orthodox `argv`. `[<program>, ...rest]`

- JS: `process.argv` gets passed to moonbit directly, so it's `["node", <script>, ...rest]`

- WASM: `moonrun`'s argv gets passed directly, no filter was made. Need to run `moonrun`'s argparser in MoonBit code _again_ before usable. **This is obviously incorrect**. Also see: https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/pull/491/files#r2055327603, https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/pull/495/files#r2055336148 -- the PRs that changed this behavior.

This renders any existing arg parser basically unusable, and **needs to be fixed**.

# Fix

Use the orthodox C-style `argv` layout: `argv[0]` is the {program, script, WASM module} being executed, and `argv[1:]` is the actual commandline args passed to it. 

**Any** other metadata args, like the runtime being used, the target, or even (I bet nobody wants this) the raw commandline args list passed to the runtime, etc. should be passed out-of-band. They should _never_ occur within `argv`.

title: Improve the user interface of `moon bench`
body:
## Which tests are considered benchmarks?

Currently, those tests with name starting with `bench` will be recognized as *benchmark-like* tests  by `moon` and will be executed to get the benchmark data. Users shall write benchmark inside these benchmark-like tests with `.bench` method of `@test.T` to ensure there's benchmark data produced. 

However, users can call still `.bench` method in a test without the `bench` prefix. In this case, the benchmark data will still be collected and statistics will be generated. The difference is that these data will be shown during `moon test`.

In brief, the `bench` prefix in a test name acts as a filter for `moon` to select which tests to run. Calling the `bench` method determines whether a benchmark for a given function will be executed and its result displayed.

It's not satisfactory and should be improved.

## Where should the `bench` function be located?

The `bench` function is now as a method of `@test.T` for historical reasons:
1. There is once a state for benchmarking, so it's defined as a method.
2. Only `@test.T` is allowed as a test argument, so it requires minimal change to fit the `bench` function as a method of it.


This design may also confuse users.

## Further improvement

1. Using attribute `#[bench]`. This a previous plan where we filter out the benchmark-like tests. This requires to modify `moon` to use the newly added `attrs` field in `test_info.json`.
2. Using test with paramter type `@bench.T`. It requires change to the compiler, and probably a breaking change to the `test_info.json` as we will need to distinguish between `no_args_test`, `with_test_T_args`, and `with_bench_T_args` now.
3. Make `bench` a function like `snapshot` since we don't have a state for benchmark now. It requires to change `moon` and modify `core` library.

Inconsistent Linker Behavior with Native Target Across `moon run` and `moon test` Commands
body:
The current native target implementation requires contradictory linker configurations when alternating between `moon run` and `moon test`, creating a development workflow conflict.

## A Simple Example

1. Create new project:
   ```bash
   moon new hello
   ```

2. Attempt native execution:
   ```bash
   moon run src/main/main.mbt --target native
   ```
   Observed Error:
   ```
    failed: cc /home/cambricon/Projects/tmp/hello/target/native/release/build/main/main.c - 
    I/home/cambricon/.moon/include -O2 /home/cambricon/.moon/lib/libmoonbitrun.o -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing - 
    lm -o /home/cambricon/Projects/tmp/hello/target/native/release/build/main/main.exe
    /usr/bin/ld: /home/cambricon/.moon/lib/libmoonbitrun.o: in function `mi_heap_set_default':
    static.c:(.text+0x3970): undefined reference to `pthread_setspecific'
    /usr/bin/ld: /home/cambricon/.moon/lib/libmoonbitrun.o: in function `mi_process_init':
    static.c:(.text+0x10f66): undefined reference to `pthread_key_create'
   ...
   ```

3. Add linker flag to `src/main/moon.pkg.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "link": {
       "native": {
         "cc-flags": "-lpthread"
       }
     }
   }
   ```
   Execution now succeeds.

4. Run native tests:
   ```bash
   moon test --target native
   ```
  error happened again:
  ```
    failed: cc /home/cambricon/Projects/tmp/hello/target/native/debug/test/lib/lib.internal_test.c - I/home/cambricon/.moon/include -O2 /home/cambricon/.moon/lib/libmoonbitrun.o -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing -lm -o /home/cambricon/Projects/tmp/hello/target/native/debug/test/lib/lib.internal_test.exe
    /usr/bin/ld: /home/cambricon/.moon/lib/libmoonbitrun.o: in function `mi_heap_set_default':
    static.c:(.text+0x3970): undefined reference to `pthread_setspecific'
    /usr/bin/ld: /home/cambricon/.moon/lib/libmoonbitrun.o: in function `mi_process_init':
    static.c:(.text+0x10f66): undefined reference to `pthread_key_create'
    ...
  ```

5. Add identical linker flag to `src/lib/moon.pkg.json`

6. Tests now succeed, but subsequent `moon run` fails with:
   ```
    failed: cc /home/cambricon/Projects/tmp/hello/target/native/release/build/lib/lib.c -I/home/cambricon/.moon/include -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing -lpthread -lm -o /home/cambricon/Projects/tmp/hello/target/native/release/build/lib/lib.exe
    /usr/bin/ld: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/crt1.o: in function `_start':
    (.text+0x24): undefined reference to `main'
    collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
    error: failed when building
    ```

   As libraries shouldn't require a `main` function, this indicates conflicting configurations.

I think it is inconvenient, users should be able to alternate between `moon test --target native` and `moon run --target native` without manual configuration changes. Coule we have better solution?

title: [Feature Request] make "cc-flags" and "cc-link-flags" address relative to package root instead of pwd
body:
# Feature Request

**Note:** While we appreciate all feature requests, please understand that not all requests can be accepted. Providing detailed information will help us better evaluate your suggestion.

## Summary

For native backend, make `"cc-flags"` and `"cc-link-flags"` address relative to package root instead of PWD, or add two arguments `cc-src` and `cc-link-src`, can help to solve compile error when reusing native-targeted packages.

## Motivation

I try to use `moonbitlang/x/fs` in a new project `my-project`. The native backend cannot find the ffi implementation file `native_stub.c`.

## Detailed Description

When using the native backend, C source files or binary library files need to be passed through `cc-flags` and `cc-link-flags`. However, the passed C files are addressed only relative to the PWD. This will lead to errors when referencing other packages that support the native backend.

Changing its behavior to address relative to the package root folder(`moon.pkg.json`), or, more clearly, adding `cc-src` and `cc-link-src` parameters with this behavior to distinguish between *FLAGS* and source files, can help to solve the problem.

## Related Issues

#555 #515 #588 [moonbitlang/x#104](https://github.com/moonbitlang/x/issues/104)

## Checklist

- [x] I have added all necessary details to make it easy for the maintainers to understand my request.

body:
# Feature Request

**Note:** While we appreciate all feature requests, please understand that not all requests can be accepted. Providing detailed information will help us better evaluate your suggestion.

## Summary

Support usage of environment variables in "cc-flags" & "cc-link-flags" field.

## Motivation

For native backend programs, I want my problem to be able to compile on linux & macOS, which sometimes may link to different system libraries, or the same library but located at different place.

However, a proper multi-platform support is somewhat complex and relies on us to maintain a list of supported platform. By using environment variables, we can let users to handle the complexity of the platforms they will be using.

## Detailed Description

I would be able to write:

```json
{
  "link": {
    "native": {
      "cc": "gcc",
      "cc-flags": "${CFLAGS}"
      "cc-link-flags": "${LDFLAGS}"
    }
  }
}
```

And moon will read the two environment variables from its environment, and interpolate them into the flags string before calling `moonc`.

## Related Issues

<!-- List any related issues, pull requests, or discussions. -->

# Feature Request

## Summary

Currently, the `moon add` only accepts `<author>/<package_name>[@<version>]`: https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/main/crates/moon/src/cli/deps.rs#L78

But internally, the dependencies can be local or from git repo.
https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/blob/main/crates/moonutil/src/dependency.rs#L28-L41
```
// Other optional fields...
/// Local path to the dependency. Overrides the version requirement.
pub path: Option<String>,
/// Git repository URL. Overrides the version requirement.
pub git: Option<String>,
/// Git branch to use.
pub git_branch: Option<String>,
```

Is there any plan to expose these two options to end user, to allow local/private dependencies?

Common use cases for local dependencies are:

- private modules that are not for opensource

title: report location of invalid package config
body:
# Feature Request

When you are trying to remove a dependency from a project, if you remove the items in deps (in moon.mod.json) first, you will get this error:

```
error: No matching module was found for xxx/xxxx...
```

This is because the packages belonging to that module were imported in some `moon.pkg.json` files. It is hard to find the invalid `moon.pkg.json` when the project grows large. So, it is better to report the location of the config files, ideally:

```
In xxx/xxx/moon.pkg.json (line n): No matching module was found for xxx/xxxx
```

title: Proposal: Add .mcignore to replace .gitignore for ignoring files in mooncakes packages
body:
Currently, when uploading packages using mooncakes, the tool relies on the .gitignore file to determine which files should be excluded from the package. However, .gitignore is intended for version control purposes, not package management.

I suggest introducing a **.mcignore file**, similar to how .npmignore is used in the Node.js ecosystem. This file would provide better control over which files are included or excluded specifically for package uploads, independent of Git settings.

## Benefits:
- Decouples file exclusion for packaging from version control rules.
- Allows more flexibility in package management, making it easier to fine-tune what is included in the final package.
- Avoids potential conflicts between packaging requirements and Git-related files.

Feature request: Add support for 'wasi' target
body:
# Support WASI target

One of the popular and emerging use cases for wasm apps is deploying/executing them in environments other than browsers, for example in the desktops, in the servers on the edge or on IOT devices. Example of these apps are backend web services, microservices in kubernetes clusters, desktop GUI, CLIs, etc.

At the moment, getting moonbit built app to deploy/run on the above environments requires using a few external tools, such as wit-bindgen, wasm-tools, wac, and possibly wasi-sdk (for c lib interop). The experience is fragmented, involves lots of trial and error and requires significant investment in terms of time and skill in understanding and using these external tools. Emphasising the last point, one basically needs to skill up on the rust language and its ecosystem to effectively use these external tools. 

A moonbit application developer writing applications for the above mentioned deployment targets would be very productive if moonbit were to support **wasi** target in lieu of current 'wasm', 'wasmgc', and 'js'.

title: resolve empty `source` to project root
body:
## Problem

A `"source": ""` config in `moon.mod.json` raises an error of:

```
$ moon run .
error: failed to load `<path-redacted>/moon.mod.json`

Caused by:
    0: `source` bad format
    1: `source` should not be empty
```

Thought it would be treated as setting the source dir to the project root but it didn't work as I expected. The new template now contains a `"source": "src"` by default, which makes me intuitively conclude that removing the `src` string would let the project root be the source dir, which is in fact not.

## Expectation

As per [the JSON schema](https://moonbitlang.github.io/moon/json_schema.html) `source` in `moon.mod.json` is allowed to be the empty string, so `"source": ""`  is a valid config.

Rather than raising an error, I would expect `"source": ""` or ``"source": "."``  to be treated as setting the source dir to the project root, i.e. the dir `moon.mod.json` is located in, providing a more seamless configuration experience.

## Alternative

Currently, by removing the `source` field manually the same goal can be achieved.

body:
# Feature Request

**Note:** While we appreciate all feature requests, please understand that not all requests can be accepted. Providing detailed information will help us better evaluate your suggestion.

## Summary

I want to be able to explicitly say some test blocks should be run in a standalone environment/thread, etc.

## Motivation

I was writing a memory allocator to manage the linear memory when using the GC proposal, and when I was adding some test to the memory allocator, I found out that the test result is not deterministic. It turns out that memory growing is a global operation and I cannot simply reset it to its original state in each test block.

## Detailed Description

In my [memory allocator code](https://github.com/tonyfettes/malloc.mbt), I use `memory.size`, `memory.grow` and various memory instructions (`i32.store` and `i32.load`) to test the functionality of my memory allocator. However, these instructions operates on the same global memory, and would be quite hard to maintain a clean state of the linear memory at the begin of each test case.

For example, there are two test blocks:

```moonbit
test {
  memory.grow 1
}

test {
  inspect!(memory.size)
}
```

If the second test case is executed before the first one, then I will see that the `memory.size` is `1`; otherwise, `memory.size` will be `2`.

I wonder if it is possible for user to specify which test cases should be run its own module instantiation/thread. My proposal was to write "isolate" at the beginning of the string of the test block to say that this test block should be run in a standalone environment.

```moonbit
test "isolate ..." {
  // ...
}
```

## Related Issues

<!-- List any related issues, pull requests, or discussions. -->

## Checklist

- [ ] I have added all necessary details to make it easy for the maintainers to understand my request.

Allow tests outside project code source directory
body:
# Feature Request

## Summary

It's an often case of mine that I need to write some standalone test programs that I don't want them to be in the source directory. Therefore, I want to be able to write/run test program outside the source directory.

## Motivation

I have written a tensor library my self at [tonyfettes/torch.mbt](https://github.com/tonyfettes/torch.mbt), and now I want to try my tensor library to build a model, and train it on the infamous [iris dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/iris).

I don't want any code related to the iris model to be inside the `src` directory since they are totally unrelated to the implementation of the tensor library.

## Detailed Description

I want to be able to develop MoonBit program with such project structure,

```
.
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
├── moon.mod.json
├── src
│   ├── distributions.mbt
│   ├── moon.pkg.json
│   ├── nn.mbt
│   ├── random.mbt
│   ├── tensor.mbt
│   ├── value.mbt
│   └── value_test.mbt
└── test
    └── iris
        ├── iris.mbt
        └── moon.pkg.json

4 directories, 12 files
```

with some extra properties such as:

- Any user of mine won't be able to use the `@test` or `@test/iris` package. They should be internal/private.

### Circumvents

1. Put all source at top-level of the directory and remove `"source": "src"` in the `moon.mod.json`, and move the test directory to `internal/test`.
2. Move the test directory to `src/internal/test`.

### Possible Implementations

1. Provided an extra option to set `"test-directory"`, for example:

   ```jsonc title="moon.mod.json"
   {
     // ...
     "test-directory": "test"
   }
   ```

4. Allow multiple directory to be used as "source directory", for example:

   ```jsonc title="moon.mod.json"
   {
     // ...
     "source": ["src", "test"]
   }
   ```

5. Treat any directory that is not the source directory as internal package.

## Related Issues

<!-- List any related issues, pull requests, or discussions. -->

## Checklist

- [ ] I have added all necessary details to make it easy for the maintainers to understand my request.

title: support build graph visualization
Do we need to ignore differences between LF and CRLF in snapshot testing?
body:
The current implementation directly compares the buffer content with the file content. However, there are cases where hidden conversions can occur, such as during a Git checkout. By default, Git may automatically convert line endings from LF to CRLF on Windows.

Ignoring differences between LF and CRLF in text comparisons might be necessary. But may cause some unexpected comparing results.

Related: https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/pull/930

body:
# Feature Request

**Note:** While we appreciate all feature requests, please understand that not all requests can be accepted. Providing detailed information will help us better evaluate your suggestion.

## Summary

It's often the case that Wasm and Wasm(GC) shares the same implementation, however, it is not possible to share their implementation since it will cause unused variable warning when using JS backend.

## Motivation

[core](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/pull/872)

## Detailed Description

In the PR above, `exp.wasm.mbt` and `exp.wasm-gc.mbt` have exactly same implementation, which makes later SE tasks harder to perform.

I want to have a file `exp.common.mbt` or `exp.default.mbt` that is used for default implementation. This means when there is a `exp.js.mbt`, JS backend will it and ignore `exp.default.mbt`; when other backends are selected, like wasm and wasm-gc, it use `exp.common.mbt` or `exp.default.mbt` instead.

## Related Issues

[core](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/pull/872)

title: Security Concern: `moon publish` should honor `.gitignore` file
body:
I had downloaded a 6.5GB (llama2-chat) file into a local copy of a repo under a `.spin` directory that was protected by `.gitignore` with a line that says `.spin`.
However, when I tried to "moon publish" the project, it obviously was attempting to upload _EVERYTHING_ it found in that directory hierarchy, including this 6.5GB.

This is a major security concern, as it is very common to have a `.env.development.local` file in a repo that contains secrets needed to run and test the project locally, and it is typically protected by having a `.env*` line in the `.gitignore` file.

`moon publish` should read and honor the contents of `.gitignore` (or provide its own equivalent mechanism) so that secrets are not leaked into public archives.
